questions.q: Factor 9x² − 49.

weeks.prep: Have your child draw a factoring flowchart (GCF? → number of terms → difference of squares / perfect square / trinomial / grouping → factor further?). Unit 8 review and test.
misconceptions: Stopping too early: x⁴ − 16 = (x² + 4)(x² − 4) is not finished — x² − 4 factors further.
Not seeing structure: (x + 2)² − 25 is a difference of squares with a = x + 2.
Dropping the GCF from the final answer.

days.guide: Your child builds the flowchart and factors 20 mixed polynomials completely, checking by multiplying.

questions.q: Factor 2x³ − 18x completely.
Factor 3x² + 12x + 12 completely.

days.guide: Treat chunks as single quantities. Your child factors structural expressions.

questions.q: Factor 4x² − 9y².
Factor (x + 2)² − 25.

days.guide: Model: a rectangle's area is x² + 8x + 15, so its sides could be (x + 3) and (x + 5). Border problem: a 10 by 8 garden with a path of width x has total area (10 + 2x)(8 + 2x).

questions.q: A rectangle has area x² + 8x + 15. Find expressions for its sides.
questions.a: x + 3 and x + 5.

days.guide: Your child completes the Unit 8 review; correct together.

questions.q: Multiply (x − 4)(2x + 3).

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test (about 50 minutes).

questions.q: Factor x² − 8x + 16.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, Desmos (type y = a(x − h)² + k and add sliders).
misconceptions: Thinking (x − 3)² shifts left: (x − h)² shifts RIGHT by h.
Using x = b/2a instead of x = −b/(2a).
Forgetting that a < 0 opens downward (a maximum, not a minimum).

days.guide: Graph y = x² from a table, then use sliders for a, h, k. Your child writes the effect of each.

questions.q: Describe y = −2(x − 3)² + 1 compared to y = x².
questions.a: Opens down, narrower (stretch by 2), vertex shifted to (3, 1).

days.guide: Model labeling vertex, axis, intercepts, max/min. Your child labels 10 parabolas.

questions.q: For y = x² − 6x + 8, give the vertex, axis of symmetry, x-intercepts, and y-intercept.
questions.a: Vertex (3, −1); axis x = 3; x-intercepts 2 and 4; y-intercept 8; minimum −1.

days.guide: Find the vertex with x = −b/(2a), then build a symmetric table around it.

questions.q: Find the vertex of y = 2x² − 8x + 3.

days.guide: Read the vertex from a graph, then use another point to find a.

questions.q: A parabola has vertex (−1, 4) and passes through (0, 2). Write its equation.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the key.

questions.q: Does y = −x² + 5 have a max or min? Value?
questions.a: Maximum of 5.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) y = (x − 2)² − 3 → vertex (2, −3), opens up, min −3. 2) y = −x² + 4x → vertex (2, 4), x-intercepts 0 and 4. 3) y = x² + 2x − 3 → vertex (−1, −4), zeros −3 and 1, y-int −3. 4) Axis of symmetry of y = 3x² − 12x + 1 → x = 2. 5) Equation with vertex (1, −2) through (3, 6): y = 2(x − 1)² − 2.

weeks.prep: Desmos. A card listing the three forms: standard y = ax² + bx + c, factored y = a(x − p)(x − q), vertex y = a(x − h)² + k.
misconceptions: Reading zeros of (x − 2)(x + 4) as −2 and 4: set each factor to 0 → x = 2 and x = −4.
When completing the square, forgetting to subtract what you added: x² + 6x + 5 = (x² + 6x + 9) − 9 + 5.
Expanding (x − 3)² as x² + 9.

days.guide: Find zeros from factored form, the axis halfway between, then the vertex.

questions.q: Sketch y = (x − 2)(x + 4): zeros and vertex?
questions.a: Zeros 2 and −4; axis x = −1; vertex (−1, −9).

days.guide: Graph from vertex form, then expand to standard form.

questions.q: Convert y = (x − 3)² − 4 to standard form.

days.guide: Complete the square: take half of b, square it, add and subtract.

questions.q: Write x² + 6x + 5 in vertex form.
Write x² − 10x + 7 in vertex form.

days.guide: Discuss: vertex form gives max height directly; factored form gives landing points (zeros); standard form gives the starting height (y-intercept).

questions.q: Which form best shows when a ball hits the ground?
questions.a: Factored form — the zeros.

days.guide: Give the forms quiz.

questions.q: Zeros of y = 2(x + 1)(x − 5)?
questions.a: x = −1 and x = 5.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) y = (x + 1)(x − 3): zeros −1 and 3; vertex (1, −4). 2) y = 2(x − 1)² + 3 → standard: 2x² − 4x + 5. 3) x² + 8x + 10 → (x + 4)² − 6. 4) x² − 4x − 5 → (x − 5)(x + 1) and (x − 2)² − 9. 5) Best form for max height → vertex; for x-intercepts → factored; for y-intercept → standard.

weeks.prep: A soft ball, stopwatch or phone video (slow-motion helps), open outdoor space. Desmos. Model: h(t) = −16t² + v₀t + h₀ (feet, seconds).
misconceptions: Treating the parabola as the ball's path sideways: h(t) graphs height versus TIME for a straight-up toss.
Using the whole parabola as the domain: time starts at 0 and ends when the ball lands.
Confusing when the max occurs (t-value) with the max height (h-value).

days.guide: Toss the ball straight up and catch it at the same height; time several flights. If thrown and caught at the same height, 0 = −16T² + v₀T, so v₀ = 16T. Your child estimates v₀.

questions.q: A ball is in the air 2.5 s before being caught at release height. Estimate v₀.

days.guide: Find the vertex: t = −b/(2a). Your child does several scenarios.

questions.q: For h = −16t² + 64t + 5, when is the max and what is it?

days.guide: Model fencing: 40 ft perimeter, width x, length 20 − x, A = x(20 − x). Find the vertex.

questions.q: What dimensions maximize area with 40 ft of fencing? Max area?
questions.a: 10 ft by 10 ft; 100 ft².

days.guide: Interpret intercepts and reasonable domain/range in context.

questions.q: For h = −16t² + 64t + 5, what does 5 mean and when does the ball land?
questions.a: 5 ft = launch height. Lands when h = 0: t = (64 + √4416)/32 ≈ 4.08 s.

questions.q: Reasonable domain and range for that model?
questions.a: Domain 0 ≤ t ≤ about 4.08 s; range 0 ≤ h ≤ 69 ft.

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test (about 50 minutes) and collect the lab write-up.

questions.q: What does the vertex of a projectile model represent?
questions.a: The maximum height and the time it occurs.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab rubric: 4 = several timed trials, average flight time, correct v₀ = 16T, max height computed (v₀²/64 above release), sources of error; 3 = minor errors; 2 = incomplete; 1 = missing. Unit 9 test sample answers: 1) y = x² − 4x − 5: vertex (2, −9), zeros −1 and 5. 2) y = −(x + 2)² + 3 → standard −x² − 4x − 1. 3) x² + 4x + 1 = (x + 2)² − 3. 4) h = −16t² + 32t + 6: max at t = 1, height 22 ft. 5) Max area with 60 ft of fence → 15 × 15 = 225 ft².

weeks.prep: Factoring flowchart; Desmos for checking.
misconceptions: Applying the zero-product property before the equation equals zero: x(x − 5) = 6 does NOT mean x = 6 or x − 5 = 6.
Taking only the positive square root: (x − 2)² = 16 gives x − 2 = ±4.
Keeping solutions that make no sense in context (negative lengths).

days.guide: Rewrite in standard form, factor, set each factor to zero.

questions.q: Solve x² − 5x = −6.
Solve 2x² = 8x.

days.guide: Isolate the square, then take ± square roots.

questions.q: Solve 3(x − 2)² = 48.

days.guide: Define the variable, write an equation, solve by factoring, reject impossible answers.

questions.q: A rectangle's length is 3 more than its width and its area is 70. Find its dimensions.

days.guide: Graph each quadratic in Desmos and compare x-intercepts with the factored solutions.

questions.q: Why do the solutions of x² − x − 6 = 0 match the x-intercepts of y = x² − x − 6?
questions.a: The x-intercepts are where y = 0, which is exactly the equation; both give x = 3 and −2.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Solve x² = 81.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) x² + 3x − 10 = 0 → x = −5, 2. 2) x² = 4x + 12 → x = 6, −2. 3) 4x² − 9 = 0 → x = ±3/2. 4) 2(x + 1)² = 50 → x = 4, −6. 5) (x − 3)² = 7 → x = 3 ± √7. 6) A number times 2 more than itself is 48 → 6 (or −8). 7) Rectangle with width w, length 2w, area 72 → 6 × 12.

weeks.prep: Algebra tiles for completing the square. A derivation sheet outline.
misconceptions: Forgetting to divide by a before completing the square.
Writing the quadratic formula with −b only over 2a or ± only on b: the whole numerator −b ± √(b² − 4ac) is over 2a.
Sign errors when b or c is negative: substitute with parentheses.

days.guide: With tiles, arrange x² + 6x into a square missing a corner; add 9 to complete it. Then symbolically.

questions.q: Solve x² + 6x = 7 by completing the square.
Solve x² − 4x − 1 = 0 by completing the square.

days.guide: Walk through deriving x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a): divide by a, move c/a, add (b/2a)², factor, square-root, isolate x. Your child writes each step with a reason.

questions.q: In the derivation, what term is added to both sides of x² + (b/a)x = −c/a?
questions.a: (b/2a)² = b²/(4a²).

days.guide: Model identifying a, b, c then substituting. Give exact and decimal answers.

questions.q: Solve 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0.
Solve x² + 5x + 6 = 0 using the formula.

days.guide: Discriminant: positive → 2 real solutions; zero → 1; negative → none. If it's not a perfect square, solutions are irrational.

questions.q: How many real solutions for x² + 2x + 5 = 0?
Why are solutions of x² − 3x + 1 = 0 irrational?
questions.a: The discriminant is 5, not a perfect square, so √5 stays irrational.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Discriminant of x² − 6x + 9?
questions.a: 0 → one real solution (x = 3).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Complete the square: x² + 8x = 9 → x = 1 or −9. 2) x² − 2x − 4 = 0 → x = 1 ± √5. 3) Formula: 3x² + 2x − 1 = 0 → x = 1/3 or −1. 4) x² − 4x + 1 = 0 → x = 2 ± √3 ≈ 3.73, 0.27. 5) Discriminant of 2x² + 3x + 5 → −31, no real solutions. 6) 4x² − 4x + 1 → 0, one solution x = 1/2.

weeks.prep: Desmos. Mixed equation list (16).
misconceptions: Always using the quadratic formula: it works, but square roots or factoring are faster when the structure fits.
Forgetting that a projectile hits the ground when h = 0 (not at the vertex).
Judging growth from small x: x² beats 2^x for small values, but 2^x wins eventually.

days.guide: For each equation, decide: no b-term → square roots; factors nicely → factoring; else formula or completing the square.

questions.q: Solve x² + x − 12 = 0.
Solve x² + 4x − 1 = 0.
questions.a: Completing the square: (x + 2)² = 5 → x = −2 ± √5.

days.guide: Set h(t) = 0 (or a target height) and solve.

questions.q: When does h = −16t² + 32t + 48 hit the ground?

days.guide: Make a table of 10x, x², 2^x for x = 1..12. Your child describes which leads when.

questions.q: Compare 10x, x², and 2^x at x = 10 and x = 12.

days.guide: Solve and check each solution in context; discard negative time or length.

questions.q: A square garden's area increases by 33 ft² when each side is lengthened by 3 ft. Original side?

days.guide: Give the applications quiz.

questions.q: Why reject t = −1 in a projectile problem?
questions.a: Time before launch isn't part of the situation.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) x² − 16 = 0 → ±4. 2) x² − 7x + 10 = 0 → 2, 5. 3) x² + 2x − 5 = 0 → −1 ± √6. 4) h = −16t² + 64t: lands at t = 4 s; max 64 ft at t = 2. 5) h = −16t² + 48t + 4 reaches 36 ft when 16t² − 48t + 32 = 0 → t = 1 s and 2 s. 6) Rectangle area 60 with length 4 more than width → 6 × 10.

weeks.prep: Desmos. Prepare 10 linear-quadratic systems and the Unit 10 review/test.
misconceptions: Expecting exactly one intersection: a line and parabola can meet 0, 1, or 2 times.
Finding x-values but not the y-values for each solution.
Interpreting only one of two valid solution times (going up and coming down).

days.guide: Graph y = x² and lines like y = 2x + 3, y = −1, y = 2x − 1 to see 2, 0, and 1 intersections.

questions.q: How many intersections do y = x² and y = −1 have?
questions.a: None — the parabola never goes below 0.

days.guide: Substitute the line into the quadratic, set to 0, solve, then find y.

questions.q: Solve y = x² and y = 2x + 3.
Solve y = x² − 4 and y = x − 2.

days.guide: Use h = −16t² + 48t + 4 and a platform/ramp at height h = 20 ft. Solve and interpret both times.

questions.q: When is the ball at 20 ft?
questions.a: 16t² − 48t + 16 = 0 → t² − 3t + 1 = 0 → t = (3 ± √5)/2 ≈ 0.38 s (going up) and 2.62 s (coming down).

days.guide: Your child completes the mixed Unit 10 review; correct and discuss method choices.

questions.q: Solve 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0.

days.guide: Give the Unit 10 test.

questions.q: Solve y = x² + 1, y = 2x.
questions.a: x² − 2x + 1 = 0 → x = 1: (1, 2), one solution.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 10 test sample answers: 1) x² − 9x + 20 = 0 → 4, 5. 2) (x + 1)² = 12 → −1 ± 2√3. 3) 2x² + x − 6 = 0 → 3/2, −2. 4) x² + 6x + 2 = 0 → −3 ± √7. 5) Discriminant of x² + x + 1 → −3, no real solutions. 6) y = x² − 2x, y = x → (0, 0), (3, 3). 7) h = −16t² + 80t: lands at t = 5 s; max 100 ft at t = 2.5. Scoring: 80%+ proficient.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, Desmos. Shipping chart example: $5 for up to 2 lb, $8 for over 2 up to 5 lb, $12 over 5 lb. Function-family cards for the sort (linear, quadratic, exponential, absolute value, square root, piecewise).
misconceptions: Shifting y = |x − 3| left: like parabolas, it shifts RIGHT 3.
Overlapping pieces in piecewise functions: each input belongs to exactly one piece — watch ≤ vs <.
Stating domain of √(x − 2) as all reals: the radicand must be ≥ 0, so x ≥ 2.

days.guide: Graph y = |x|, then use a, h, k as with parabolas. Your child graphs 8 and describes transformations.

questions.q: Describe y = 2|x − 3| + 1.
questions.a: V-shape opening up, vertex (3, 1), twice as steep as y = |x|.

days.guide: Graph each piece only on its interval, using open/closed dots. Evaluate inputs using the right piece.

questions.q: Using the shipping chart, what does a 2-lb package cost? A 4.5-lb package?

days.guide: Graph y = √x from a table (0, 1, 4, 9), then shift.

questions.q: Domain and range of y = √(x − 2) + 3?
questions.a: Domain x ≥ 2; range y ≥ 3.

days.guide: Sort cards by family using table patterns (constant difference, constant ratio, second differences, V shape, half-parabola).

questions.q: A table has first differences 3, 5, 7, 9. What family?
questions.a: Quadratic (constant second differences of 2).

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Vertex of y = −|x + 1| + 4?
questions.a: (−1, 4), opens down.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) y = |x + 2| − 3 → vertex (−2, −3), opens up. 2) y = −3|x| → opens down, steeper. 3) f(x) = {x + 1 if x < 0; 2x if x ≥ 0}: f(−3) = −2, f(0) = 0, f(4) = 8. 4) y = √(x + 4) − 1: domain x ≥ −4, range y ≥ −1. 5) Table 2, 6, 18, 54 → exponential. 6) Table 1, 4, 9, 16 → quadratic.

weeks.prep: Assemble a cumulative review packet from unit tests. Schedule a quiet 2-hour final exam block.
misconceptions: Treating the final as only recent material: review early units (equations, inequalities) too.
Not showing work, which loses partial credit and makes errors hard to find.
Panicking on unfamiliar-looking problems: identify the function family or equation type first.

days.guide: Your child completes the Units 1–5 review; correct errors together.

questions.q: Solve the system x + 2y = 7, 3x − y = 7.
questions.a: From elimination: x = 3, y = 2.

questions.q: Write the line through (0, −3) with slope 4.

days.guide: Your child completes the Units 6–7 review.

questions.q: Median and IQR of 2, 5, 6, 8, 10, 13, 15, 20?
questions.a: Median 9; Q1 5.5, Q3 14, IQR 8.5.

questions.q: $500 grows 6% per year. Value after 3 years?

days.guide: Your child completes the Units 8–11 review.

questions.q: Factor 2x² − x − 6.
Solve x² − 6x + 4 = 0.

days.guide: Give a timed practice final; review errors by topic.

questions.q: Domain of y = √(x + 5)?

days.guide: Give the final exam (about 2 hours). Grade with the key and celebrate completing Algebra I.

questions.q: Which grows fastest eventually: 1000x, 50x², or 1.01^x?

PE.overview: PE 9 is a high-school course centered on personal fitness: students learn FITT, heart-rate training and FITNESSGRAM testing, then apply them across running and track, racket sports, dance, balance and tumbling, yoga and core, aquatics, strength training, jump rope, disc golf and a lifetime activity, finishing with a self-designed fitness plan and portfolio. Every session needs a dynamic warm-up, at least 30 minutes of purposeful activity and a cool-down; the parent sets up safely, gives one or two technique cues at a time, and checks understanding with the questions here. Keep all test data, goal sheets, logs and videos in a fitness portfolio — it is assembled in week 36. Supervise all aquatics closely (a lifeguarded pool is best), spot tumbling and partner balances, and stop for pain, dizziness or chest discomfort.

weeks.prep: Athletic shoes, water bottle, activity-log template. Set up a 5-station circuit (one per health-related component). Write a 10-question components quiz.
misconceptions: Confusing muscular strength and muscular endurance. Correct: strength is maximum force in one effort; endurance is repeating or sustaining a contraction over time.
Thinking body composition is just weight. Correct: it's the proportion of fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone, water).

days.guide: Teach the five components (cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition). Circuit: jumping jacks (cardio), wall sit or heavy carry (strength), push-ups (endurance), sit-and-reach stretch (flexibility), discussion card (body composition).

questions.q: Classify: a 1-mile run, one maximal push of a heavy object, 40 curl-ups.
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance; muscular strength; muscular endurance.

days.guide: Teach a 10-minute dynamic warm-up and do a 15-minute walk/jog.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a dynamic warm-up?
questions.a: To gradually raise heart rate, body temperature and range of motion so muscles and joints are ready, reducing injury risk.

days.guide: Set up the weekly log; complete a 30-minute moderate activity.

questions.q: What does moderate intensity feel like?
questions.a: Breathing harder, can talk but not sing (about 5–6 on a 10-point RPE).

days.guide: Teach static stretching after activity (hold 15–30 s, no bouncing). 20-minute circuit and cool-down stretches.

questions.q: When is static stretching best used?
questions.a: After activity during the cool-down, when muscles are warm.

days.guide: Child leads a family member through the warm-up; give the quiz.

questions.q: Name the five health-related fitness components.
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) cardiorespiratory endurance – heart/lungs supply oxygen over time 2) muscular strength – max force once 3) muscular endurance – repeated contractions 4) flexibility – range of motion at a joint 5) body composition – fat vs lean mass 6) dynamic warm-up before, static stretching after 7) example of cardio: running/swimming 8) example of strength: heavy lift 9) example of endurance: push-ups test 10) hold static stretches 15–30 s. Warm-up demo: proficient = 8+ moves, correct form, clear counts, gradual intensity.

weeks.prep: Stopwatch or phone; optional HR app. Teach the radial or carotid pulse (count 15 s × 4). RPE (0–10) chart.
misconceptions: Measuring pulse with the thumb. Correct: use index and middle fingers; the thumb has its own pulse.
Thinking 220 − age is exact. Correct: it's an estimate; individuals vary by ±10–12 bpm, so also use RPE.

days.guide: Measure resting HR three mornings; compute max and 60–85% zone.

questions.q: For a 15-year-old, what is the estimated max HR and 60–85% target zone?

days.guide: 20 minutes of jog, walk and sprint intervals; check HR and RPE after each.

questions.q: Which interval should produce the highest HR and RPE?
questions.a: The sprint interval.

days.guide: Design a FITT cardio workout and complete it.

questions.q: Write FITT for a cardio workout.
questions.a: Example: F 4 days/week; I 70–80% max HR (~145–165 bpm); T 30 minutes; T jogging.

days.guide: 25-minute interval workout: 1 min hard, 2 min easy, staying in zone.

questions.q: Why does interval training work?
questions.a: Alternating hard and easy efforts allows more total time at high intensity, improving aerobic and anaerobic fitness.

days.guide: Give the quiz; collect the log.

questions.q: Your 15-second pulse count is 38. What's your HR?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) max HR = 220 − age 2) target zone 60–85% 3) 16-year-old max 204, zone ≈ 122–173 4) 15-s count × 4 5) FITT = Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type 6) lower resting HR generally reflects better cardio fitness 7) RPE = rating of perceived exertion 8) interval training alternates hard and easy. FITT plan: all four elements labeled and realistic.

weeks.prep: Cones/tape for a 20 m PACER lane, PACER audio, measuring tape, curl-up measuring strip (FITNESSGRAM uses a 4.5-inch strip for ages 10 and up; 3-inch for ages 5–9), mat, cadence audio. Fitness portfolio folder.
misconceptions: Treating the PACER as a sprint. Correct: start slowly; speed increases each level.
Bouncing off the floor on curl-ups or sagging on push-ups. Correct: controlled form; stop at the second form correction.

days.guide: Full warm-up; PACER (or mile). Record laps or time.

questions.q: How do you score the PACER?
questions.a: Total laps completed; the test ends on the second missed beep.

days.guide: Curl-up form: knees ~140°, feet flat, arms straight, fingertips slide across the strip, head returns to mat; one every 3 s; max 75.

questions.q: What is the cadence for curl-ups?
questions.a: One curl-up every 3 seconds (20 per minute).

days.guide: 90° push-ups: body straight, lower until upper arms parallel to floor (elbows at 90°), one every 3 s.

questions.q: What ends the push-up test?
questions.a: The second form correction (or stopping/failing to keep cadence).

days.guide: 30-minute easy walk and 15 minutes mobility (hip circles, thoracic rotation, ankle mobility).

questions.q: Why include active recovery days?
questions.a: Light movement increases blood flow and aids recovery without adding stress.

days.guide: Compare results to Healthy Fitness Zone (HFZ) charts and record.

questions.q: What is the Healthy Fitness Zone?
questions.a: FITNESSGRAM's criterion-referenced standard showing the level of fitness associated with good health for age and sex.

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline results recorded: proficient = PACER/mile, curl-ups and push-ups all recorded with date, units and HFZ status (Healthy Fitness Zone or Needs Improvement) in the portfolio.

weeks.prep: Yardstick and 12-inch box for sit-and-reach; ruler for trunk lift; SMART goal sheet.
misconceptions: Hyperextending on the trunk lift. Correct: lift slowly to a maximum of 12 inches.
Focusing only on weight. Correct: body composition is one part of health; fitness, habits and how you feel matter too.

days.guide: Trunk lift (max 12 in) and back-saver sit-and-reach (each leg).

questions.q: What does the trunk lift measure?
questions.a: Trunk extensor strength and flexibility (lower back).

days.guide: Explain body composition (percent body fat; methods include skinfolds, bioelectrical impedance, BMI as a screening estimate) and its limits; 30-minute workout.

questions.q: Why is BMI an imperfect measure for athletes?
questions.a: It uses only height and weight, so muscular people can be classified as 'overweight' despite low body fat.

days.guide: Write two SMART goals from baseline.

questions.q: Make 'do more push-ups' SMART.
questions.a: 'Increase my 90° push-ups from 12 to 18 by week 18 by doing 3 sets of push-ups 3 days a week.'

days.guide: 30-minute workout targeting the weakest component.

questions.q: If flexibility is weakest, what would you do?
questions.a: Stretch major muscle groups 3+ days a week, holding 15–30 s, plus yoga.

days.guide: Submit the goal sheet.

questions.q: What does 'Time-bound' mean?
questions.a: The goal has a specific deadline.

weeks.assessment_key: SMART goal sheet: proficient = baseline data for all tests, two goals each meeting all five SMART criteria tied to a specific weak area, and a weekly action plan (FITT) for each.

weeks.prep: Phone for video, stopwatch, a measured 400 m (track or measured route). Running-form checklist (tall posture, slight forward lean, relaxed shoulders, 90° arm swing front-to-back, midfoot strike under hips, quick cadence).
misconceptions: Overstriding (landing on heel far ahead). Correct: shorter, quicker steps landing under the hips.
Arms crossing the body. Correct: swing forward and back, hands relaxed, 'cheek to pocket.'

days.guide: Teach form; do 6 drills (A-skips, B-skips, high knees, butt kicks, carioca, strides) and a 15-minute run.

questions.q: What is an A-skip?
questions.a: A skipping drill driving one knee up to hip height with the opposite arm, then pawing the foot down under the hip.

days.guide: Film running; note two corrections.

questions.q: Why is heel-striking far in front of the body inefficient?
questions.a: It acts as a brake and increases impact forces.

days.guide: 4×400 m (or 2-min repeats) within 3 seconds.

questions.q: If your 400s are 2:00, 1:52, 2:05, 1:58, were they within 3 seconds?
questions.a: No — the range is 1:52 to 2:05 (13 seconds).

days.guide: 25–30 minute easy run or run/walk.

questions.q: How should an easy run feel?
questions.a: Conversational pace (RPE ~3–4).

days.guide: 1-mile time trial with splits; compare to baseline.

questions.q: Your quarter splits were 2:10, 2:15, 2:20, 2:05. Total?

weeks.assessment_key: Mile time trial: recorded with four splits and comparison to baseline. Video analysis: proficient = identifies two specific form issues against the checklist with cues/drills to fix them.

weeks.prep: Cones at 0, 10, 20, 40 m; stopwatch; phone camera.
misconceptions: Standing upright immediately out of the start. Correct: maintain forward lean during the drive phase (first ~10–20 m).
Tense, side-to-side arms. Correct: powerful front-to-back arm action, relaxed hands.

days.guide: Wall drills, high knees, acceleration runs; teach drive phase.

questions.q: What is the drive phase?
questions.a: The first part of a sprint where the body leans forward and pushes back powerfully into the ground to accelerate.

days.guide: Three-point and standing starts over 20 m.

questions.q: Why lean forward at the start?
questions.a: It directs force horizontally (backward into the ground), producing forward acceleration.

days.guide: Time 6×40 m with full recovery (2–3 min).

questions.q: Why take full recovery between sprints?
questions.a: To restore phosphocreatine energy so each sprint is at maximum speed and quality.

days.guide: Film sprints; correct arm action.

questions.q: How should the arms move?
questions.a: Bent ~90°, swinging from the shoulders front to back, hands from hip to cheek height, not crossing the midline.

days.guide: 40 m sprint test; written explanation of force and lean.

questions.q: How does Newton's third law apply to sprinting?
questions.a: The runner pushes back and down on the ground; the ground pushes forward and up with an equal and opposite force, propelling the runner.

weeks.assessment_key: Written explanation proficient: explains pushing backward against the ground creates an equal, opposite ground reaction force (Newton's 3rd law); forward lean directs more of that force horizontally to accelerate; as speed builds the body rises to upright for maximum velocity; arm action balances leg drive. Sprint test recorded.

weeks.prep: Tape measure, soft ball or frisbee, sand or soft grass, cones for distance marks, protractor sketch for angles.
misconceptions: Landing stiff-legged. Correct: land with knees bent, arms forward to avoid falling back.
Thinking 45° is always best. Correct: with release above the ground, the optimal angle is a bit below 45°.

days.guide: Teach arm swing and two-foot takeoff; measure 5 jumps.

questions.q: Where do you measure a jump?
questions.a: From the takeoff line to the back of the closest landing mark (usually the heel).

days.guide: Short approach (5–7 steps), one-foot takeoff, two-foot landing on grass/sand.

questions.q: Why does an approach increase distance?
questions.a: It adds horizontal speed (momentum) at takeoff.

days.guide: Overhand throw: side to target, step with opposite foot, hip-shoulder rotation, follow-through.

questions.q: What body sequence produces a powerful throw?
questions.a: Legs → hips → trunk → shoulder → elbow → wrist (kinetic chain).

days.guide: Test release angles (about 30°, 40°, 50°) and record.

questions.q: Which angle likely produced the longest throw?
questions.a: Around 35–42° for a release above ground level; very high angles lose horizontal speed, very low ones hit the ground early.

days.guide: Mini-meet; record best marks.

questions.q: What is a personal best?
questions.a: The best mark you've achieved in an event.

weeks.assessment_key: Mini-meet results recorded with units; release-angle data table with 3+ angles and distances, and a conclusion identifying the best angle with explanation (balance of height/time in air and horizontal speed; release height lowers the optimum below 45°).

weeks.prep: Stopwatch, route map with a hill; option to swim, bike or hike.
misconceptions: Running every run hard. Correct: most runs should be easy; hard days need recovery.
Walking down hills too fast. Correct: walk-down is recovery.

days.guide: 25-minute fartlek with surges (e.g., sprint to next tree, jog to recover).

questions.q: What is fartlek training?
questions.a: 'Speed play' — continuous running with unstructured surges of faster running.

days.guide: 6 hill repeats with walk-down.

questions.q: What do hill repeats build?
questions.a: Leg strength, power and cardio fitness with less impact than flat sprinting.

days.guide: 40 minutes swim/bike/hike at target HR.

questions.q: Why cross-train?
questions.a: Builds fitness while reducing repetitive stress injuries and boredom.

days.guide: 20-minute recovery run and stretching.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a recovery run?
questions.a: Light activity that promotes blood flow and adaptation without added stress.

days.guide: Retake mile or PACER; compare to week 3.

questions.q: Your PACER went from 42 to 50 laps. What percent improvement?

weeks.assessment_key: Retest comparison: proficient = retest recorded, change calculated (difference and percent), connects change to training types done in weeks 5–8, updates HFZ status.

weeks.prep: Badminton rackets, shuttlecocks, net or string at about 5 ft (official 5 ft 1 in at posts). Targets (hoops/tape) for serves.
misconceptions: Gripping the racket like a frying pan (panhandle). Correct: 'handshake' forehand grip; rotate thumb onto the flat bevel for backhand.
Serving above the waist. Correct: the shuttle must be hit below 1.15 m (about waist height), with an underhand motion.

days.guide: Forehand and backhand grips, ready position; rally 100 hits.

questions.q: Describe the forehand grip.
questions.a: Shake hands with the handle, forming a V between thumb and index finger along the side; hold loosely.

days.guide: Short and long serves into targets.

questions.q: When is a short serve used?
questions.a: In doubles especially, to land just past the short service line and prevent an attack.

days.guide: Overhead forehand clears with follow-through.

questions.q: What is a clear?
questions.a: A high, deep shot to the opponent's back line to push them back and gain time.

days.guide: Drop shots and net play.

questions.q: Why use a drop shot?
questions.a: It lands just over the net, forcing a deep opponent to rush forward.

days.guide: Skills test: serve accuracy and rally count.

questions.q: What's a legal badminton serve?
questions.a: Underhand, below about waist height (1.15 m), diagonal into the opponent's service court, feet stationary.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills test: serve accuracy (e.g., 10 serves to target: 7+ proficient), longest cooperative rally (20+ proficient), correct grips and ready position observed.

weeks.prep: Badminton set; court diagram showing singles (long and narrow) and doubles (short and wide service court; full width in play) boundaries.
misconceptions: Thinking only the server scores. Correct: badminton uses rally scoring — a point every rally.
Both doubles partners chasing the same shuttle. Correct: side-by-side on defense, front-back on attack; call 'mine.'

days.guide: Teach rally scoring: games to 21, win by 2, cap at 30; best of three games. Server serves from right court when score is even, left when odd.

questions.q: Score is 20-20. How does the game end?
questions.a: A player must win by 2 (e.g., 22-20); if it reaches 29-29, the next point (30) wins.

days.guide: Move opponents with clears and drops.

questions.q: Why alternate clears and drops?
questions.a: It forces the opponent to cover the full length of the court, tiring them and creating openings.

days.guide: Teach the smash (steep downward overhead).

questions.q: When should you smash?
questions.a: When the shuttle is high and short (in the front-mid court), giving a steep angle downward.

days.guide: Doubles formations: side-by-side defending, front-back attacking.

questions.q: When does a doubles team go front-back?
questions.a: When attacking (after a smash or drop), with the back player hitting down and the front player covering the net.

days.guide: Round-robin; self-evaluate sportsmanship.

questions.q: Name two sportsmanship behaviors.
questions.a: Calling lines honestly, shaking hands, encouraging partners, accepting calls.

weeks.assessment_key: Game play rubric: Skills (clears, drops, serve), Strategy (moves opponent, uses formations), Rules/scoring (keeps score correctly), Sportsmanship (fair calls, respect). Each 1–4; proficient = 3+ in every row.

weeks.prep: Pickleball paddles, balls, a public court (or tape a 20 × 44 ft court with a 7-ft non-volley zone).
misconceptions: Volleying while standing in the kitchen. Correct: no volleys while touching the non-volley zone (7 ft from the net).
Rushing the net after serving. Correct: the two-bounce rule means the serving team must let the return bounce.

days.guide: Grip, forehand, backhand; underhand serve below the waist, diagonal, landing beyond the kitchen.

questions.q: Describe a legal pickleball serve.
questions.a: Underhand, contact below the waist, paddle moving upward, one foot behind the baseline, diagonal to the opposite service court beyond the kitchen line.

days.guide: Two-bounce rule and non-volley zone.

questions.q: What is the two-bounce rule?
questions.a: The serve must bounce, and the return must bounce, before either team may volley.

days.guide: Dinks and volleys at the kitchen line.

questions.q: What is a dink?
questions.a: A soft shot that arcs over the net and lands in the opponent's kitchen.

days.guide: Third-shot drop; doubles.

questions.q: Why use a third-shot drop?
questions.a: A soft shot into the kitchen lets the serving team move up to the net safely.

days.guide: Skills test and rules quiz.

questions.q: Can the receiving team score a point?
questions.a: No — in traditional scoring, only the serving team scores.

weeks.assessment_key: Rules quiz key: 1) games to 11, win by 2 2) only serving team scores 3) serve underhand, below waist, diagonal 4) two-bounce rule 5) kitchen = 7 ft non-volley zone 6) no volley while in kitchen (including follow-through) 7) doubles score call: server score, receiver score, server number (e.g., '4-2-1') 8) ball on the line is in (except kitchen line on serve). Skills test: 7/10 legal serves, 10-shot dink rally.

weeks.prep: Rackets/paddles, bracket sheet, scorecards. Invite family/friends. Line-calling rules: call your own side; if unsure, the ball is 'in.'
misconceptions: Calling close balls 'out.' Correct: if not sure, it's in.
Teaching too much at once. Correct: one cue at a time with demonstration.

days.guide: Teach officiating and fair line calls.

questions.q: In recreational play, who calls the lines?
questions.a: Each player/team calls the lines on their own side; give the benefit of doubt to the opponent.

days.guide: Badminton tournament games.

questions.q: What's the score call before serving?
questions.a: Server's score first, then receiver's.

days.guide: Pickleball tournament games.

questions.q: What does '0-0-2' mean at the start of a doubles game?
questions.a: Serving team 0, receiving team 0, second server — the first serving team gets only one server to start.

days.guide: Teach a younger sibling or friend a basic stroke.

questions.q: What's a good teaching order?
questions.a: Explain briefly, demonstrate, let them try, give one cue, praise.

days.guide: Write reflection on strategy and sportsmanship.

questions.q: What strategy worked best?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers cite specific shots and situations.

weeks.assessment_key: Tournament reflection: 4 = describes strategies used in both sports with specific examples, evaluates what worked, describes sportsmanship and officiating fairness, and reflects on teaching; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = general; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Music player, open space; songs at several tempos; 'Cupid Shuffle' or 'Electric Slide' tutorial video; dance-fitness video and HR monitor.
misconceptions: Starting on the wrong count. Correct: listen for the downbeat ('1') of the phrase.
Watching feet instead of listening. Correct: learn steps slowly, then add music.

days.guide: Clap and step to songs; count 8-count phrases.

questions.q: What is tempo?
questions.a: The speed of the beat, measured in beats per minute (bpm).

days.guide: Teach grapevine (side, behind, side, touch), step-touch, pivot turn, kick-ball-change.

questions.q: Describe a grapevine right.
questions.a: Step right, cross left behind, step right, touch (or tap) left beside right.

days.guide: Learn the line dance.

questions.q: In the Cupid Shuffle, what are the first moves?
questions.a: Step/shuffle to the right four counts, then to the left four counts, then kick heels, then walk it by and turn.

days.guide: 30-minute dance-fitness video; track HR.

questions.q: Was your HR in the target zone?
questions.a: Answers vary; compare to the 60–85% zone calculated in week 2.

days.guide: Perform the line dance; self-assess timing.

questions.q: Why is dance considered a lifetime activity?
questions.a: It can be done at any age, alone or socially, and builds cardio fitness and coordination.

weeks.assessment_key: Line dance performance: 4 = all steps correct, on the beat, smooth transitions, completes full sequence with wall changes; 3 = minor errors; 2 = frequent off-beat; 1 = cannot complete.

weeks.prep: Music and tutorial videos for zapateado (ballet folklórico), the hora (Israeli circle dance, e.g., 'Hava Nagila'), Tinikling (Philippines; two long poles or tape lines) and square-dance calls.
misconceptions: Thinking Tinikling is Korean. Correct: Tinikling is the national folk dance of the Philippines, imitating the tikling bird stepping between bamboo traps.
Getting feet caught in Tinikling poles. Correct: practice with tape lines first; pole clappers keep a steady 3-count (tap, tap, close).

days.guide: Teach basic zapateado (heel-toe stamps, rhythmic patterns).

questions.q: Where does ballet folklórico come from?
questions.a: Mexico — traditional regional dances, popularized as a stage form in the 1950s by Amalia Hernández.

days.guide: Teach the hora in a circle: step left, cross right behind, step left, hop/kick, etc.

questions.q: What occasion is the hora often danced at?
questions.a: Celebrations such as Jewish weddings and bar/bat mitzvahs.

days.guide: Teach Tinikling basic: two hops between lines/poles, one hop outside, in 3/4 rhythm.

questions.q: What does Tinikling imitate?
questions.a: The tikling bird stepping between grass stems or dodging bamboo traps set by farmers.

days.guide: Teach square-dance calls: honor, do-si-do, swing, promenade, allemande left.

questions.q: What does 'allemande left' mean?
questions.a: Turn to your corner, join left hands (or forearms) and walk around each other back to place.

days.guide: Perform one dance and explain its origin.

questions.q: What should an origin explanation include?
questions.a: Country/culture, when or why it's danced, and what movements represent.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance and explanation: 4 = performs dance accurately on the beat and explains origin (country, cultural meaning, traditional occasion or costume) accurately; 3 = minor errors; 2 = performance only or inaccurate origin; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Music (clean version), phone for filming; choreography worksheet with 8-count boxes.
misconceptions: Making every move at the same level and speed. Correct: vary levels (high/middle/low), pathways (straight/curved/zigzag) and dynamics (sharp/smooth, fast/slow).
Forgetting choreography. Correct: write it down in 8-counts and rehearse in sections.

days.guide: Teach levels, pathways, dynamics with examples.

questions.q: Give an example of each element.
questions.a: Level: a jump (high) or floor roll (low); pathway: zigzag across the room; dynamics: sharp punch vs. slow melt.

days.guide: Create 32 counts.

questions.q: How many 8-counts is 32 counts?
questions.a: Four.

days.guide: Expand to 64 counts with a partner formation change.

questions.q: Name two formation changes.
questions.a: Switching sides, moving from side-by-side to one behind the other, mirroring, canon.

days.guide: Rehearse, film, adjust timing.

questions.q: Why film rehearsals?
questions.a: To see timing and spacing errors you can't feel while dancing.

days.guide: Perform for family.

questions.q: What makes choreography interesting to watch?
questions.a: Variety in levels, pathways and dynamics, and movement that matches the music.

weeks.assessment_key: Choreography rubric (4 levels): Composition (64 counts, uses levels, pathways, dynamics, formation change), Musicality (on the beat, matches phrasing), Execution (confident, clean), Effort/presentation. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Music; Zumba-style video; space for a 'dress rehearsal' with video.
misconceptions: Thinking dance isn't 'real' exercise. Correct: a 30-minute dance workout can reach vigorous intensity.
Teaching too fast. Correct: break moves down, use counts and mirror the learner.

days.guide: 30-minute workout; compare HR to a running session.

questions.q: Did dance reach your target zone?
questions.a: Answers vary; compare average HR to week 2 zone and running data.

days.guide: Polish choreography.

questions.q: What does 'polish' mean?
questions.a: Cleaning details: sharp arms, matching timing, clear facial expression, spacing.

days.guide: Teach part of the dance.

questions.q: How do you teach a dance phrase?
questions.a: Break into small chunks, count aloud, demonstrate facing the same direction or mirrored, repeat and add music.

days.guide: Dress rehearsal on video.

questions.q: What would you fix after watching the video?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers name specific counts or moves.

days.guide: Final performance and reflection.

questions.q: How can dance be lifelong fitness?
questions.a: Social dance classes, dance-fitness, cultural groups — enjoyable cardio and coordination at any age.

weeks.assessment_key: Final dance performance: same rubric as week 15 plus reflection (4 = explains fitness benefits with HR data, social and cultural value, and personal plan to keep dancing).

weeks.prep: Mat or carpet; a tape line on the floor; space for partner balances with spotter.
misconceptions: Thinking balance is just strength. Correct: balance depends on keeping the center of gravity over the base of support.
Partner balances without communication. Correct: agree on signals and come down slowly.

days.guide: Experiment: narrow vs. wide stance, high vs. low center of gravity.

questions.q: Why is a wide, low stance more stable?
questions.a: A wider base of support and lower center of gravity keep the center of gravity over the base more easily.

days.guide: Hold 10 balances 10 s each (V-sit, arabesque, tripod, etc.).

questions.q: Why is the tripod stable?
questions.a: Head and two hands form a triangle — a wide three-point base under the center of gravity.

days.guide: Walk the line forward/backward; turns.

questions.q: What is dynamic balance?
questions.a: Maintaining balance while moving.

days.guide: Safe partner balances (counterbalance and countertension).

questions.q: Difference between counterbalance and countertension?
questions.a: Counterbalance: partners lean toward/push against each other; countertension: partners pull away from each other while holding on.

days.guide: Perform a sequence; explain center of gravity.

questions.q: Define center of gravity.
questions.a: The point where the body's weight is evenly distributed; balance is kept when it stays above the base of support.

weeks.assessment_key: Balance sequence: 4 = 5+ balances (static, dynamic, partner) held 3+ s with smooth transitions, explanation of center of gravity and base of support with examples; 3 = minor wobbles or weak explanation; 2 = few balances; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Thick mat; spotting plan for the cartwheel; push-up and curl-up test materials; week 3 data.
misconceptions: Rolling on the head/neck. Correct: tuck chin to chest and roll across the shoulders and back.
Cartwheel with bent arms and legs. Correct: straight arms, hand-hand-foot-foot in a line.

days.guide: Log rolls, forward rolls (chin tucked, push with hands) and backward shoulder rolls (over one shoulder).

questions.q: What is the key safety cue for a forward roll?
questions.a: Tuck your chin to your chest so you roll on your upper back, not your head/neck.

days.guide: Cartwheel progressions: lunge start, hands down in a line, kick legs over, land facing start; parent spots at the hips.

questions.q: What is the order of contact in a cartwheel?
questions.a: Hand, hand, foot, foot — in a straight line.

days.guide: Retest push-ups and curl-ups; compare.

questions.q: Your curl-ups went from 30 to 41. What's the change?
questions.a: +11 curl-ups, about 37% improvement.

days.guide: Link rolls and balances into a routine.

questions.q: Why plan transitions?
questions.a: Smooth links show control and keep the routine flowing safely.

days.guide: Perform the routine and update goals.

questions.q: If you met your goal early, what next?
questions.a: Set a new, higher target with a date.

weeks.assessment_key: Tumbling routine: 4 = includes at least two rolls, a cartwheel (or progression), two balances, smooth transitions, safe technique; goal sheet updated with retest data. 3 = minor technique errors; 2 = unsafe or incomplete elements; 1 = not attempted.

weeks.prep: Yoga mat; a beginner yoga video; sit-and-reach box. List of 10 foundational poses (mountain, forward fold, downward dog, plank, cobra, child's pose, warrior I, warrior II, triangle, bridge).
misconceptions: Forcing poses into pain. Correct: move to gentle tension and breathe; use modifications.
Holding the breath. Correct: steady nasal breathing, inhaling to lengthen, exhaling to fold or twist.

days.guide: Teach 10 poses with breathing.

questions.q: What is child's pose used for?
questions.a: Rest and gentle stretch of the back, hips and shoulders.

days.guide: Sun Salutation A, repeated.

questions.q: Which pose follows plank/chaturanga in Sun Salutation A?
questions.a: Upward-facing dog (or cobra), then downward dog.

days.guide: 30-minute flexibility routine; measure sit-and-reach.

questions.q: How long should static stretches be held to improve flexibility?
questions.a: About 15–30 seconds (up to 60), repeated 2–4 times.

days.guide: Tree, warrior III, half-moon.

questions.q: What helps balance in half-moon?
questions.a: Fixing the gaze on a point, engaging the core, a strong standing leg and using a block if needed.

days.guide: Child leads a 15-minute flow.

questions.q: What should a leader cue?
questions.a: Breath, alignment, transitions and modifications.

weeks.assessment_key: Yoga flow leadership: 4 = 15 minutes, logical sequence (warm-up, standing, balance, floor, relaxation), clear breath and alignment cues, offers modifications; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = disorganized; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Mat; core anatomy diagram (rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, internal/external obliques, erector spinae, multifidus, glutes, pelvic floor, diaphragm). Stopwatch for plank test.
misconceptions: Thinking crunches are the best core exercise. Correct: the core's main job is stabilizing the spine; planks, bird-dogs and anti-rotation work train that.
Sagging hips in plank. Correct: squeeze glutes and brace so the body is a straight line.

days.guide: Teach core muscles; 15-minute circuit.

questions.q: Name three core muscles and a job of each.
questions.a: Rectus abdominis – flexes the trunk; obliques – rotate and side-bend; transverse abdominis – braces/stabilizes; erector spinae – extends the spine.

days.guide: Plank, side plank, bird-dog progressions.

questions.q: What does a side plank target?
questions.a: Obliques and the lateral hip muscles (gluteus medius) along with shoulder stability.

days.guide: Combine balance and core in a stability circuit.

questions.q: Why combine balance and core?
questions.a: A strong core keeps the center of gravity controlled over the base of support.

days.guide: 30-minute Pilates-style workout.

questions.q: What is a Pilates principle?
questions.a: Control, centering (core), concentration, precision, breath, flow.

days.guide: Plank hold test and curl-up retest.

questions.q: When should a plank test stop?
questions.a: When form breaks (hips sag or pike) or the person can no longer hold the straight line.

weeks.assessment_key: Core assessment: plank time and curl-ups recorded and compared to baseline; proficient = plank 60+ s with good form and curl-ups at or above Healthy Fitness Zone, or measurable improvement from baseline.

weeks.prep: Life jacket (Coast Guard–approved), rope or garden hose, empty gallon jug with a little water, a pole/broom. American Red Cross water-safety video. NOAA rip-current diagrams.
misconceptions: Thinking drowning looks like splashing and yelling. Correct: it's often silent — head low, mouth at water level, unable to call or wave.
Jumping in to rescue. Correct: reach or throw, don't go — untrained rescuers often drown.

days.guide: Watch the video; list silent signs; 30-minute cardio.

questions.q: List three silent signs of drowning.
questions.a: Head low with mouth at water level, head tilted back, eyes glassy or closed, vertical body with no kick, trying to roll onto the back, climbing-ladder motion.

days.guide: Learn to spot (gap in waves, darker narrow channel, foam moving seaward) and escape a rip current; draw an escape plan.

questions.q: How do you escape a rip current?
questions.a: Don't fight it; swim parallel to shore until free, then angle back to shore; or float and wave for help.

days.guide: Reach with a pole and throw a rope or jug to a target 15 ft away, 10 times each.

questions.q: Why lie down or brace when reaching?
questions.a: To keep a low center of gravity so you aren't pulled into the water.

days.guide: Fit a life jacket: USCG label, correct size by weight/chest, buckled, snug — lift at shoulders and it shouldn't rise past the chin/ears. 20-minute core circuit.

questions.q: How do you check a life jacket fits?
questions.a: Fasten it, then have someone pull up at the shoulders; it shouldn't ride up over the chin or ears.

days.guide: Quiz and throwing-assist demo.

questions.q: What does 'Reach, Throw, Don't Go' mean?
questions.a: Help from land: reach with an object or throw a floating object; don't swim to a struggling person.

weeks.assessment_key: Water safety quiz key: 1) drowning is often silent 2) signs: head low, vertical, no waving 3) rip current: swim parallel 4) reach, throw, don't go 5) life jacket USCG-approved, snug, sized by weight 6) swim with a buddy and near lifeguards 7) enter unknown water feet-first. Throwing assist: proficient = braced low stance, calls to victim, throws past and pulls the line to the victim, 7/10 within reach.

weeks.prep: Lifeguarded community pool (or land-based alternative: bench for arm motion and breathing), goggles, kickboard. Stay within arm's reach of a weak swimmer.
misconceptions: Lifting the head forward to breathe in freestyle. Correct: rotate the head to the side with one goggle in the water.
Kicking from the knees. Correct: kick from the hips with nearly straight legs and loose ankles.

days.guide: Back and front floats (30 s), push-off glides.

questions.q: What helps you float on your back?
questions.a: Relax, head back with ears in water, chest up, arms out, slow breathing — a full breath increases buoyancy.

days.guide: Eggbeater and scissor kicks; tread 3×1 minute.

questions.q: Why learn to tread water?
questions.a: To stay at the surface with your head up to breathe and call for help.

days.guide: Flutter kick 8 lengths with kickboard.

questions.q: Where should a flutter kick come from?
questions.a: The hips, with long legs, slight knee bend and pointed toes.

days.guide: Freestyle with bilateral breathing every three strokes, 8×25 yd.

questions.q: Why breathe every three strokes?
questions.a: It alternates sides, balancing the stroke and building symmetry.

days.guide: Skills check: float 1 min, tread 2 min, 50 yd freestyle.

questions.q: What's the correct freestyle arm entry?
questions.a: Hand enters in front of the shoulder, fingertips first, then extends forward before the pull.

weeks.assessment_key: Swim skills check: float 1 minute (pass/fail), tread 2 minutes (pass/fail), 50 yd freestyle continuous with side breathing (pass/fail); land-based alternative: demonstrates arm stroke, side breathing and kick on a bench with correct technique. All three = proficient.

weeks.prep: Pool access, phone for video (with permission at public pools), technique checklists for backstroke and breaststroke.
misconceptions: Sitting low in the water on backstroke. Correct: hips up, ears in the water, eyes up.
Breaststroke flutter kick. Correct: whip kick — heels to buttocks, feet turn out, kick around and together.

days.guide: Streamline push-offs; measure glide.

questions.q: Describe a streamline position.
questions.a: Arms overhead, one hand on top of the other, biceps squeezing the ears, body tight and straight.

days.guide: Backstroke arm rotation (pinky enters first) and flutter kick; 6×25.

questions.q: Which part of the hand enters first in backstroke?
questions.a: The pinky finger.

days.guide: Whip kick at the wall, then with a kickboard.

questions.q: Describe the breaststroke kick.
questions.a: Bend knees bringing heels toward the buttocks, turn feet out, then kick out and around, snapping legs together.

days.guide: Combine pull, breathe, kick, glide; film one length.

questions.q: What is the breaststroke timing?
questions.a: Pull and breathe, kick, then glide — 'pull, breathe, kick, glide.'

days.guide: Compare video to checklist; demonstrate both strokes.

questions.q: Which strokes are swum on the front?
questions.a: Freestyle, breaststroke and butterfly; backstroke is on the back.

weeks.assessment_key: Stroke demonstration and video analysis: proficient = swims 25 yd of each stroke with checklist points (backstroke: hips up, straight-arm recovery, pinky entry; breaststroke: whip kick, glide, breath with pull) and identifies two corrections from the video.

weeks.prep: Pool access; pace clock; chest-deep area for water aerobics; HELP position diagram.
misconceptions: Thinking you can't get a hard workout in water. Correct: water resistance and swimming can reach high heart rates.
Diving into unknown water. Correct: always enter feet-first unless the depth is known to be safe (at least 9 ft for diving).

days.guide: 8×50 yd on 1:30; record HR.

questions.q: What does '8 × 50 on 1:30' mean?
questions.a: Swim 50 yards eight times, starting each one every 1 minute 30 seconds; rest is whatever time is left.

days.guide: 25-minute water-aerobics routine.

questions.q: Why is water exercise easier on joints?
questions.a: Buoyancy reduces body weight on joints, while water resistance still works muscles.

days.guide: Survival floating, HELP position (with life jacket: knees to chest, arms crossed), feet-first entry.

questions.q: What is the HELP position and why use it?
questions.a: Heat Escape Lessening Posture: in a life jacket, draw knees to chest and hug them to reduce heat loss in cold water.

days.guide: Continuous 15–20 minute swim.

questions.q: How do you pace a long swim?
questions.a: Start easy, breathe rhythmically, switch strokes to rest if needed.

days.guide: Final assessment: 100 yd mixed, 3-minute tread, safety questions.

questions.q: If you fall into cold water, what should you do first?
questions.a: Stay calm and control breathing for the first minute (cold shock), keep your head above water, then float or get out.

weeks.assessment_key: Final aquatics assessment: 100 yards mixed strokes continuously (pass), tread 3 minutes (pass), safety questions: silent drowning signs, rip current escape, reach-throw-don't go, life jacket fit, feet-first entry, HELP position — 5/6 correct. Proficient = pass both swims and 5/6.

weeks.prep: Resistance bands, dumbbells or water jugs, mat, mirror; muscle chart; technique checklist for squat, lunge, hip hinge (Romanian deadlift), push-up, band row.
misconceptions: Rounding the back in a hip hinge. Correct: push hips back with a neutral spine and slight knee bend.
Lifting too heavy too soon. Correct: master form with body weight first; progress gradually.

days.guide: Label muscle groups with bodyweight exercises; 20-minute circuit.

questions.q: Pair: hamstrings, triceps, pectorals.
questions.a: Hamstrings – glute bridge or hip hinge; triceps – bench dips or close-grip push-ups; pectorals – push-ups.

days.guide: Squat, lunge, hip hinge with mirror; 3×10.

questions.q: What is the difference between a squat and a hinge?
questions.a: A squat bends knees and hips more equally (more quad); a hinge pushes the hips back with little knee bend (more hamstrings/glutes).

days.guide: Push-ups (with incline or knee modifications) and band rows; 3×10–12.

questions.q: Give a push-up modification.
questions.a: Hands on a bench or wall (incline) or from knees.

days.guide: Compare heavy low-rep vs. light high-rep sets.

questions.q: Which rep range builds muscular endurance?
questions.a: Higher reps (about 12–20+) with lighter load.

days.guide: Technique check and quiz.

questions.q: Define a rep and a set.
questions.a: A rep is one complete movement; a set is a group of reps done in a row.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) rep vs set 2) strength: ~1–6 reps heavy (for teens, focus 6–12 with excellent form) 3) endurance: 12–20+ reps light 4) rest 48 h before training the same muscle hard 5) breathe out on effort 6) warm up first 7) spotter for heavy free weights 8) progressive overload. Technique check: 5 lifts scored 0–2 each; 8+/10 proficient.

weeks.prep: Bands, dumbbells or jugs; workout log (exercise, sets, reps, load, RPE).
misconceptions: Doing the same workout forever with no change. Correct: progressive overload — small increases in reps, sets or resistance.
Skipping rest days. Correct: muscles adapt during recovery; wait ~48 hours before working the same muscles hard.

days.guide: Design a 30-minute routine with 6 exercises (squat, push-up, row, lunge, overhead press, plank), sets/reps.

questions.q: Why include both push and pull exercises?
questions.a: To balance opposing muscle groups and support good posture and joint health.

days.guide: Complete Workout A; log.

questions.q: What should your log include?
questions.a: Exercise, sets, reps, load, RPE and notes on form.

days.guide: 25-minute mobility; why rest days matter.

questions.q: Why are rest days important?
questions.a: Muscles repair and get stronger during recovery; rest reduces injury and overtraining risk.

days.guide: Repeat Workout A adding reps or resistance.

questions.q: Give an example of overload.
questions.a: Going from 3×10 to 3×12 with the same band, or to a heavier band at 3×10.

days.guide: Film one set of each exercise and self-correct.

questions.q: Name one thing to check on video for a squat.
questions.a: Knees tracking over toes, neutral back, depth, heels down.

weeks.assessment_key: Strength plan and log: 4 = 6 exercises covering push/pull/legs/core with sets/reps/rest, two logged workouts showing overload, form self-corrections noted; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = incomplete logging; 1 = no plan.

weeks.prep: PACER audio, measuring tape, mat, fall baseline data. Explain the California PFT (FITNESSGRAM) is given in grades 5, 7 and 9.
misconceptions: Not pacing the PACER. Correct: run just fast enough to beat each beep; turn efficiently.
Practicing only on test day. Correct: train components weekly.

days.guide: PACER practice with pacing strategy.

questions.q: What is a good PACER pacing strategy?
questions.a: Arrive at the line just as the beep sounds, pivot quickly, and conserve energy in early levels.

days.guide: Push-up cadence practice; improvement circuit.

questions.q: Give a push-up improvement exercise.
questions.a: Incline push-ups, negative (slow lowering) push-ups, plank holds.

days.guide: Curl-ups, trunk lift, sit-and-reach with flexibility work.

questions.q: Which stretches help sit-and-reach?
questions.a: Hamstring and lower back stretches (seated forward fold, PNF hamstring stretch).

days.guide: 35-minute workout targeting the lowest component.

questions.q: If cardio is lowest, what workout?
questions.a: Intervals or a 30+ minute run/bike in the target zone.

days.guide: Full PFT practice; compare to fall.

questions.q: Why compare to your own baseline?
questions.a: Progress against yourself shows improvement regardless of others.

weeks.assessment_key: PFT practice results: proficient = all tests completed with correct protocol, recorded in portfolio and compared to fall baseline with HFZ status noted.

weeks.prep: All FITNESSGRAM testing materials; graph paper or spreadsheet.
misconceptions: Testing tired. Correct: rest the day before and warm up well.
Ignoring components that declined. Correct: analyze why and plan improvement.

days.guide: PACER or mile.

questions.q: What does the PACER estimate?
questions.a: Aerobic capacity (VO2max).

days.guide: Curl-up and push-up tests.

questions.q: What do curl-ups measure?
questions.a: Abdominal muscular strength and endurance.

days.guide: Trunk lift and sit-and-reach.

questions.q: What does sit-and-reach measure?
questions.a: Hamstring and lower back flexibility.

days.guide: Graph fall vs. spring.

questions.q: What type of graph compares two test dates for several components?
questions.a: A double bar graph (or clustered bar chart).

days.guide: Write a 1-page analysis.

questions.q: Your mile went from 9:30 to 8:45. How much faster?
questions.a: 45 seconds faster.

weeks.assessment_key: Progress analysis: 4 = all components graphed fall vs. spring, changes calculated, HFZ status for each, explains reasons using training evidence, evaluates SMART goals; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = data without analysis; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Jump rope per student; music for routine. Rope sizing: stand on the middle; handles should reach the armpits (beginners) or chest.
misconceptions: Jumping too high. Correct: small jumps (1–2 inches) on the balls of the feet.
Turning with the arms/shoulders. Correct: turn with the wrists, elbows close to the body.

days.guide: Size rope; basic bounce and alternate step 10×1 min.

questions.q: How do you size a jump rope?
questions.a: Stand on the middle with one foot; handles should reach about armpit height.

days.guide: Criss-cross, side swing, boxer step.

questions.q: Describe a criss-cross.
questions.a: Cross arms at the waist on the downswing so you jump through the crossed loop, then uncross.

days.guide: 20-minute interval workout; track HR.

questions.q: Is jumping rope moderate or vigorous?
questions.a: Vigorous for most people at a steady pace.

days.guide: Create a 1-minute routine with 5 tricks.

questions.q: How do you link tricks smoothly?
questions.a: Use a basic bounce between tricks and plan them on the beat.

days.guide: Perform the routine and 1-minute speed test.

questions.q: How is a speed test counted?
questions.a: Count each time the right foot touches (or every rotation) in 1 minute.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine: 4 = 5 tricks, on the beat, smooth transitions, ~1 minute, few misses; speed jump recorded. 3 = 4 tricks or several misses; 2 = 2–3 tricks; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Discs, a local disc golf course or targets (hoop/trash can). Note: hyzer = outer edge tilted down; anhyzer = outer edge tilted up.
misconceptions: Throwing with only the arm. Correct: reach back, pull across the chest with the body, snap the wrist.
Confusing hyzer and anhyzer. Correct: for a right-hand backhand throw, hyzer curves left and anhyzer curves right.

days.guide: Backhand grip, reach-back, follow-through; 30 throws at a target.

questions.q: Describe a power grip for backhand.
questions.a: Four fingers curled under the rim, thumb on top of the flight plate.

days.guide: Forehand (sidearm) throw; 30 throws.

questions.q: Describe the forehand grip.
questions.a: Index and middle fingers under the rim against the inside edge, thumb on top, like a sidearm throw.

days.guide: Putting from 10, 15, 20 ft.

questions.q: Why is putting important?
questions.a: Most strokes are saved or lost on short throws to the basket.

days.guide: Experiment with hyzer and anhyzer.

questions.q: For a right-handed backhand, which way does a hyzer release curve?
questions.a: To the left.

days.guide: Skills test: accuracy throws and putting percentage.

questions.q: You made 14 of 20 putts. Percentage?

weeks.assessment_key: Skills test: accuracy throws (e.g., 10 throws to land within 10 ft of a target at 50 ft: 5+ proficient), putting percentage from 15 ft (60%+ proficient), plus correct description of hyzer/anhyzer flight.

weeks.prep: Discs, scorecards, local course map (or 9-hole backyard course).
misconceptions: Throwing out of turn. Correct: on the fairway the player farthest from the basket throws first; on the tee, lowest score on the previous hole goes first.
Trying for distance on every throw. Correct: choose the safest shot that sets up an easy putt.

days.guide: Rules and etiquette; play 9.

questions.q: Who throws first from the tee after the first hole?
questions.a: The player with the lowest score on the previous hole.

days.guide: Plan shots; play 9 noting choices.

questions.q: What is course management?
questions.a: Choosing shots based on hazards, distance and your skills to minimize strokes.

days.guide: Practice costliest shots.

questions.q: Why practice weaknesses?
questions.a: They cost the most strokes, so improvement there lowers scores fastest.

days.guide: Play 18 (or two 9s).

questions.q: Par for the course is 27 for 9 holes; you shot 31. What's your score?

days.guide: Compare scorecards; reflect on strategy.

questions.q: Name one etiquette rule.
questions.a: Don't throw until the group ahead is out of range; stay quiet and still while others throw; pick up trash.

weeks.assessment_key: Scorecards complete and totaled relative to par. Strategy reflection: 4 = compares rounds with numbers, identifies costly shot types, describes specific strategy changes and their results; 3 = general comparison; 2 = scores only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Equipment for the chosen activity (racket, bike and helmet, hiking pack, climbing gym pass). Find a free community lesson or tutorial.
misconceptions: Choosing an activity that's not realistic long-term. Correct: consider cost, location, season and enjoyment.
Skipping safety gear. Correct: research required gear (helmet, harness, sun protection).

days.guide: Choose an activity; research rules and safety.

questions.q: Name two safety rules for your activity.
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., cycling: helmet, ride with traffic; hiking: water, map, tell someone your route.

days.guide: Take a lesson or follow a tutorial; practice 40 minutes.

questions.q: What did you learn first?
questions.a: Answers vary; usually basic technique and safety.

days.guide: Practice 40 minutes; film one skill.

questions.q: What does the video show about your technique?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers compare to a model.

days.guide: Compare fitness benefits with HR and FITT.

questions.q: Which components does your activity build?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., cycling – cardio endurance and leg muscular endurance.

days.guide: Present a 3-minute talk.

questions.q: What should a 'how to start' talk include?
questions.a: Cost, equipment, where to do it locally, safety, beginner steps, fitness benefits.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = explains rules, safety, equipment, cost, local access, fitness benefits with HR/FITT data and how to start, 3 minutes, clear delivery; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing safety or fitness data; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Fitness portfolio, calendar, 4-week planning template with FITT for cardio, strength and flexibility.
misconceptions: Making a plan that's too ambitious. Correct: start realistic and progress.
Ignoring barriers. Correct: plan specific strategies for time, weather and cost.

days.guide: Review data; identify two priorities.

questions.q: How do you choose priorities?
questions.a: Pick components outside the Healthy Fitness Zone or furthest from goals, plus what matters to you.

days.guide: Write a 4-week plan with FITT.

questions.q: FITT for flexibility?
questions.a: Example: F 3–5 days/week; I mild tension; T hold 15–30 s, 2–4 reps per stretch, 15 min; T static stretching/yoga.

days.guide: Identify barriers and strategies.

questions.q: Give a strategy for 'no time.'
questions.a: Short 10-minute workouts, schedule exercise like an appointment, active transport.

days.guide: Start plan; log day 1.

questions.q: Why log right away?
questions.a: Accurate records and accountability.

days.guide: Submit for feedback.

questions.q: What feedback would improve the plan?
questions.a: Answers vary; check balance, rest days and progression.

weeks.assessment_key: Personal fitness plan: 4 = 4 weeks, FITT for cardio/strength/flexibility, progression week to week, rest days, warm-up/cool-down, barriers and strategies, tied to two data-based priorities; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing components; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Activity log, HR app or watch.
misconceptions: Training at the wrong intensity. Correct: check HR or RPE against the plan.
Not adjusting the plan. Correct: modify based on how sessions feel and log data.

days.guide: Cardio session; log HR.

questions.q: Was your average HR in the planned zone?
questions.a: Answers vary; compare with planned FITT intensity.

days.guide: Strength session.

questions.q: Did you use progressive overload?
questions.a: Answers vary; look for an increase in reps, sets or resistance from last time.

days.guide: Flexibility/yoga session.

questions.q: How long did you hold each stretch?
questions.a: Should be about 15–30 seconds.

days.guide: Lifetime activity session.

questions.q: Why include a choice day?
questions.a: Enjoyment builds adherence.

days.guide: Review the log and adjust.

questions.q: What adjustment might you make if every session felt RPE 9?
questions.a: Lower intensity or volume and add recovery.

weeks.assessment_key: Activity log: proficient = 4+ sessions logged with type, duration, HR/RPE and notes, and at least one written adjustment based on the data.

weeks.prep: Activity log, stopwatch, PACER audio; earlier results from weeks 3, 8 and 28; article on intrinsic vs. extrinsic motivation.
misconceptions: Only using extrinsic motivators. Correct: build intrinsic motivation through enjoyment, mastery and choice.
Leading a workout without a warm-up. Correct: always warm up and cool down.

days.guide: Retest mile or PACER; compare to weeks 3, 8 and 28.

questions.q: What trend do your four results show?
questions.a: Answers vary; describe direction and size of change.

days.guide: Strength session with one added set or heavier resistance; log.

questions.q: What principle does adding a set demonstrate?
questions.a: Progressive overload.

days.guide: Read about motivation; write strategies; 30-minute workout.

questions.q: Give one intrinsic and one extrinsic motivator.
questions.a: Intrinsic: enjoying how running feels. Extrinsic: earning a reward or praise.

days.guide: Plan and lead a 30-minute family workout.

questions.q: What three parts must your workout have?
questions.a: Warm-up, main workout, cool-down.

days.guide: Write one-page evaluation with adherence and two adjustments.

questions.q: You completed 14 of 16 planned sessions. Adherence?

weeks.assessment_key: Plan evaluation: 4 = adherence % calculated, retest results compared across four dates with trend, evidence-based assessment of what worked, two specific adjustments; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = little data; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Fitness portfolio, calendar, all data, graphs, goal sheets, logs and skill videos. Summer plan template.
misconceptions: Planning outdoor workouts at midday in summer heat. Correct: exercise early or late, hydrate and have indoor backups.
Reflecting only on fitness scores. Correct: include skills, sportsmanship and habits.

days.guide: 45 minutes of favorite activity; record HR and RPE.

questions.q: Why might enjoyment matter most for lifelong fitness?
questions.a: People continue activities they enjoy, which leads to long-term health.

days.guide: Assemble portfolio.

questions.q: What belongs in the portfolio?
questions.a: Baseline and spring PFT data, graphs, goal sheets, logs and skill videos.

days.guide: Write a 1-page reflection.

questions.q: What is one area of growth besides fitness?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., sportsmanship, leadership, a new skill.

days.guide: Write an 8-week summer plan with 4+ active days/week and hot-day backups.

questions.q: Give a hot-day backup.
questions.a: Swim, indoor workout, exercise early morning or evening, mall walking.

days.guide: Family game day; self-assess sportsmanship.

questions.q: Name a sign of good sportsmanship.
questions.a: Shaking hands, fair calls, encouraging others, winning and losing gracefully.

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio and reflection: 4 = complete portfolio (all data, graphs, goals, logs, videos), reflection with specific evidence of growth in fitness, skill and sportsmanship, and an 8-week summer plan with 4+ active days/week and backups; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing sections; 1 = incomplete.

SCI.overview: Biology – The Living Earth combines reading, discussion, and a hands-on investigation almost every week. Preview each lab with the materials list, enforce safety (goggles, adult handling of heat, iodine, and alcohol, handwashing after dissections), and have your child record everything in a claim–evidence–reasoning notebook. Emphasize explaining 'why' with data, and use the Friday quizzes to decide what to reteach.

weeks.prep: Notebook, meter stick, 4 m of string, 4 stakes or rocks, hand lens. Pick two survey spots (one sunny, one shady). Home lab safety: goggles for chemicals, never taste lab materials, wash hands, adult supervision for heat or chemicals.
misconceptions: Thinking abiotic means 'dead things': abiotic factors are nonliving parts of the environment (light, temperature, water, soil); a dead leaf came from a living thing (biotic origin).
Confusing population and community: a population is one species; a community is all populations in an area.
CER claims without data: evidence must cite actual measurements or counts.

days.guide: Set up the notebook in claim–evidence–reasoning format and go over safety rules together; your child writes and signs a safety contract.

questions.q: Why should you never taste or smell lab materials directly?
questions.a: They may be toxic or irritating; waft odors toward you instead and never taste anything in a lab.

days.guide: Read about levels of organization; your child builds a concept map with local examples.

questions.q: Put in order from smallest to largest: community, organism, biosphere, population, ecosystem.
questions.a: Organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.

questions.q: What is the difference between a community and an ecosystem?
questions.a: A community is all the living populations in an area; an ecosystem includes the community plus the abiotic factors.

days.guide: Mark a 1 m² quadrat; your child records every organism and abiotic factor (light, moisture, temperature, soil).

questions.q: Name two biotic and two abiotic factors you might find in a yard quadrat.
questions.a: Biotic: grass, ants, clover, earthworms. Abiotic: sunlight, soil moisture, temperature, rocks.

days.guide: Repeat in a second spot; graph species counts side by side.

questions.q: Predict: will a sunny or shady quadrat have more grass? Why?
questions.a: Usually the sunny one, because grass needs high light for photosynthesis; shade favors moss or shade-tolerant plants.

days.guide: Your child writes a CER on one abiotic factor that differed; give the vocabulary quiz.

questions.q: Define 'abiotic factor'.
questions.a: A nonliving physical or chemical part of an ecosystem, such as light, temperature, water, or soil.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = claim answers the question; evidence uses specific data (numbers, units, observations); reasoning connects the evidence to a scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence with partial reasoning; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect. Vocabulary quiz: biotic = living factors; abiotic = nonliving factors; population = one species in an area; community = all populations in an area; ecosystem = community + abiotic environment; biosphere = all ecosystems on Earth; quadrat = square sampling area; species = organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

weeks.prep: Three clean plastic bottles, three balloons, active dry yeast, sugar, warm (not hot, about 40°C/105°F) water, string and ruler for circumference, timer. Dried beans and graph paper. Find the St. Matthew Island reindeer data (29 reindeer introduced in 1944; about 6,000 by 1963; 42 by 1966).
misconceptions: Thinking populations grow forever: resources limit growth; logistic growth levels off at carrying capacity (K).

Confusing density-dependent and density-independent factors: density-dependent effects get stronger as the population gets crowded (food, disease); density-independent factors affect populations regardless of size (fire, freeze).
Believing carrying capacity is fixed: overuse can damage the habitat and lower K.

days.guide: Graph sample data for exponential (J-curve) and logistic (S-curve) growth; mark K.

questions.q: Describe the shape of a logistic growth curve and where carrying capacity is.
questions.a: S-shaped: slow start, rapid growth, then leveling off; K is the level where the curve flattens.

days.guide: Mix 1 tsp yeast + 1 cup warm water in each bottle with 0, 1, or 2 tsp sugar; attach balloons; measure circumference every 10 minutes.

questions.q: Predict which balloon inflates most and why.
questions.a: The 2-tsp bottle — yeast use sugar for respiration/fermentation and release CO2; more food supports more activity. The 0-sugar bottle barely inflates.

questions.q: What is the independent variable?
questions.a: Amount of sugar; the dependent variable is balloon circumference.

days.guide: Analyze the yeast data; classify limiting factors.
