questions.q: Classify: disease, wildfire, food supply, drought.
questions.a: Density-dependent: disease, food supply. Density-independent: wildfire, drought (weather).

days.guide: Analyze the reindeer data; explain the crash.

questions.q: Why did the St. Matthew Island reindeer crash?
questions.a: With no predators, the population overshot carrying capacity, overgrazed the slow-growing lichen, and then starved during a harsh winter (1963–64), dropping from about 6,000 to 42.

days.guide: Quiz with a graph interpretation.

questions.q: On a logistic curve, when is the population growing fastest?
questions.a: In the middle (about half of K), where the curve is steepest.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = testable question, hypothesis, identified variables (independent, dependent, controlled), clear data table and labeled graph, conclusion that uses data and explains the science, sources of error; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing graph or analysis; 1 = incomplete. Quiz answers: 1) J-curve = exponential, unlimited resources. 2) S-curve = logistic. 3) K = carrying capacity — the maximum population the environment can support. 4) Limiting factor examples (food, space, water). 5) Density-dependent example: disease. 6) Density-independent: hurricane. 7) Graph interpretation: identify K as the plateau value and the fastest growth at the inflection point.

weeks.prep: Quadrat data from Week 1; calculator. Print the lynx–hare (Hudson's Bay Company pelt) graph and a sea otter–urchin–kelp diagram. Simpson's index formula: D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/[N(N − 1)].
misconceptions: Calling all close relationships 'symbiosis = helpful': symbiosis includes mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0), and parasitism (+/−).
Thinking predators always 'win': predator and prey populations cycle together.
Equating diversity with number of species only: diversity also depends on evenness.

days.guide: Your child classifies 15 species pairs: predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism.

questions.q: Classify: bees and California poppies; ticks on deer; barnacles on a whale.
questions.a: Mutualism (+/+); parasitism (+/−); commensalism (+/0).

days.guide: Graph lynx–hare data; explain cycles.

questions.q: Why do lynx population peaks come slightly after hare peaks?
questions.a: More hares means more food, so lynx populations rise; then lynx overeat hares, hares decline, and lynx decline afterward — a lag of a year or two in roughly 10-year cycles.

days.guide: Read about otters and kelp; draw the trophic cascade.

questions.q: What happens to kelp forests if sea otters disappear?
questions.a: Sea urchins (otter prey) increase and overgraze kelp, creating 'urchin barrens'; otters are a keystone species.

days.guide: Calculate Simpson's index for both quadrats.

questions.q: Quadrat counts: 5 clover, 3 grass, 2 dandelions. Find Simpson's diversity index (1 − D).
Which is more diverse: 8, 1, 1 or 5, 3, 2?
questions.a: 5, 3, 2 (index 0.69 vs. 0.38) — more even.

days.guide: Quiz on interactions and diversity.

questions.q: What is a keystone species?
questions.a: A species with a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance (e.g., sea otters).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/−, predation +/−, competition −/−. 2) Lynx–hare cycle explanation (lag). 3) Otters → urchins ↓ → kelp ↑. 4) Simpson's index for 4, 4, 2 → N = 10, Σ = 12 + 12 + 2 = 26, 26/90 = 0.289, index 0.71. 5) Higher index = more diverse. Diversity calculation scored for correct N, Σn(n−1), and interpretation.

weeks.prep: Purchase a sterilized owl pellet kit (heat-treated) or use a virtual pellet (e.g., KidWings). Tweezers, gloves, paper plate, bone chart. Wash hands after dissection.
misconceptions: Arrows pointing from predator to prey: food-web arrows show energy flow — from the organism eaten to the eater.
Thinking 90% of energy 'disappears': it is used for life processes and lost as heat, not destroyed.
Assuming top predators are most numerous: fewer organisms can be supported at higher trophic levels.

days.guide: Your child builds a chaparral food web with 12+ organisms.

questions.q: Give a 4-link chaparral food chain.
questions.a: Chamise/manzanita → brush rabbit or deer mouse → gopher snake → red-tailed hawk (other valid chains accepted).

questions.q: Which direction should arrows point?
questions.a: From food to consumer — the direction energy flows.

days.guide: Dissect the pellet; sort bones; estimate prey eaten (count skulls).

questions.q: How can you tell how many animals an owl ate from a pellet?
questions.a: Count skulls or pairs of jaws — each skull is one prey animal.

days.guide: Apply the 10% rule from 10,000 kcal.

questions.q: Starting with 10,000 kcal in producers, how much reaches tertiary consumers?
questions.a: Primary 1,000; secondary 100; tertiary 10 kcal.

days.guide: Explain why biomass pyramids narrow and where energy goes.

questions.q: Where does the 'missing' 90% of energy go at each level?
questions.a: Used for cellular respiration (movement, growth, body heat) and lost as heat, or not eaten/digested (waste).

days.guide: Energy-flow quiz.

questions.q: If a hawk gets 5 kcal, how much producer energy supported it in a 4-level chain?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) 20,000 kcal producers → 2,000 → 200 → 20 kcal. 2) Arrow direction: toward the consumer. 3) Trophic level of a snake eating mice that eat seeds: third (secondary consumer). 4) Why fewer top predators: less energy available. 5) Decomposers recycle matter, not energy. Dissection data sheet: bones sorted by type, prey identified by skull, count of prey individuals, sketch.

weeks.prep: Sugar water (1:1) in a bottle cap; ant trail (outdoors); timer. Find a wildfire-recovery case study (e.g., chaparral regrowth after a fire — many chaparral plants resprout or have fire-triggered seeds). Prepare the Unit 1 test.
misconceptions: Thinking animals cooperate 'to help the species': behaviors persist because they increase the survival and reproduction of individuals and relatives.
Believing ecosystems return exactly to how they were: they may recover, or shift to a new state if disturbance is extreme or frequent.
Counting only one observation as evidence: repeat counts at intervals.

days.guide: Read about bee swarming, fish schooling, and wolf packs; list survival advantages.

questions.q: How does schooling help fish survive?
questions.a: It confuses predators (hard to target one fish), and many eyes detect danger sooner.

days.guide: Place sugar water near an ant trail; count ants every 5 minutes for 30 minutes.

questions.q: Predict how ant numbers at the sugar will change, and why.
questions.a: They increase over time because scouts lay pheromone trails that recruit nestmates (recruitment), then may level off.

days.guide: Analyze a chaparral wildfire recovery case study.

questions.q: How do many chaparral plants recover after fire?
questions.a: Some resprout from burls/roots; others have seeds that germinate after heat or smoke; but fires that are too frequent can convert chaparral to non-native grassland.

days.guide: Write a CER on whether group behavior increases survival using two data sources.

questions.q: What makes evidence strong in a CER?
questions.a: Specific, relevant data from reliable sources, with numbers and comparisons.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test.

questions.q: What does the 10% rule predict for 50,000 kcal of producers at the secondary consumer level?
questions.a: 500 kcal.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test sample answers: 1) Levels of organization order. 2) Logistic curve and K. 3) Density-dependent vs. independent examples. 4) Interaction types. 5) Keystone species (sea otter). 6) Simpson's index for 6, 2, 2 → Σ = 30 + 2 + 2 = 34, 34/90 = 0.378, index 0.62. 7) 10% rule calculation. 8) Group behavior advantage example. 9) Ecosystem resilience after disturbance. Scoring: 80%+ proficient. CER rubric: 4 = claim answers the question; evidence uses specific data (numbers, units, observations); reasoning connects the evidence to a scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence with partial reasoning; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect.

weeks.prep: Toilet paper roll (at least 46 squares; 1 square = 100 million years) or 460 squares (1 square = 10 million years); markers. Steel wool (soap-free), white vinegar, jars. Images of Shark Bay stromatolites.
misconceptions: Thinking early Earth had oxygen like today: early atmosphere had almost no free O₂; it accumulated after cyanobacteria (Great Oxidation Event ~2.4 billion years ago).
Imagining humans appeared early: on a 4.6-billion-year timeline, humans occupy the last tiny fraction of the final square.
Treating Earth and life as separate: each changed the other (coevolution).

days.guide: Build the timeline: Earth forms 4.6 bya; first life ~3.5–3.8 bya; Great Oxidation ~2.4 bya; multicellular life later; dinosaurs; humans at the very end.

questions.q: On a 460-square timeline (1 square = 10 million years), where does the Great Oxidation Event (2.4 bya) fall?
questions.a: 240 squares from the 'today' end (about square 220 from the start).

days.guide: Soak steel wool in vinegar (removes coating), place in a jar, observe rust.

questions.q: How does rusting steel wool model banded iron formations?
questions.a: Iron reacts with oxygen to form iron oxide (rust); in ancient oceans, oxygen from cyanobacteria reacted with dissolved iron, which settled as iron-rich layers.

days.guide: Examine stromatolite images.

questions.q: What are stromatolites and why do they matter?
questions.a: Layered structures built by cyanobacteria mats trapping sediment; ancient ones are among the oldest evidence of life, and their photosynthesis released the oxygen that changed the atmosphere.

days.guide: Your child writes an argument on how life and atmosphere changed each other.

questions.q: Give one way life changed Earth and one way Earth changed life.
questions.a: Life → cyanobacteria added O₂ to the atmosphere (and an ozone layer formed). Earth → rising oxygen allowed aerobic respiration and complex life, and killed off many anaerobic organisms.

days.guide: Quiz on early atmosphere.

questions.q: About when did oxygen begin to accumulate in the atmosphere?
questions.a: About 2.4 billion years ago (the Great Oxidation Event).

weeks.assessment_key: Argument rubric: 4 = claim that life and atmosphere coevolved, evidence from stromatolites, banded iron formations, and timing of the Great Oxidation Event, reasoning about photosynthesis and aerobic life; 3 = two pieces of evidence; 2 = one; 1 = none. Quiz answers: 1) Earth age 4.6 billion years. 2) Early atmosphere: CO₂, N₂, water vapor, little O₂. 3) Cyanobacteria produced oxygen. 4) Banded iron formations = iron + oxygen layers. 5) Ozone layer formed from O₂, shielding land life from UV.

weeks.prep: Fresh spinach, hole punch or straw, baking soda, dish soap, 10 mL plastic syringe (no needle), clear cups, lamp, timer, ruler. Practice infiltrating disks once before teaching (pull plunger to vacuum until disks sink).
misconceptions: Thinking plants get their mass from soil: most of a plant's mass comes from carbon in CO₂ from the air.
Believing plants don't respire: plants do both photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
Saying light energy 'becomes' glucose: light energy is converted to chemical energy stored in glucose bonds.

days.guide: Draw the input–output model.

questions.q: Write the balanced equation for photosynthesis.
questions.a: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

questions.q: Where does the oxygen released come from?
questions.a: From splitting water molecules in the light reactions.

days.guide: Punch 10 disks; infiltrate with baking-soda solution (with a drop of soap) using the syringe; place under light and record time to float.

questions.q: Why do the disks float?
questions.a: Photosynthesis produces O₂ gas, which fills the air spaces in the leaf, making the disks buoyant.

questions.q: What does the baking soda provide?
questions.a: A source of CO₂ (as bicarbonate) for photosynthesis.

days.guide: Repeat at two lamp distances; graph time for 50% to float.

questions.q: Predict: will disks float faster near or far from the lamp?
questions.a: Nearer — more light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis (up to a limit).

days.guide: Label the chloroplast; flowchart light reactions and Calvin cycle.

questions.q: Where do the light reactions and Calvin cycle occur?
questions.a: Light reactions in the thylakoid membranes; Calvin cycle in the stroma.

questions.q: What do the light reactions supply to the Calvin cycle?
questions.a: ATP and NADPH.

days.guide: Lab report and quiz.

questions.q: What gas do plants take in for photosynthesis?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = testable question, hypothesis, identified variables (independent, dependent, controlled), clear data table and labeled graph, conclusion that uses data and explains the science, sources of error; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing graph or analysis; 1 = incomplete. Quiz answers: 1) Equation (above). 2) Chlorophyll absorbs light (mainly red and blue). 3) Thylakoid/stroma locations. 4) O₂ from water. 5) Light intensity increases rate until another factor limits. 6) Most plant mass comes from CO₂.

weeks.prep: Red cabbage indicator (boil chopped red cabbage 10 minutes, strain, cool) or bromothymol blue; straws; yeast and sugar; two bottles with balloons. Safety: blow OUT only through the straw — never inhale indicator.
misconceptions: Thinking respiration = breathing: cellular respiration is the chemical process in cells that releases energy from glucose.
Believing fermentation produces lots of energy: it yields only 2 ATP per glucose versus about 30–38 in aerobic respiration.
Thinking ATP is stored long-term: cells constantly regenerate ATP; it's an energy 'currency,' not storage.

days.guide: Model with molecule cards: bonds broken, bonds formed, energy released.

questions.q: Write the equation for cellular respiration.
questions.a: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP).

questions.q: How are photosynthesis and respiration related?
questions.a: They are reverse processes; the products of one are the reactants of the other.

days.guide: Blow through a straw into indicator at rest and after exercise; compare color.

questions.q: Predict the color change after exercise and explain.
questions.a: Red cabbage turns from purple toward pink/red (bromothymol blue turns green/yellow) faster after exercise, because more CO₂ is exhaled, forming carbonic acid.

days.guide: Compare yeast with and without oxygen; connect to bread and yogurt.

questions.q: What does yeast produce during fermentation?
questions.a: Ethanol and CO₂ (the CO₂ makes bread rise).

questions.q: What type of fermentation makes yogurt?
questions.a: Lactic acid fermentation by bacteria.

days.guide: Explain ATP with an analogy (a rechargeable battery).

questions.q: How does ATP release energy?
questions.a: Breaking the bond to the third phosphate (ATP → ADP + P) releases energy for cell work.

days.guide: Quiz comparing photosynthesis and respiration.

questions.q: Which organisms do cellular respiration?
questions.a: Nearly all organisms — plants, animals, fungi, and many microbes.

weeks.assessment_key: Indicator lab write-up: 4 = prediction, data (color and time) before/after exercise, explanation linking exercise → more respiration → more CO₂ → acid → color change. Quiz answers: 1) Photosynthesis: chloroplast, stores energy, uses CO₂ + H₂O. 2) Respiration: mitochondria, releases energy, uses glucose + O₂. 3) Aerobic ~30–38 ATP vs. fermentation 2 ATP. 4) Yeast fermentation products. 5) ATP → ADP + P releases energy.

weeks.prep: Iodine tincture (poison — adult use only, keep away from mouth), brown paper bag, droppers, foods: bread, potato, apple, butter, nuts, cooked egg white, cracker. Paper clips.
misconceptions: Thinking all carbohydrates are sugar: starch and cellulose are complex polysaccharides made of glucose.
Believing proteins are only for muscles: proteins also act as enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and transporters.
Confusing dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis: synthesis removes water to join monomers; hydrolysis adds water to split them.

days.guide: Build the four-macromolecule chart.

questions.q: Give the monomer of each macromolecule.
questions.a: Carbohydrates — monosaccharides (glucose); proteins — amino acids; nucleic acids — nucleotides; lipids — not true polymers (often glycerol + fatty acids).

days.guide: Test foods with iodine (starch turns blue-black) and brown paper (translucent spot = lipid).

questions.q: A potato turns blue-black with iodine. What does it contain?
questions.a: Starch.

questions.q: Butter leaves a translucent spot on paper. What does it contain?
questions.a: Lipid (fat).

days.guide: Explain that plants use glucose's carbon skeletons plus nitrogen (from soil nitrates) to build amino acids.

questions.q: Which element must be added to glucose-derived carbon skeletons to make amino acids?
questions.a: Nitrogen (from soil nitrates or ammonium, ultimately from nitrogen fixation).

days.guide: Build paper clip chains: remove a 'water' card for each link (dehydration synthesis); add one to split (hydrolysis).

questions.q: How many water molecules are released when 5 monomers join in a chain?
questions.a: 4 (one per bond).

days.guide: Biomolecules quiz.

questions.q: Which macromolecule stores genetic information?
questions.a: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).

weeks.assessment_key: Food test data table: proficient = each food tested for starch and lipid with result and observation; correct interpretations (bread, potato, cracker: starch; butter, nuts: lipid; apple: little starch; egg white: protein, neither test positive). Quiz answers: 1) Monomers (above). 2) Enzymes are proteins. 3) Starch test = iodine blue-black. 4) Lipids: energy storage, membranes. 5) Dehydration synthesis joins monomers releasing water. 6) Hydrolysis breaks polymers with water.

weeks.prep: Print the Keeling curve data (NOAA Global Monitoring Lab, Mauna Loa monthly CO₂). Carbonated water, red cabbage indicator, cups. Reference values: atmosphere holds about 870 GtC; 1 ppm CO₂ ≈ 2.13 GtC; fossil fuels emit about 10 GtC per year. Prepare the Unit 2 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the seasonal wiggle is from human activity: it's from Northern Hemisphere plant growth (photosynthesis) in summer and decay/respiration in winter.
Believing all emitted CO₂ stays in the air: roughly half is absorbed by oceans and land plants.
Thinking the ocean sink is harmless: absorbed CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering ocean pH.

days.guide: Draw the carbon cycle across spheres with flux arrows (photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, ocean exchange, sedimentation).

questions.q: Name two processes that move carbon from the biosphere to the atmosphere.
questions.a: Cellular respiration and decomposition (also burning/combustion of biomass).

days.guide: Graph Mauna Loa data; explain the seasonal pattern.

questions.q: Why does CO₂ fall each Northern Hemisphere summer?
questions.a: Plants in the Northern Hemisphere (which has more land) photosynthesize more, removing CO₂.

questions.q: About how much has CO₂ risen since 1958?
questions.a: From about 315 ppm to over 420 ppm in recent years.

days.guide: Use reservoir values to compute fossil fuel impact.

questions.q: If about 10 GtC are emitted per year and about 45% stays in the air, how much does CO₂ rise per year (1 ppm ≈ 2.13 GtC)?
questions.a: 4.5 GtC ÷ 2.13 ≈ 2.1 ppm per year — close to the observed rate.

days.guide: Add carbonated water to cabbage indicator; compare to plain water.

questions.q: What happens to indicator when CO₂-rich water is added, and what does it model?
questions.a: It shifts toward pink/red (more acidic) — modeling ocean acidification as oceans absorb CO₂.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test.

questions.q: Which organelle performs photosynthesis?
questions.a: Chloroplast.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test sample answers: 1) Great Oxidation Event ~2.4 bya by cyanobacteria. 2) Photosynthesis and respiration equations. 3) Leaf disks float due to O₂. 4) Light reactions/Calvin cycle locations. 5) Fermentation vs. aerobic ATP. 6) Macromolecule monomers. 7) Carbon cycle processes. 8) Keeling curve trend and seasonal cycle. 9) Ocean acidification. 10) Calculation: 6 GtC added to air ≈ 2.8 ppm. Scoring: 80%+ proficient.

weeks.prep: Clear jar, sand, soil, gravel, a small 'fossil' (shell or toy) per layer; 100 pennies and a shoebox for half-life; clay. Reference: carbon-14 half-life is about 5,730 years.
misconceptions: Thinking deeper layers are always younger: by the law of superposition, lower (undisturbed) layers are older.
Believing radioactive decay depends on temperature or conditions: half-lives are constant.
Viewing transitional fossils as 'half-and-half' creatures: they show mixtures of ancestral and new traits.

days.guide: Layer the jar with a 'fossil' in each layer; your child explains relative dating.

questions.q: In undisturbed layers, which fossils are oldest?
questions.a: Those in the bottom layers (law of superposition).

days.guide: Shake pennies, remove 'decayed' (heads), record; each shake = one half-life.

questions.q: A fossil has 25% of its original carbon-14. How old is it?
questions.a: Two half-lives: 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years.

questions.q: After 3 half-lives, what fraction of the parent isotope remains?

days.guide: Analyze Tiktaalik and the whale sequence (Pakicetus → Ambulocetus → Rodhocetus → Basilosaurus → modern whales).

questions.q: What features make Tiktaalik transitional?
questions.a: Fish features (scales, fins, gills) plus tetrapod-like features (a flat head, a mobile neck, sturdy fin bones like a wrist, lungs).

questions.q: What traits changed in the whale sequence?
questions.a: Hind limbs shrank, nostrils moved back toward a blowhole, bodies became streamlined for swimming.

days.guide: Place fossil groups on the geologic time scale.

questions.q: Which came first: fish, dinosaurs, or flowering plants?
questions.a: Fish (Cambrian/Ordovician), then dinosaurs (Triassic), then flowering plants (Cretaceous).

days.guide: Fossil-evidence quiz.

questions.q: What is a transitional fossil?
questions.a: A fossil showing traits intermediate between an ancestral group and its descendants.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Superposition. 2) Index fossils help date layers. 3) Half-life definition. 4) 1/16 remaining = 4 half-lives. 5) C-14 dating useful up to ~50,000 years. 6) Tiktaalik features. 7) Whale sequence traits. 8) Order: bacteria → fish → amphibians → reptiles/dinosaurs → mammals radiate → humans.

weeks.prep: Raw chicken wing (from the grocery), gloves, scissors, paper towels; disinfect surfaces and wash hands (Salmonella). Cytochrome c comparison table (humans and chimpanzees identical; rhesus monkey differs by 1 amino acid; horse by about 12; yeast by about 44). Trait table for 6 animals.
misconceptions: Confusing homologous and analogous: homologous = same underlying structure from common ancestry (human arm, bat wing); analogous = similar function, different origin (bird wing, insect wing).
Reading a cladogram as a ladder of 'higher' animals: branch points show common ancestors; all living groups are equally 'evolved.'
Thinking embryos look identical: they share features (pharyngeal pouches, tails) but differ.

days.guide: Dissect the wing; identify humerus, radius, ulna, wrist/digits; compare to a human arm.

questions.q: Which bones in the chicken wing match the human arm?
questions.a: Humerus (upper), radius and ulna (forearm), and reduced wrist and finger bones.

days.guide: Sort 12 structures.

questions.q: Classify: bat wing and human hand; butterfly wing and bird wing.
questions.a: Homologous; analogous.

days.guide: Rank relatedness by cytochrome c differences.

questions.q: Human cytochrome c differs from rhesus monkey by 1 amino acid and from horse by about 12. Which is more closely related to humans?
questions.a: Rhesus monkey — fewer differences indicate a more recent common ancestor.

days.guide: Build a cladogram from shared derived traits.

questions.q: What does a branch point on a cladogram represent?
questions.a: A common ancestor where a new shared derived trait appeared.

days.guide: Your child creates a brochure communicating multiple lines of evidence.

questions.q: Name four lines of evidence for common ancestry.
questions.a: Fossils, comparative anatomy (homologous structures), embryology, molecular (DNA/protein) similarities (also biogeography).

weeks.assessment_key: Brochure rubric (HS-LS4-1): 4 = at least four lines of evidence with specific examples (e.g., whale fossils, forelimb homology, vertebrate embryos, cytochrome c data), clear explanation of how each supports common ancestry, accurate visuals; 3 = three lines; 2 = two or vague; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Dried beans or pasta in 4–5 colors (50 of each), two fabrics with different patterns, timer (15 seconds per predation round). Darwin's finches reading.
misconceptions: Believing individuals evolve or 'try' to adapt: populations evolve; individuals don't change their genes in response to need.
'Survival of the fittest' = strongest: fitness means reproductive success in a specific environment.
Thinking mutations arise because they're needed: variation is random; selection is not.

days.guide: Read about Darwin's finches; list the four factors.

questions.q: What are the four factors of natural selection?
questions.a: Variation; inheritance (traits are heritable); overproduction/competition; differential survival and reproduction.

days.guide: Spread beans; 'predator' picks as many as possible in 15 seconds; survivors 'reproduce' (add one of same color per survivor).

questions.q: Predict which bean colors will survive best on the patterned fabric.
questions.a: Colors that match the background (camouflaged), because predators find conspicuous beans faster.

days.guide: Graph color frequency over generations.

questions.q: If camouflaged beans went from 20% to 45% of the population, what happened?
questions.a: Natural selection increased the frequency of the better-camouflaged trait.

days.guide: Analyze peppered moths and antibiotic resistance.

questions.q: Why did dark peppered moths increase during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.a: Soot darkened tree bark, so dark moths were better hidden from birds and survived to reproduce more.

questions.q: Why is finishing antibiotics as prescribed important?
questions.a: Stopping early can leave the most resistant bacteria alive to multiply, selecting for resistance.

days.guide: Natural selection quiz.

questions.q: Does an individual bacterium become resistant because it was exposed to an antibiotic?
questions.a: No — resistant variants already exist (from mutation); the antibiotic kills the susceptible ones, so resistant ones multiply.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = testable question, hypothesis, identified variables (independent, dependent, controlled), clear data table and labeled graph, conclusion that uses data and explains the science, sources of error; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing graph or analysis; 1 = incomplete. Quiz answers: 1) Four factors (above). 2) Fitness = reproductive success. 3) Peppered moth explanation. 4) Antibiotic resistance explanation. 5) Variation arises from mutation and sexual reproduction. 6) Populations, not individuals, evolve.

weeks.prep: Stream HHMI BioInteractive 'The Making of the Fittest: Natural Selection and Adaptation' (rock pocket mice, about 10 minutes). Spreadsheet software.
misconceptions: Thinking the mice turned dark because they lived on dark rocks: the dark-fur mutation arose randomly; predators selected it.
Ignoring probability: a small advantage can change frequencies a lot over many generations.
Confusing frequency (proportion) with number of individuals.

days.guide: Watch the film; record evidence of selection.

questions.q: Why are dark mice common on lava flows but light mice common on sandy desert?
questions.a: Predators (owls, hawks) more easily see mice that contrast with the background, so matching fur survives and reproduces more.

days.guide: Calculate trait proportions over generations from data.

questions.q: A population of 200 mice has 50 dark mice. What is the dark-fur frequency? If it becomes 120 of 200, what is the change?
questions.a: 0.25 → 0.60; an increase of 0.35 (35 percentage points).

days.guide: Spreadsheet: new p = 1.1p / (1.1p + (1 − p)); graph 20 generations.

questions.q: Starting at 10% dark mice with a 10% survival advantage, about what frequency after 20 generations?

days.guide: Write a CER explaining dark fur on lava flows.

questions.q: What gene was linked to dark fur in some rock pocket mice?
questions.a: Mutations in the Mc1r gene (melanocortin-1 receptor) in Arizona populations.

days.guide: Quiz on probability and selection.

questions.q: If a trait has no survival advantage, what happens to its frequency (ignoring chance)?
questions.a: It stays about the same.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = claim answers the question; evidence uses specific data (numbers, units, observations); reasoning connects the evidence to a scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence with partial reasoning; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect. Proficient CER: claim — dark fur became common on lava because of natural selection; evidence — predation rates/survival data and frequency changes from the film; reasoning — random mutation produced dark fur, which was camouflaged on dark rock, so those mice survived and reproduced more, passing on the allele. Quiz answers: frequency calculations as above; 10% advantage model reaches ~0.87 after 20 generations starting at 0.5.

weeks.prep: A bag of mixed-color beads or M&Ms (at least 100), several cups. Reading on Ellis–van Creveld syndrome in the Old Order Amish of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania.
misconceptions: Thinking evolution = natural selection only: drift, gene flow, mutation, and nonrandom mating also change allele frequencies.
Believing genetic drift favors 'better' alleles: drift is random and strongest in small populations.
Confusing founder effect and bottleneck: founder = a small group starts a new population; bottleneck = a population is drastically reduced.

days.guide: Draw 10 beads from a large population cup vs. 4 from a small one repeatedly; compare color frequencies.

questions.q: Why does genetic drift affect small populations more?
questions.a: Chance events have a larger effect on proportions when there are few individuals; alleles can be lost or fixed quickly.

days.guide: Read about Ellis–van Creveld syndrome in the Amish.

questions.q: Why is Ellis–van Creveld syndrome more common among the Lancaster County Amish?
questions.a: The community descends from a small group of founders, at least one of whom carried the allele; marrying within the group kept its frequency high (founder effect).

days.guide: Move beads between two cup populations each generation; track convergence.

questions.q: What does gene flow do to two populations' allele frequencies over time?
questions.a: Makes them more similar (reduces differences between populations).

days.guide: Make a comparison chart: mutation, selection, drift (founder, bottleneck), gene flow.

questions.q: Example of a bottleneck?
questions.a: Northern elephant seals were hunted down to perhaps 20–100 individuals by the 1890s; today's large population has very low genetic diversity.

days.guide: Mechanisms quiz.

questions.q: Which mechanism is the original source of new alleles?
questions.a: Mutation.

weeks.assessment_key: Mechanisms quiz answers: 1) Natural selection — nonrandom, adaptive. 2) Genetic drift — random, strongest in small populations. 3) Founder effect — Amish/Ellis–van Creveld. 4) Bottleneck — northern elephant seals or cheetahs. 5) Gene flow — migration between populations, reduces differences. 6) Mutation — source of new alleles.

weeks.prep: Map of Ensatina salamander subspecies around California's Central Valley (search 'Ensatina ring species map', e.g., UC Berkeley Understanding Evolution). Hawaiian honeycreeper beak images.
misconceptions: Thinking species are always clearly separate: ring species and hybrids show speciation is a gradual process.
Confusing prezygotic and postzygotic barriers: prezygotic prevent mating/fertilization; postzygotic affect the hybrid after fertilization.
Believing new species appear in one generation (usually they accumulate differences over many).

days.guide: Discuss the biological species concept and its limits.

questions.q: What is the biological species concept?
questions.a: Populations whose members can interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring.

questions.q: Name one limitation.
questions.a: It can't be applied to asexual organisms or fossils, and some species hybridize.

days.guide: Map Ensatina subspecies.

questions.q: Why are Ensatina salamanders called a ring species?
questions.a: Neighboring populations around the Central Valley interbreed, but where the two ends of the ring meet in Southern California, the forms rarely interbreed and act like separate species.

days.guide: Classify 10 barriers.

questions.q: Classify: two frog species breed in different months; a mule (horse × donkey) is sterile.
questions.a: Temporal isolation (prezygotic); hybrid sterility (postzygotic).

days.guide: Analyze Hawaiian honeycreepers.

questions.q: How do Hawaiian honeycreepers show adaptive radiation?
questions.a: A single finch-like ancestor colonized the islands and diversified into many species with beaks adapted to different foods (nectar, seeds, insects).

days.guide: Speciation quiz.

questions.q: Which type of speciation results from a geographic barrier?
questions.a: Allopatric speciation.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Biological species concept. 2) Allopatric vs. sympatric speciation. 3) Prezygotic examples: temporal, behavioral (bird songs), mechanical, habitat, gametic. 4) Postzygotic: hybrid sterility (mule), hybrid inviability. 5) Ensatina ring species. 6) Honeycreeper adaptive radiation.

weeks.prep: Print a graph of extinction rates over the Phanerozoic showing the 'Big Five' (end-Ordovician ~445 mya, Late Devonian ~372 mya, end-Permian ~252 mya, end-Triassic ~201 mya, end-Cretaceous 66 mya). Information on the iridium layer and Chicxulub crater. Prepare the Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Believing all dinosaurs vanished: birds are living dinosaurs.
Thinking extinction is rare/unnatural: most species that ever lived are extinct; background extinction is normal, but mass extinctions are sudden spikes.
Claiming a sixth mass extinction is either proven or a hoax: evaluate rates — current extinction rates are estimated far above background, but we have not (yet) lost ~75% of species.

days.guide: Analyze the extinction graph; list the five and causes.

questions.q: Which was the largest mass extinction and what likely caused it?
questions.a: The end-Permian (~252 mya), when roughly 90% or more of marine species died; linked to massive Siberian Traps volcanism, warming, and ocean acidification/low oxygen.

days.guide: Evaluate the asteroid evidence.

questions.q: What evidence supports an asteroid impact at the K-Pg boundary?
questions.a: A worldwide iridium-rich clay layer (iridium is rare on Earth, common in asteroids), shocked quartz, tektites, and the Chicxulub crater in the Yucatán dated to 66 million years ago.

days.guide: Explain the mammal radiation.

questions.q: Why did mammals diversify after the dinosaurs went extinct?
questions.a: Many ecological niches were empty, so surviving small mammals radiated into new forms (adaptive radiation).

days.guide: Evaluate the sixth-extinction claim with data.

questions.q: What evidence supports a current extinction crisis?
questions.a: Extinction rates far above background rates and sharp population declines driven by habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, overharvesting, and climate change.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: When did the non-avian dinosaurs go extinct?
questions.a: About 66 million years ago.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test sample answers: superposition; half-life math; transitional fossils; homologous vs. analogous; cytochrome c reasoning; cladogram reading; four factors of natural selection; peppered moths; frequency calculations; drift vs. selection; founder effect; species concept; isolation mechanisms; K-Pg evidence. Scoring: 80%+ proficient.

weeks.prep: Semester review guide covering ecosystems, energy/matter, and evolution. Index cards for flashcards. Plan a 90-minute exam block.
misconceptions: Memorizing diagrams without understanding arrows: explain each arrow aloud.
Mixing up photosynthesis and respiration locations and products.
Using 'adapt' to mean individuals change on purpose.

days.guide: One-page summary of ecosystem concepts with diagrams.

questions.q: Explain carrying capacity in one sentence.
questions.a: The maximum population size an environment can sustain given its resources.

days.guide: Redraw photosynthesis, respiration, and carbon cycle models from memory.

questions.q: Where does carbon in a tree's wood come from?
questions.a: CO₂ from the air, fixed during photosynthesis.

days.guide: Make evolution flashcards.

questions.q: Explain natural selection in two sentences.
questions.a: Individuals in a population vary in heritable traits. Those with traits better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations.

days.guide: Practice exam; correct mistakes.

questions.q: Using the 10% rule, how much energy reaches the third trophic level from 8,000 kcal of producers?
questions.a: 80 kcal.

days.guide: Give the semester exam.

questions.q: What is a keystone species example from California?
questions.a: Sea otters (kelp forests).

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam: multiple choice and short answers on Units 1–3 scored with the unit keys; constructed responses scored with the CER rubric. CER rubric: 4 = claim answers the question; evidence uses specific data (numbers, units, observations); reasoning connects the evidence to a scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence with partial reasoning; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect.

weeks.prep: Strawberries (2–3), zip-top bag, dish soap, salt, water, coffee filter, clear cup, rubbing alcohol chilled in the freezer at least 1 hour (adult handles; flammable). Paper DNA model template. Reading on Rosalind Franklin and Photo 51.
misconceptions: Thinking you can see the double helix in the extracted DNA: you see millions of tangled DNA strands clumped together, not the helix.
Pairing A with G: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G (in DNA).
Believing replication makes one new and one totally old molecule: it is semiconservative — each new molecule has one old and one new strand.

days.guide: Mash strawberries with extraction buffer (soap, salt, water), filter, layer cold alcohol, spool DNA.

questions.q: What do the soap, salt, and cold alcohol each do?
questions.a: Soap breaks down cell and nuclear membranes (lipids); salt helps DNA clump by neutralizing its charges; cold alcohol makes DNA precipitate (DNA doesn't dissolve in alcohol).

questions.q: Why are strawberries good for DNA extraction?
questions.a: They are octoploid (8 copies of each chromosome set) and soft, so they yield lots of DNA.

days.guide: Build the paper model with base pairs and antiparallel strands.

questions.q: Write the complementary strand: 5'-ATGCCA-3'.
questions.a: 3'-TACGGT-5'.

days.guide: Read about Franklin, Watson, Crick, and Photo 51.

questions.q: What did Photo 51 reveal, and who made it?
questions.a: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction image (with Raymond Gosling, 1952) showed DNA's helical structure; Watson and Crick used it to build their 1953 double-helix model.

days.guide: Model semiconservative replication.

questions.q: After one round of replication, what does each new DNA molecule contain?
questions.a: One original (parent) strand and one newly made strand.

days.guide: Quiz on DNA.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a nucleotide?
questions.a: A phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar, and a nitrogenous base.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = testable question, hypothesis, identified variables (independent, dependent, controlled), clear data table and labeled graph, conclusion that uses data and explains the science, sources of error; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing graph or analysis; 1 = incomplete. Quiz answers: 1) Base pairing A–T, C–G. 2) Nucleotide parts. 3) Sugar-phosphate backbone, bases inside. 4) Semiconservative replication. 5) Enzyme that unzips DNA: helicase; builds new strands: DNA polymerase. 6) Franklin's Photo 51.

weeks.prep: Print a codon chart (mRNA codons). Beads or paper strips for amino acids. Prepare 5 DNA template sequences.
misconceptions: Transcribing with T: RNA uses U (uracil) instead of T.
Translating the DNA directly: translate the mRNA codons.
Thinking each gene makes a trait directly: genes code for proteins, whose structure and function produce traits.

days.guide: Draw the central dogma.

questions.q: What are the three processes of the central dogma and where do they occur in eukaryotes?
questions.a: Replication (DNA → DNA, nucleus), transcription (DNA → mRNA, nucleus), translation (mRNA → protein, ribosomes in cytoplasm).

days.guide: Transcribe template sequences; mark start and stop codons.

questions.q: Transcribe the DNA template TAC GGA TTC ACT into mRNA.
questions.a: AUG CCU AAG UGA.

days.guide: Translate using the codon chart; build paper chains.

questions.q: Translate AUG CCU AAG UGA.
questions.a: Met – Pro – Lys – stop.

days.guide: Explain how sequence determines shape and function.

questions.q: How can changing one amino acid change hemoglobin?
questions.a: In sickle-cell hemoglobin, valine replaces glutamic acid, causing molecules to stick together and deform red blood cells.

days.guide: Protein synthesis quiz.

questions.q: What is a codon?
questions.a: A sequence of three mRNA bases coding for one amino acid (or stop).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Central dogma. 2) Transcribe TAC AAA CCG ATT → AUG UUU GGC UAA. 3) Translate AUG UUU GGC UAA → Met–Phe–Gly–stop. 4) tRNA carries amino acids, anticodons match codons. 5) Ribosome = site of translation. 6) Protein shape determines function.

weeks.prep: Pipe cleaners in 2 colors (maternal/paternal), beads for centromeres. A comparison table template.
misconceptions: Thinking meiosis makes identical cells: it makes four genetically different haploid cells.
Confusing chromosomes and chromatids: after replication, each chromosome has two sister chromatids.
Believing differentiated cells have different DNA: they have the same DNA but express different genes.

days.guide: Model interphase and mitosis stages (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) and cytokinesis.

questions.q: In a human body cell, how many chromosomes do the two daughter cells have after mitosis?
questions.a: 46 each — identical to the parent cell.

days.guide: Model meiosis I and II.

questions.q: How many cells and how many chromosomes result from meiosis in humans?
questions.a: Four haploid cells with 23 chromosomes each.

days.guide: Demonstrate crossing over and independent assortment.

questions.q: How does crossing over increase variation?
questions.a: Homologous chromosomes exchange segments in prophase I, creating new allele combinations.

days.guide: Complete the mitosis vs. meiosis table; explain differentiation.

questions.q: Give one purpose of mitosis and one of meiosis.
questions.a: Mitosis: growth and repair. Meiosis: making gametes (eggs and sperm).

days.guide: Cell division quiz.

questions.q: In which phase do chromosomes line up in the middle?
questions.a: Metaphase.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Phases of mitosis in order (PMAT). 2) Mitosis: 2 identical diploid cells. 3) Meiosis: 4 unique haploid cells. 4) Crossing over in prophase I. 5) Independent assortment in metaphase I. 6) Differentiation = different gene expression.

weeks.prep: Coins (2 per pair), Punnett square worksheets.
misconceptions: Confusing genotype and phenotype: genotype = alleles (Pp); phenotype = observable trait (purple).
Thinking a 3:1 ratio guarantees 3 of 4 offspring: it gives probabilities, not exact outcomes.
Assuming dominant means more common: dominance is about expression, not frequency.

days.guide: Read about Mendel; define allele, homozygous, heterozygous, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype.

questions.q: What did Mendel find when he crossed two hybrid (Pp) purple-flowered pea plants?
questions.a: About 3 purple : 1 white in the offspring.

days.guide: Solve 10 monohybrid crosses.

questions.q: Cross Pp × Pp. Give genotype and phenotype ratios.
questions.a: Genotypes 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp; phenotypes 3 purple : 1 white.

questions.q: Cross Tt × tt (T = tall).
questions.a: 1 Tt : 1 tt; 1 tall : 1 short.

days.guide: Flip two coins (heads = A, tails = a) 40 times; compare to 1:2:1.

questions.q: Expected counts for 40 tosses of Aa × Aa?
questions.a: 10 AA, 20 Aa, 10 aa.

days.guide: Solve dihybrid crosses.

questions.q: In RrYy × RrYy, what fraction are round and yellow (both dominant)?

days.guide: Genetics quiz.

questions.q: What is the probability of aa from Aa × Aa?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Definitions. 2) Bb × bb → 50% brown, 50% blue (if B = brown). 3) Hh × Hh → 1:2:1, 3:1. 4) Test cross purpose. 5) RrYy × RrYy → 9:3:3:1. 6) Probability of rryy → 1/16.

weeks.prep: Pedigree worksheets; tape measure for family heights.
misconceptions: Thinking codominance and incomplete dominance are the same: incomplete = blend (pink); codominance = both shown (AB blood, roan).
Believing females can't have sex-linked recessive traits: they can, if they inherit two recessive alleles, but it's rarer.
Assuming every trait has 2 forms: many traits (height, skin color) are polygenic with continuous variation.

days.guide: Solve incomplete dominance and codominance problems.

questions.q: Cross two pink snapdragons (RW × RW).
questions.a: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

questions.q: Parents with blood types Iᴬi and Iᴮi — possible children?
questions.a: AB, A, B, and O, each with probability 1/4.

days.guide: Solve sex-linked problems.

questions.q: A carrier mother (XᴮXᵇ) and a father with normal vision (XᴮY): chance a son is color-blind? A daughter?
questions.a: Sons: 50%. Daughters: 0% affected (50% carriers).

questions.q: Why are males more often affected?
questions.a: Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed.

days.guide: Analyze pedigrees.

questions.q: Two unaffected parents have an affected child. What inheritance pattern is likely?
questions.a: Recessive (both parents are carriers).

days.guide: Measure and graph family heights.

questions.q: What shape does a polygenic trait's distribution usually show?
questions.a: A bell-shaped (normal) curve.

days.guide: Quiz; pedigree analysis.

questions.q: In a pedigree, what does a shaded square represent?
questions.a: An affected male.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Incomplete dominance ratio 1:2:1. 2) Codominance blood type cross. 3) Sex-linked cross (above). 4) Hemophilia father (XʰY) × normal mother (XᴴXᴴ) → all daughters carriers, all sons unaffected. 5) Pedigree symbols. Pedigree analysis: proficient = correctly identifies pattern with reasoning (skipped generations → recessive; mostly males → X-linked).

weeks.prep: UV-sensitive beads (online or craft store), sunscreen, a clear plastic bag. Mutation worksheet with a sentence of three-letter words (THE FAT CAT ATE THE RAT). Prepare the Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Thinking all mutations are harmful: many are neutral, and some are beneficial (e.g., sickle-cell carriers resist malaria).
Believing a point mutation always changes the protein: a silent mutation may code the same amino acid.
Confusing CRISPR with cloning: CRISPR edits specific DNA sequences.

days.guide: Model substitution, insertion, and deletion with THE FAT CAT ATE THE RAT.

questions.q: Delete the first A: what happens and what type of mutation is it?
questions.a: THE FTC ATA TET HER AT — every word after the deletion changes: a frameshift mutation.

questions.q: Which is usually more damaging, a substitution or a frameshift?
questions.a: Frameshift — it changes every codon after the mutation.

days.guide: Expose UV beads to sunlight with and without sunscreen.

questions.q: Predict what happens to beads covered with sunscreen.
questions.a: They change color less, because sunscreen blocks some UV — the same UV that can damage DNA in skin cells.

days.guide: Explain sickle cell.

questions.q: What single change causes sickle-cell disease?
questions.a: An A→T substitution in the β-globin gene (GAG → GTG) replaces glutamic acid with valine.

questions.q: Why is the sickle allele common where malaria is common?
questions.a: Carriers (heterozygotes) are more resistant to malaria, so they survive and reproduce more.

days.guide: Research CRISPR; write a claim about its ethical use.

questions.q: What does CRISPR-Cas9 do?
questions.a: A guide RNA leads the Cas9 enzyme to a specific DNA sequence, where it cuts so the DNA can be edited.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test.

questions.q: Transcribe DNA template TAC CTT into mRNA.
questions.a: AUG GAA.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test sample answers: DNA structure and base pairing; semiconservative replication; transcription/translation of a given sequence; mitosis vs. meiosis; Punnett squares (3:1, 1:2:1, 9:3:3:1); blood types; sex-linked cross; pedigree pattern; mutation types; sickle cell; CRISPR. Scoring: 80%+ proficient. CRISPR claim rubric: 4 = clear claim, scientific explanation, ethical reasoning considering benefits and risks.

weeks.prep: Onion, iodine (adult handles), microscope or phone microscope clip, slides/cover slips (or clear tape on glass). Organelle list.
misconceptions: Thinking plant cells lack mitochondria: plant cells have both chloroplasts and mitochondria.
Believing prokaryotes have no DNA: they have DNA but no nucleus.
Expecting to see chloroplasts in onion bulb cells: onion bulbs grow underground and don't photosynthesize.

days.guide: Read about cell theory; compare prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

questions.q: State the three parts of cell theory.
questions.a: All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells come from pre-existing cells.

questions.q: Main difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
questions.a: Eukaryotes have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotes don't.

days.guide: Prepare an onion slide; stain; sketch.

questions.q: What structures will you see in stained onion cells?
questions.a: Cell walls (rectangular outlines), nuclei (stained dark), cytoplasm — but no chloroplasts.

days.guide: Create a city analogy chart.

questions.q: Give a city analogy for the mitochondrion and the ribosome.
questions.a: Mitochondrion = power plant (releases energy as ATP); ribosome = factory workers building proteins.

days.guide: Compare nerve, muscle, and blood cells.

questions.q: How does a nerve cell's shape relate to its function?
questions.a: Long extensions (axons and dendrites) carry signals over long distances.

days.guide: Cell structure quiz.

questions.q: Which organelle packages and ships proteins?
questions.a: The Golgi apparatus.

weeks.assessment_key: Microscope sketch: proficient = labeled cell wall, nucleus, cytoplasm, magnification noted, accurate proportions. Quiz answers: nucleus (DNA), mitochondria (respiration), chloroplast (photosynthesis), ribosome (protein synthesis), ER (transport/synthesis), Golgi (packaging), cell membrane (controls entry/exit), cell wall (support, plants).

weeks.prep: Two raw eggs, white vinegar (shells dissolve in 24–48 hours — start before Day 2), corn syrup, water, kitchen scale, cups. Paper cutouts for the sodium-potassium pump.
misconceptions: Thinking solutes move in osmosis: in osmosis, WATER moves across a membrane toward higher solute concentration.
Confusing hypertonic and hypotonic: hypertonic solution has more solute than the cell (cell shrinks).
Believing all transport needs energy: diffusion and osmosis are passive.

days.guide: Draw the phospholipid bilayer.

questions.q: Why is the membrane called selectively permeable?
questions.a: It lets some substances (small nonpolar molecules, water) cross easily while blocking or regulating others (ions, large molecules).

days.guide: Remove shells in vinegar; weigh eggs; place one in water, one in corn syrup.

questions.q: Predict the mass change of an egg in corn syrup and in water.
questions.a: Corn syrup (hypertonic): mass decreases as water leaves. Water (hypotonic): mass increases as water enters.

days.guide: Calculate percent mass change.

questions.q: An egg went from 70 g to 80 g. Percent change?

days.guide: Model the sodium-potassium pump.

questions.q: Why does the sodium-potassium pump need ATP?
questions.a: It moves ions against their concentration gradients (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP) — active transport.

days.guide: Transport quiz.

questions.q: What happens to a red blood cell placed in pure water?
questions.a: Water enters and it swells and may burst (hypotonic).

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = testable question, hypothesis, identified variables (independent, dependent, controlled), clear data table and labeled graph, conclusion that uses data and explains the science, sources of error; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing graph or analysis; 1 = incomplete. Quiz answers: 1) Osmosis definition. 2) Hypertonic/hypotonic/isotonic. 3) Diffusion is passive. 4) Facilitated diffusion uses protein channels, no ATP. 5) Active transport uses ATP. 6) Endocytosis/exocytosis for large particles.

weeks.prep: Store-bought chicken or pig heart, dissection scissors, gloves, tray; wash surfaces and hands. Celery stalks with leaves, food coloring, cups.
misconceptions: Thinking blood is blue in veins: deoxygenated blood is dark red.
Believing body systems work alone: e.g., exercise needs muscular, circulatory, respiratory, and nervous systems together.
Mixing up xylem and phloem: xylem carries water up from roots; phloem carries sugars.

days.guide: Build a cell → tissue → organ → system → organism model using digestion.

questions.q: Give the levels of organization for the stomach.
questions.a: Smooth muscle cell → muscle tissue → stomach (organ) → digestive system → organism.

days.guide: Trace interactions during exercise.

questions.q: How do the respiratory and circulatory systems work together during exercise?
questions.a: Breathing rate increases to bring in more O₂ and remove CO₂; heart rate increases to deliver O₂ to muscles and carry CO₂ to lungs.

days.guide: Dissect the heart; identify chambers.

questions.q: Which chamber has the thickest wall and why?
questions.a: The left ventricle — it pumps blood to the entire body.

days.guide: Put celery in colored water; observe after several hours.

questions.q: What does the colored celery show?
questions.a: Xylem tubes carry water up the stem; the colored dots in a cross-section are xylem bundles.

days.guide: Systems quiz.

questions.q: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?
questions.a: The right side (right ventricle).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Levels of organization. 2) Blood path: body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body. 3) Exercise interactions. 4) Xylem vs. phloem. 5) Stomata exchange gases. Dissection sheet: proficient = labeled four chambers, aorta, valves (if visible), comparison of ventricle walls.

weeks.prep: Thermometer, stopwatch, safe exercise space (jumping jacks or stairs). Check with your child's doctor if any health condition limits exercise.
misconceptions: Thinking homeostasis means nothing changes: values fluctuate around a set point.
Confusing negative and positive feedback: negative feedback reverses change; positive feedback amplifies it.
Believing insulin raises blood sugar: insulin lowers it; glucagon raises it.

days.guide: Diagram negative feedback for temperature and glucose.

questions.q: Describe how the body responds when blood glucose rises after a meal.
questions.a: The pancreas releases insulin; cells take up glucose and the liver stores it as glycogen, lowering blood glucose back to set point.

questions.q: How does the body cool when temperature rises?
questions.a: Sweating and dilating skin blood vessels release heat.

days.guide: Measure heart and breathing rates at rest, during, and after exercise (every minute for 5 minutes after).

questions.q: Predict heart rate during and after exercise.
questions.a: It rises during exercise and gradually returns toward resting rate afterward.

days.guide: Graph results; explain return toward set point.

questions.q: Why does heart rate return to normal after exercise?
questions.a: Negative feedback: as CO₂ and O₂ demand return to normal, the nervous system slows heart and breathing rates.

days.guide: Compare positive and negative feedback.

questions.q: Give an example of positive feedback.
questions.a: Childbirth: contractions trigger more oxytocin, causing stronger contractions until birth (also blood clotting).

days.guide: Write the lab report.

questions.q: What is the set point for human body temperature?

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = testable question, hypothesis, identified variables (independent, dependent, controlled), clear data table and labeled graph, conclusion that uses data and explains the science, sources of error; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing graph or analysis; 1 = incomplete. Proficient analysis: identifies independent variable (activity level/time), dependent variables (heart and breathing rates), graphs data, explains the rise as increased demand for O₂ and CO₂ removal, and the recovery as negative feedback restoring set points.

weeks.prep: Pothos cutting with at least one node; jar of water; window light. Readings on stem cells and cancer (OpenStax Biology).
misconceptions: Thinking differentiated cells lose genes: they keep all genes but switch some on and off.
Believing cancer is 'catching': cancer results from mutations that disrupt cell-cycle control.
Assuming all stem cells are embryonic: adult stem cells (e.g., bone marrow) and induced pluripotent stem cells exist.

days.guide: Explain gene expression and differentiation.

questions.q: How can a muscle cell and a nerve cell have the same DNA but look different?
questions.a: They express different genes, making different proteins.

days.guide: Root a pothos cutting at a node; observe over weeks.

questions.q: Where do new roots grow from on a pothos cutting and why?
questions.a: From the nodes, where meristem-like cells can divide and differentiate into roots.

days.guide: Read about stem cell types.

questions.q: What is the difference between embryonic and adult stem cells?
questions.a: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (can become almost any cell); adult stem cells are more limited (e.g., blood stem cells make blood cells).

days.guide: Explain cancer as checkpoint failure.

questions.q: How does cancer develop?
questions.a: Mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle (e.g., checkpoints, tumor suppressors like p53) let cells divide uncontrollably, forming tumors.

days.guide: Differentiation quiz.

questions.q: What is a medical use of stem cells today?
questions.a: Bone marrow (hematopoietic stem cell) transplants for leukemia.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Differentiation = gene expression. 2) Stem cell definition. 3) Embryonic vs. adult vs. iPS. 4) Cell cycle checkpoints. 5) Cancer = uncontrolled division. 6) Plant meristems.

weeks.prep: 3% hydrogen peroxide, raw potato cubes (or liver), test tubes or small cups, ruler, thermometer; ice water, room temperature, and boiled potato. Goggles. Prepare the Unit 5 review and test.
misconceptions: Thinking enzymes are used up: enzymes are reusable catalysts.
Believing 'hotter is always faster': past the optimum, enzymes denature and stop working.
Confusing denaturing with killing: denaturing is a change in a protein's shape that destroys its active site.

days.guide: Draw lock-and-key and induced fit.

questions.q: Why is each enzyme specific to its substrate?
questions.a: The active site's shape fits only certain substrates.

days.guide: Test catalase at three temperatures; measure foam height.

questions.q: What reaction does catalase speed up?
questions.a: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (the bubbles are oxygen).

questions.q: Predict foam heights for cold, room-temperature, and boiled potato.
questions.a: Cold: moderate/less; room/warm: most; boiled: little or none.

days.guide: Graph and explain.

questions.q: Why does boiled potato produce almost no foam?
questions.a: High heat denatured the catalase, changing the active site's shape so it can't bind H₂O₂.

days.guide: Unit 5 review guide.

questions.q: Name the four levels of organization from cell to system.
questions.a: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test.

questions.q: What does a catalyst do?
questions.a: It speeds up a reaction by lowering activation energy without being used up.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = testable question, hypothesis, identified variables (independent, dependent, controlled), clear data table and labeled graph, conclusion that uses data and explains the science, sources of error; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing graph or analysis; 1 = incomplete. Unit 5 test sample answers: cell theory; organelle functions; prokaryote vs. eukaryote; osmosis predictions; active transport; heart blood path; feedback loops (insulin/glucagon); positive vs. negative feedback; differentiation; enzymes and denaturation. Scoring: 80%+ proficient.

weeks.prep: Local news articles on invasive species or pollution; pH strips; clean jars for water samples (tap, rain, pond/creek — wear gloves at natural water). Monarch data (Xerces Society Western Monarch Count).
misconceptions: Thinking invasive = any non-native species: invasive species cause harm and spread aggressively; many non-natives are harmless.
Assuming pH alone shows water is safe: many pollutants don't change pH.
Blaming one cause for monarch decline: habitat loss (milkweed and overwintering sites), pesticides, and climate all contribute.

days.guide: Teach HIPPO with an example of each.

questions.q: What does HIPPO stand for?
questions.a: Habitat loss, Invasive species, Pollution, Population (human growth), Overharvesting.

days.guide: Research a California invasive species.

questions.q: How do quagga mussels harm California waterways?
questions.a: They spread rapidly (since arriving in Lake Mead in 2007), clog water pipes and infrastructure, and filter out plankton that native food webs depend on.

days.guide: Test water samples with pH strips.

questions.q: Drinking water pH guidelines are about 6.5–8.5. A creek sample reads 5.0. What might this mean?
questions.a: It is acidic — possibly from acid runoff or pollution; more testing is needed.

days.guide: Analyze monarch decline data.

questions.q: What happened to the western monarch overwintering count?
questions.a: It fell from millions in the 1980s to fewer than 2,000 butterflies counted in 2020, with partial rebounds in some later years.

days.guide: Human-impacts quiz.

questions.q: Give one action that helps monarchs.
questions.a: Plant native milkweed and nectar flowers, reduce pesticide use, protect overwintering groves.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) HIPPO components. 2) Invasive species example and impact. 3) Biomagnification of pollutants up food chains. 4) Overharvesting example (e.g., abalone in California). 5) Monarch decline causes. 6) Habitat fragmentation definition.

weeks.prep: Two identical jars, two thermometers, plastic wrap, a lamp (or sunlight), timer. En-ROADS climate simulator (en-roads.climateinteractive.org). Reading on coral bleaching and Sierra snowpack.
misconceptions: Confusing weather and climate: weather is short-term; climate is long-term averages.
Thinking the greenhouse effect is bad in itself: the natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable; the problem is its enhancement by added greenhouse gases.
Mixing up the ozone hole with climate change: they are different problems.

days.guide: Measure temperature in covered vs. uncovered jars every 2 minutes for 20 minutes.

questions.q: Predict which jar warms more and why.
questions.a: The covered jar — the plastic traps warm air (a partial model of greenhouse gases trapping heat).

days.guide: Use En-ROADS to test scenarios.

questions.q: Which En-ROADS changes reduce projected warming most?
questions.a: Large changes such as carbon pricing and reducing coal/oil use, along with energy efficiency and renewables (answers vary; the key is reducing emissions).

days.guide: Analyze coral reefs and Sierra snowpack.

questions.q: What causes coral bleaching?
questions.a: Warm water stresses corals, which expel their symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae), turning white and starving.

questions.q: Why does Sierra snowpack matter to California?
questions.a: It acts as natural water storage, supplying roughly 30% of the state's water as it melts; warming causes less snow and earlier melt.

days.guide: Evaluate claims about kelp forests shifting to urchin barrens.

questions.q: What caused much of Northern California's bull kelp loss after 2014?
questions.a: A marine heatwave plus sea star wasting disease, which killed sunflower sea stars (urchin predators), letting purple urchins explode and graze kelp — more than 90% loss in some areas.

days.guide: Quiz on climate and ecosystems.

questions.q: Name two major greenhouse gases.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide and methane (also water vapor, nitrous oxide).

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = testable question, hypothesis, identified variables (independent, dependent, controlled), clear data table and labeled graph, conclusion that uses data and explains the science, sources of error; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing graph or analysis; 1 = incomplete. Quiz answers: 1) Greenhouse effect. 2) CO₂ and methane sources. 3) Coral bleaching. 4) Snowpack and water supply. 5) Kelp-urchin shift. 6) Weather vs. climate.

weeks.prep: Local environmental reports (county or state parks, Xerces Society, CA Department of Fish and Wildlife). Engineering design process poster: define, research, brainstorm, prototype, test, iterate.
misconceptions: Defining the problem as a solution ('we need a bee hotel'): define the need ('native bees lack nesting sites in our neighborhood').
Vague criteria ('it should work well'): make criteria measurable (e.g., 'attracts at least 3 bee species in 4 weeks').
Ignoring constraints such as cost, time, and safety.

days.guide: Choose a local biodiversity problem.

questions.q: What makes a good engineering problem for this project?
questions.a: Specific, local, connected to biodiversity, and realistically addressable with available resources.

days.guide: Define criteria and constraints.

questions.q: What is the difference between a criterion and a constraint?
questions.a: A criterion is a goal the solution should meet (what success looks like); a constraint is a limit (cost, time, materials).

days.guide: Research existing solutions.

questions.q: Name one existing solution to native pollinator decline.
questions.a: Planting native flowering plants and pollinator gardens (also nesting habitats, reduced pesticides).

days.guide: Break the problem into 3–4 sub-problems and rank them.

questions.q: Why break a big problem into sub-problems?
questions.a: Smaller parts are easier to solve and test, and ranking helps focus effort on what matters most.

days.guide: Submit the problem statement for feedback; revise.

questions.q: Write a sample problem statement.
questions.a: 'Native bees in our neighborhood lack nesting sites and early-spring flowers; we need a low-cost solution under $30 that increases visits by native bees.'

weeks.assessment_key: Problem statement rubric: 4 = specific local problem with evidence, at least three measurable criteria and three realistic constraints, sub-problems ranked with reasoning; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = vague criteria; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Spreadsheet; recycled materials (cans, untreated wood blocks, hollow stems, cardboard tubes) for a prototype; drill (adult use) for bee-hotel holes.
misconceptions: Picking the first idea: evaluate multiple solutions with a decision matrix.
Simulations with unrealistic numbers: base rates on research data.
Treating failure as the end: iteration is part of engineering.

days.guide: Brainstorm three solutions; score with a decision matrix.

questions.q: What is a decision matrix?
questions.a: A table that scores each solution against weighted criteria to compare options objectively.

days.guide: Build a prototype or detailed plan.

questions.q: What hole diameters suit native bee hotels?
questions.a: A range of roughly 3–10 mm, about 10–15 cm deep, with closed backs (various species prefer different sizes).

days.guide: Create a spreadsheet simulation of the solution's effect on a population.

questions.q: If a bee population grows 15% per year with the solution vs. 2% without, starting at 100, what are populations after 3 years?

days.guide: Revise and document changes.

questions.q: Why document design changes?
questions.a: To show what was learned from testing and justify decisions.

days.guide: 3-minute check-in presentation; record feedback.

questions.q: What three items should the check-in include?
questions.a: The design, the simulation graph, and revisions with reasons.

weeks.assessment_key: Prototype/design rubric: 4 = design clearly addresses criteria and constraints, decision matrix justifies choice, simulation uses researched values and shows predicted impact, revisions documented with reasons; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = little iteration or unjustified simulation; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Presentation software; timer; invite family or co-op audience for Day 5.
misconceptions: Presenting only benefits: credible engineering presentations discuss trade-offs and limitations.
Ignoring stakeholders (neighbors, landowners, wildlife agencies).
Reading slides instead of explaining data.

days.guide: Evaluate costs, benefits, trade-offs.

questions.q: Give a trade-off for a pollinator garden.
questions.a: Higher water use or initial cost vs. long-term biodiversity benefit; native plants may need establishment watering but less water later.

days.guide: Consider stakeholders; revise.

questions.q: Name three stakeholders for a neighborhood habitat project.
questions.a: Homeowners/neighbors, local government or HOA, wildlife agencies or conservation groups (also gardeners, beekeepers).

days.guide: Prepare a 6-minute presentation.

questions.q: What sections should the presentation include?
questions.a: Problem, data, design, simulation results, trade-offs, and next steps.

days.guide: Rehearse twice with a timer; revise.

questions.q: How do you make data clear in a presentation?
questions.a: Use simple labeled graphs and state the key takeaway aloud.

days.guide: Present to an audience.

questions.q: How should you respond to a question you can't answer?
questions.a: Acknowledge it, explain how you could find out, and note it as future work.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = clearly defined problem with data, design and simulation explained, trade-offs and stakeholders addressed, visuals effective, within 6 minutes, answers questions; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing trade-offs or data; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Final review guide; flashcards; practice exam. Plan a 2-hour exam block.
misconceptions: Studying only by re-reading: test yourself by redrawing models and solving problems.
Skipping Unit 1–2 content: the final is cumulative.
Leaving out units in calculations.

days.guide: Redraw food web, energy pyramid, photosynthesis, respiration, and carbon cycle models; check them.

questions.q: Which process removes CO₂ from the atmosphere?
questions.a: Photosynthesis (also ocean absorption).

days.guide: Practice 20 genetics and evolution problems.

questions.q: Cross XᴴXʰ × XᴴY. Chance a son has hemophilia?
If 36 of 100 mice show a recessive phenotype, is the trait likely to increase if it's camouflaging?
questions.a: Yes — natural selection would increase a trait that improves survival.

days.guide: Review homeostasis feedback loops and human-impact cases.

questions.q: What hormone raises blood glucose?
questions.a: Glucagon.

days.guide: Practice exam; review errors.

questions.q: Percent change from 50 g to 45 g?

days.guide: Final exam.

questions.q: What is the main source of new genetic variation?
questions.a: Mutation (with recombination in sexual reproduction).

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam: cumulative items scored with unit keys (energy pyramids, photosynthesis/respiration, carbon cycle, evidence for evolution, natural selection, Punnett squares, protein synthesis, membrane transport, homeostasis, human impacts). Constructed responses scored with the CER rubric. 90%+ A, 80–89 B, 70–79 C.

VAPA.overview: VAPA 9 is a high-school foundations of visual art course: drawing (contour, proportion, value, perspective), color and painting, printmaking and graphic design, sculpture and clay, portraiture across cultures, photography, collage, digital art and a self-directed body of work, ending in a curated exhibition. Each day follows look–practice–make: study a master work or demonstration, practice a technique in the sketchbook, then apply it to a finished piece; use the Feldman method (describe, analyze, interpret, judge) for all critiques. The parent's role is coach and critic: set up materials and lighting, ask the check questions, and praise specific choices. Keep everything — the semester and final portfolios depend on the sketchbook and process photos.

weeks.prep: 9×12 sketchbook, graphite pencils 2H–6B, kneaded eraser, mirror, shoe, plant, kitchen utensils, banana, paper bag. Explain the pencil scale: H = harder/lighter, B = softer/darker.
misconceptions: Drawing symbols ('what an eye looks like') instead of observing. Correct: look at the subject most of the time.
Starting with 6B. Correct: begin lightly with 2H/HB and build darks with B pencils.

days.guide: Cover lettering in three styles; draw the non-dominant hand for 10 minutes.

questions.q: What does 'H' and 'B' mean on a pencil?
questions.a: H = hard (lighter lines), B = black/soft (darker lines); higher numbers mean more of that quality.

days.guide: Five 3-minute blind contours (shoe, plant, face in mirror).

questions.q: What is blind contour drawing?
questions.a: Drawing the edges of a subject while looking only at the subject, never the paper.

days.guide: Modified contour of utensils, glancing at the paper only at corners.

questions.q: How is modified contour different from blind contour?
questions.a: You may glance at the paper occasionally (e.g., at corners or junctions) to keep proportions, but mostly look at the subject.

days.guide: Cross-contour banana and crumpled bag.

questions.q: What does cross-contour show that outline doesn't?
questions.a: The surface form and volume, using lines that wrap around the object.

days.guide: Choose the best contour drawing; write a 5-sentence reflection.

questions.q: What is a contour?
questions.a: The edge of a form, including outer edges and interior edges like folds or overlaps.

weeks.assessment_key: Sketchbook check: 4 = 10+ contour drawings (hand, 5 blind, modified, 2 cross-contour, more) showing careful observation, varied line weight, and a 5-sentence reflection naming a specific improvement; 3 = 10 drawings, general reflection; 2 = 6–9 drawings; 1 = fewer than 6.

weeks.prep: Sketchbook, pencil, timer, three household objects, a chair and plant. Teach sighting: arm straight, close one eye, pencil as a measuring stick.
misconceptions: Bending the elbow while sighting. Correct: lock the arm straight so measurements stay consistent.
Focusing on details too early. Correct: block in big shapes and proportions first.

days.guide: Block in a still life with basic shapes, then refine.

questions.q: Why start with geometric shapes?
questions.a: They establish proportion, placement and structure before details.

days.guide: Sight-measure a chair.

questions.q: How does sighting work?
questions.a: Hold the pencil at arm's length, align the tip with one edge and mark with the thumb to measure a unit, then compare other lengths and angles to it.

days.guide: Twenty 30-second gesture drawings.

questions.q: What should a gesture drawing capture?
questions.a: The action, movement and overall pose — the 'line of action' — not details.

days.guide: Draw only the negative spaces around a chair or plant.

questions.q: What is negative space?
questions.a: The empty space around and between objects.

days.guide: 45-minute proportion drawing; self-check with sighting.

questions.q: Why does drawing negative space fix errors?
questions.a: Negative shapes are unfamiliar, so you draw what you see instead of what you assume.

weeks.assessment_key: Proportion still life: 4 = accurate relative sizes and placement verified by sighting, correct ellipses/angles, refined edges, composition fills the page; 3 = minor proportion errors; 2 = noticeable distortions; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Pencils 2H–6B, blending stump, fine-tip pen, white egg, lamp, phone camera, sphere/cube/cylinder objects (ball, box, can).
misconceptions: Blending everything with a finger. Correct: use a stump or tissue; fingers leave oils and smudges.
Making the cast shadow lighter than the form shadow. Correct: the cast shadow's core (near the object) is usually the darkest area.

days.guide: 9-step value scales in four techniques.

questions.q: Name four shading techniques.
questions.a: Blending, hatching, cross-hatching, stippling.

days.guide: Render sphere, cube, cylinder with five lighting zones.

questions.q: List the five parts of light on a form.
questions.a: Highlight, midtone (light), core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow.

days.guide: Photograph an egg from three angles; draw the best.

questions.q: Why use a single light source?
questions.a: It creates clear, consistent shadows that reveal form.

days.guide: Shade the egg in pen with hatching only.

questions.q: How do you create darker values with pen?
questions.a: Lines closer together, layered cross-hatching or thicker lines.

days.guide: Critique comparing pencil and pen versions.

questions.q: What vocabulary describes the difference?
questions.a: Value range, contrast, texture, line quality.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: value scales smooth with 9 distinct steps in each technique (4); forms show all five light zones (4); egg drawings accurate with consistent light (4); critique uses element vocabulary (4). Proficient = 3+ in each.

weeks.prep: 3–5 white objects (eggs, mugs, bowls, crumpled paper), one strong lamp, good drawing paper.
misconceptions: Using too little contrast. Correct: commit to the darkest darks early to set the range.
Outlining shadows. Correct: shadows have soft or hard edges, not outlines.

days.guide: Arrange objects; three thumbnails; pick one.

questions.q: What makes a strong still-life composition?
