questions.a: Overlapping objects, varied heights, an odd number of objects, asymmetrical balance and a clear focal point.

days.guide: Block in with sighting.

questions.q: Why block in lightly?
questions.a: So proportions can be corrected easily.

days.guide: Lay in darks and lights, then midtones.

questions.q: Why establish darks first?
questions.a: It sets the full value range so midtones can be judged against it.

days.guide: Refine edges, textures, cast shadows.

questions.q: What is edge quality?
questions.a: How sharp or soft a transition is; varying edges creates depth and focus.

days.guide: Write criteria and self-evaluate.

questions.q: Give an example of a strong success criterion.
questions.a: 'The drawing includes at least 7 distinct values from white to near black.'

weeks.assessment_key: Still life rubric: Composition (thumbnail-based, balanced), Proportion (accurate), Value (full range, form zones on each object), Edges/Texture (varied, believable), Craftsmanship. 4 levels each; proficient = 3+. Self-written criteria scored for specificity.

weeks.prep: Crayons and thin paper for rubbings; vine and compressed charcoal; India ink, brush, three cups for dilutions; spray fixative or hairspray (use outdoors).
misconceptions: Pressing hard with compressed charcoal at the start. Correct: start with vine charcoal (soft, erasable), then add compressed for darks.
Ink washes too dark. Correct: test dilutions on scrap first.

days.guide: Ten labeled crayon rubbings (frottage).

questions.q: What is frottage?
questions.a: Making a rubbing of a textured surface with a crayon or pencil on paper.

days.guide: Close-up texture studies of bark, fabric, metal.

questions.q: How can you draw metal's texture?
questions.a: High contrast, sharp highlights and reflections next to dark areas.

days.guide: Charcoal paper bag using subtractive eraser drawing.

questions.q: What is subtractive drawing?
questions.a: Covering the paper with a tone, then erasing to create lights.

days.guide: Ink-wash houseplant with three dilutions.

questions.q: How do you make a light ink wash?
questions.a: Mix a small amount of ink with a lot of water.

days.guide: Assemble best three drawings; document growth.

questions.q: Why document with photos and captions?
questions.a: It records growth and process for the portfolio.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 portfolio review: 4 = three strong drawings showing contour, proportion, value and texture, clear photos with captions describing technique and growth; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = weak documentation; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Ruler, pencil, paper; printout of Leonardo's 'The Last Supper' (c. 1495–98).
misconceptions: Placing the vanishing point off the horizon. Correct: the VP always sits on the horizon line (eye level).
Drawing vertical lines toward the VP in one-point. Correct: verticals stay vertical; only orthogonals converge.

days.guide: Trace orthogonals on 'The Last Supper' to find the VP.

questions.q: Where is the vanishing point in 'The Last Supper'?
questions.a: At Christ's head (near his right temple), at the center, drawing all eyes to him.

days.guide: Floating boxes in one-point.

questions.q: What are orthogonals?
questions.a: Lines that recede toward the vanishing point.

days.guide: Draw a hallway or room interior.

questions.q: Where do the floor and ceiling lines meet?
questions.a: They converge at the vanishing point.

days.guide: Draw a one-point street scene.

questions.q: How do windows change as buildings recede?
questions.a: They get smaller and closer together, following orthogonals.

days.guide: Add value and details.

questions.q: How does value add depth?
questions.a: Contrast and darker values in front, lighter in distance, plus shadows, make space believable.

weeks.assessment_key: One-point drawing: 4 = single VP on horizon line, all orthogonals converge accurately, verticals/horizontals true, detail and value add depth; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = many errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Ruler, long paper (tape two sheets) for far-apart vanishing points.
misconceptions: VPs too close, causing distortion. Correct: place them far apart, even off the page.
Forgetting eye level. Correct: you see tops of objects below the horizon and bottoms above.

days.guide: Two-point boxes at different heights.

questions.q: What stays vertical in two-point perspective?
questions.a: All vertical edges.

days.guide: Draw your house or a local building.

questions.q: How many VPs does a building corner facing you use?
questions.a: Two — one for each side receding away.

days.guide: Bird's-eye and worm's-eye boxes (three-point).

questions.q: What is a bird's-eye view?
questions.a: Looking down from high above; verticals converge to a third vanishing point below.

days.guide: Imaginary city block.

questions.q: How can you add variety to a city block?
questions.a: Vary building heights, rooflines, windows, signs and overlapping.

days.guide: Self-critique with checklist.

questions.q: What's one item on your checklist?
questions.a: All horizontal edges go to the correct VP; verticals are vertical.

weeks.assessment_key: Two-point city drawing: 4 = two VPs on horizon, all edges converge correctly, multiple buildings with overlap, varied detail, clean ruler lines; 3 = minor errors; 2 = frequent errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Pencils, landscape photos; images of a Song dynasty landscape (e.g., Fan Kuan's 'Travelers among Mountains and Streams,' c. 1000, or Guo Xi's 'Early Spring,' 1072) and Hudson River School paintings (Thomas Cole, Albert Bierstadt, Frederic Church).
misconceptions: Drawing distant objects as dark and detailed as near ones. Correct: distant objects are lighter, bluer, lower contrast and less detailed.
Thinking linear perspective is the only way to show depth. Correct: Chinese painters used mist, overlapping and vertical placement.

days.guide: Study a Song landscape; identify mist and depth.

questions.q: How do Song landscape painters show depth?
questions.a: Mist separating foreground, middle and background; overlapping forms; placing distant elements higher; fading ink tones.

days.guide: Draw a landscape outdoors with three grounds.

questions.q: Define foreground, middle ground, background.
questions.a: Areas closest, in the middle and farthest from the viewer.

days.guide: Redo the landscape with value fading in distance.

questions.q: What is atmospheric perspective?
questions.a: Distant objects appear lighter, cooler (bluer), blurrier and lower in contrast because of air and particles.

days.guide: Compare Chinese and Hudson River School landscapes in writing.

questions.q: Name one difference.
questions.a: Song paintings use ink, vertical scrolls, mist and a moving viewpoint; Hudson River School uses oil paint, dramatic light and realistic detail celebrating the American wilderness.

days.guide: Unit 2 review.

questions.q: Which perspective techniques have you used?
questions.a: One-point, two-point, three-point and atmospheric perspective.

weeks.assessment_key: Landscape drawing and comparison: drawing 4 = clear foreground/middle/background with atmospheric value change; comparison 4 = accurate details of both traditions (medium, format, depth techniques, purpose), with visual evidence and a conclusion; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = superficial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Tempera or acrylic primaries plus white and black, palette, brushes, water, paper. Images of Picasso Blue Period works ('The Old Guitarist,' 1903–04). Write a 10-question color quiz.
misconceptions: Muddy mixtures from too many colors. Correct: mix two at a time; clean brushes.
Confusing triadic and complementary. Correct: triadic = three evenly spaced; complementary = two opposites.

days.guide: Mix a 12-step color wheel.

questions.q: How do you mix a tertiary color?
questions.a: Mix a primary with a neighboring secondary, e.g., blue + green = blue-green.

days.guide: Tint and shade scales.

questions.q: Tint vs. shade?
questions.a: Tint = color + white; shade = color + black.

days.guide: Four squares in complementary, analogous, triadic, monochromatic.

questions.q: Give a triadic scheme.
questions.a: Red, yellow, blue (or orange, green, violet).

days.guide: Analyze Blue Period color and mood.

questions.q: Why did Picasso use blue in this period?
questions.a: Blues express melancholy and poverty; the period followed the suicide of his friend Carlos Casagemas.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Name a complementary pair.
questions.a: Red–green, blue–orange, yellow–violet.

weeks.assessment_key: Color quiz key: 1) primaries red, yellow, blue 2) secondaries orange, green, violet 3) tertiary definition 4) complementary = opposite 5) analogous = adjacent 6) triadic = 3 evenly spaced 7) monochromatic = one hue + tints/shades 8) tint 9) shade 10) warm vs cool colors. Color wheel: 12 accurate, evenly mixed segments.

weeks.prep: Watercolor set, watercolor paper (140 lb), salt, white crayon, paper towels, two water jars. Safety: don't pour pigment water down storm drains; dispose in a sink or let it evaporate and trash solids.
misconceptions: Overworking wet paint. Correct: let layers dry before glazing; work quickly in washes.
Using white paint for lights. Correct: in transparent watercolor, the paper is the white — plan and save it.

days.guide: Safe handling and cleanup.

questions.q: Why not pour paint water into a storm drain?
questions.a: Storm drains flow untreated into creeks and the ocean; pigments can pollute water.

days.guide: Paint the sampler grid of six techniques.

questions.q: What is glazing?
questions.a: Painting a transparent layer over a dry layer to change color or value.

days.guide: Three sky studies.

questions.q: What technique makes soft clouds?
questions.a: Wet-on-wet, or lifting color with a tissue while wet.

days.guide: Botanical study with glazing.

questions.q: How do you keep highlights white?
questions.a: Paint around them, use wax resist or lift.

days.guide: Label the sampler; choose a technique.

questions.q: What does salt do on wet watercolor?
questions.a: It absorbs pigment and water, creating starburst textures.

weeks.assessment_key: Technique sampler: 6 labeled techniques each clearly demonstrated (wet-on-wet soft bleeds, graded wash smooth, glazing visible layers, salt texture, lifting lights, wax resist). 6/6 proficient.

weeks.prep: Paints, canvas board or heavy paper; images of Monet's 'Haystacks' (Grainstacks) series (1890–91).
misconceptions: Blending colors smoothly on the canvas. Correct: Impressionist broken color places dabs side by side to mix optically.
Thinking shadows are gray/black. Correct: Impressionists painted colored shadows (often blues and violets).

days.guide: Study 'Haystacks' and explain how light changes color.

questions.q: Why did Monet paint the same subject many times?
questions.a: To capture how changing light, weather and seasons alter color and atmosphere.

days.guide: Three small studies of one view at different times.

questions.q: How does color change from midday to sunset?
questions.a: Midday light is cooler and brighter with short shadows; sunset is warmer (orange/pink) with long, blue-violet shadows.

days.guide: Start a landscape in broken color.

questions.q: What is broken color?
questions.a: Short strokes of unmixed or lightly mixed color placed side by side so the eye blends them.

days.guide: Finish the landscape.

questions.q: What is plein air painting?
questions.a: Painting outdoors directly from the scene.

days.guide: Write an interpretation of a Monet painting citing visual evidence.

questions.q: Interpret a Monet sunset haystack.
questions.a: Example: warm oranges and long violet shadows suggest the quiet end of a day and the passing of time, shown by the glowing edges where low sun hits the stack.

weeks.assessment_key: Landscape painting: 4 = broken-color brushwork, color reflects a specific time of day, colored shadows, three grounds; interpretation 4 = claim about meaning/mood supported by at least three specific visual details (color, brushwork, light); 3 = two details; 2 = description only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Paints, paper; images of Matisse 'Woman with a Hat' (1905), Munch 'The Scream' (1893), Kirchner's Berlin street scenes (1913–15).
misconceptions: Thinking arbitrary color is random. Correct: Fauves and Expressionists chose non-naturalistic color deliberately for emotion.
Confusing Fauvism and Expressionism. Correct: Fauvism (France) emphasized bold joyous color; German Expressionism emphasized anxiety and inner feeling with distortion.

days.guide: Analyze 'Woman with a Hat'; list arbitrary colors.

questions.q: Why were the Fauves called 'wild beasts'?
questions.a: A critic at the 1905 Salon d'Automne was shocked by their violent, non-natural colors and called them 'fauves.'

days.guide: Analyze 'The Scream' and Kirchner's street scenes.

questions.q: How does Munch show anxiety in 'The Scream'?
questions.a: Swirling blood-orange sky, distorted figure, wavy lines and a sharply angled bridge create a sense of panic.

days.guide: Paint a familiar place in arbitrary colors for a mood.

questions.q: Which colors might express calm?
questions.a: Cool blues, greens and soft violets, with smooth strokes.

days.guide: Finish and title.

questions.q: Why does a title matter?
questions.a: It guides the viewer's interpretation.

days.guide: Write an artist statement explaining color choices.

questions.q: What is arbitrary color?
questions.a: Color chosen for expression rather than to match reality.

weeks.assessment_key: Expressive painting and statement: 4 = bold intentional arbitrary color clearly creating a named mood, expressive brushwork, statement links specific color choices to the mood and to Fauvist/Expressionist influence; 3 = mood clear, weaker explanation; 2 = colors mostly naturalistic; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Finished paintings from weeks 11–12; image of a Frida Kahlo painting (e.g., 'The Two Fridas,' 1939).
misconceptions: Jumping to judgment first. Correct: describe and analyze before interpreting and judging.
Revising by starting over. Correct: target specific issues identified in critique.

days.guide: Teach Feldman's four steps; critique a Kahlo painting.

questions.q: Interpret 'The Two Fridas.'
questions.a: Two seated Fridas — one in a European dress, one in Tehuana dress — share a heart connected by a vein, suggesting her dual heritage and the emotional pain of her divorce from Diego Rivera.

days.guide: Critique both of your paintings.

questions.q: What do you discuss in 'Analyze'?
questions.a: How elements and principles (color, line, balance, emphasis) are organized.

days.guide: Revise one painting.

questions.q: What did you change and why?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers cite the critique.

days.guide: Photograph and document work.

questions.q: How should you photograph flat art?
questions.a: Square to the camera, even natural light, no glare, cropped to the edges.

days.guide: Unit 3 portfolio check.

questions.q: Which painting best shows growth?
questions.a: Answers vary; give evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Critique writing: 4 = all four Feldman steps with specific evidence for the Kahlo and own paintings; revised painting shows clear improvement tied to critique; 3 = steps present, evidence thin; 2 = missing steps; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Magazines, scissors, glue, colored paper. List of principles: balance, emphasis, contrast, movement, rhythm, pattern, proportion/scale, unity, variety.
misconceptions: Confusing elements and principles. Correct: elements (line, shape, form, color, value, texture, space) are the tools; principles are how they're arranged.
Thinking asymmetrical means unbalanced. Correct: asymmetrical balance uses different elements of equal visual weight.

days.guide: Find magazine examples of each principle.

questions.q: Define emphasis.
questions.a: Creating a focal point that draws the viewer's eye first.

days.guide: Cut-paper symmetrical, asymmetrical, radial balance.

questions.q: Give an example of radial balance.
questions.a: A flower, a mandala or a rose window — designs radiate from a center.

days.guide: Contrast composition with a focal point.

questions.q: Name two ways to create emphasis.
questions.a: Contrast in color or value, isolation, placement, size, converging lines.

days.guide: Rhythm/pattern design.

questions.q: Difference between pattern and rhythm?
questions.a: Pattern is a repeated element; rhythm is the visual movement created by repetition (regular, alternating, progressive).

days.guide: Principles quiz.

questions.q: What is unity?
questions.a: The sense that all parts of an artwork belong together.

weeks.assessment_key: Principles quiz key: balance (symmetrical/asymmetrical/radial), emphasis (focal point), contrast, movement (path of the eye), rhythm (repetition creating movement), pattern (repeated motif), proportion/scale, unity (wholeness), variety (difference for interest); identify elements vs principles. Reference sheet: one labeled example per principle.

weeks.prep: Foam printing plates (or soft-cut linoleum), pencil; images of Hokusai's 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa' (c. 1830–32) and José Guadalupe Posada's calaveras (e.g., 'La Calavera Catrina'); Taller de Gráfica Popular prints (founded 1937).
misconceptions: Forgetting prints reverse. Correct: transfer the design in mirror image, especially lettering.
Thinking in lines only. Correct: relief prints are about bold black and white shapes.

days.guide: Study 'The Great Wave' and ukiyo-e.

questions.q: What does ukiyo-e mean and how were prints made?
questions.a: 'Pictures of the floating world'; designers, carvers and printers collaborated, carving a separate woodblock for each color.

days.guide: Study Posada and the TGP.

questions.q: What are Posada's calaveras?
questions.a: Satirical skeleton images in prints for popular broadsheets mocking society and politics in Mexico; 'La Calavera Catrina' satirized upper-class pretensions.

days.guide: Three thumbnails thinking in black and white.

questions.q: In relief printing, what prints — the raised or carved areas?
questions.a: The raised (uncarved) surface takes ink and prints; carved areas stay paper-colored.

days.guide: Transfer in reverse to a foam plate.

questions.q: How do you reverse a design?
questions.a: Trace it, flip the tracing over and transfer, or draw it in mirror image.

days.guide: Explain printmaking as public art.

questions.q: Why is printmaking good for public messages?
questions.a: Multiple copies can be made cheaply and distributed widely as posters and broadsheets.

weeks.assessment_key: Print design: 4 = strong black/white shape balance, community theme, reversed text/design, ready to carve; written explanation cites ukiyo-e mass production and Posada/TGP political prints as public art; 3 = minor issues; 2 = too detailed/linear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Carving tools (or pencil/ballpoint for foam), bench hook, block printing ink (water-based), brayer, inking plate (glass or tray), paper, spoon or baren.
misconceptions: Carving toward the hand. Correct: always carve away from the body and hold the block behind the tool (use a bench hook).
Over-inking. Correct: roll a thin, even layer that 'hisses' like velvet.

days.guide: Tool safety demonstration.

questions.q: What is the most important carving safety rule?
questions.a: Always carve away from your hands and body.

days.guide: Carve or press the plate.

questions.q: Why carve shallow first?
questions.a: You can always remove more, but can't add material back.

days.guide: Pull a proof; adjust.

questions.q: What is a proof?
questions.a: A test print to check the image before printing the edition.

days.guide: Print an edition of 5; number and sign.

questions.q: How is an edition numbered and signed?
questions.a: In pencil below the image: edition number like 1/5 at left, title in center, signature (and date) at right.

days.guide: Select the best print; critique.

questions.q: What makes a 'good' print in an edition?
questions.a: Even ink coverage, clean margins, consistent across copies.

weeks.assessment_key: Print edition: 4 = 5 consistent, clean prints with even inking and margins, correctly numbered (1/5–5/5), titled and signed in pencil; critique evaluates the best print; 3 = minor inconsistencies; 2 = uneven or unsigned; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Poster board or a free design app, markers; Library of Congress WPA poster collection (1936–43). Pick a real community event.
misconceptions: Making all text the same size. Correct: create hierarchy — title largest, key info next, details smallest.
Using too many colors and fonts. Correct: limit to three colors and two typefaces.

days.guide: Analyze five WPA posters.

questions.q: What is visual hierarchy?
questions.a: Arranging elements by size, color and placement so viewers notice the most important information first.

days.guide: Six thumbnails for a real event.

questions.q: What information must an event poster include?
questions.a: What, when, where (and who/how to join).

days.guide: Hand-letter the title in two styles.

questions.q: How can lettering show mood?
questions.a: Bold blocky letters feel strong; flowing script feels elegant; playful letters feel fun.

days.guide: Final 11×17 poster in three colors.

questions.q: Why limit the palette?
questions.a: It unifies the design and matches how WPA silkscreen posters were printed.

days.guide: 5-second test with a fresh viewer.

questions.q: What does the 5-second test check?
questions.a: Whether the key information (event, date, place) is readable at a glance.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric: Hierarchy (title, then date/place, then details), Readability (passes 5-second test), Design principles (balance, emphasis, unity), Limited palette and lettering. 4 levels; proficient = 3+.

weeks.prep: All semester work, phone camera, neutral backdrop (white sheet or wall), natural light.
misconceptions: Choosing only one medium. Correct: show range.
Vague reflections. Correct: state goal, process and specific changes.

days.guide: Select six pieces showing range.

questions.q: Why show range?
questions.a: It demonstrates skills across media and techniques.

days.guide: Photograph squarely in natural light; crop/label.

questions.q: How do you avoid distortion when photographing art?
questions.a: Hold the camera parallel to the artwork, centered, and fill the frame.

days.guide: 100-word reflections.

questions.q: What three questions should each reflection answer?
questions.a: What was the goal? What was the process? What would you change?

days.guide: Present with an in-depth Feldman critique.

questions.q: What are the four Feldman steps?
questions.a: Describe, analyze, interpret, judge.

days.guide: Compare week 1 to recent drawing; write three goals.

questions.q: Give an example of a strong art goal.
questions.a: 'Improve proportion accuracy by doing three sighting drawings per week.'

weeks.assessment_key: Semester portfolio: 4 = six well-documented pieces across 4+ media, 100-word reflections with goal/process/change, confident presentation with complete Feldman critique, three specific goals; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = thin reflections; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Cardstock, scissors, glue, craft knife and cutting mat (supervise knife use), lamp. Images: Michelangelo's 'David' (1501–04), Barbara Hepworth's pierced forms, Ruth Asawa's looped-wire sculptures.
misconceptions: Making a sculpture that only works from the front. Correct: sculpture in the round should be interesting from every side.
Ignoring negative space. Correct: holes and openings are part of the form (as in Hepworth and Asawa).

days.guide: Compare the three sculptors' use of space.

questions.q: How does Hepworth use space differently from Michelangelo?
questions.a: Hepworth pierces holes through her abstract forms so negative space becomes part of the sculpture; Michelangelo carved a solid figure from marble.

days.guide: Technique sampler: score, fold, curl, tab, slot.

questions.q: Why score paper before folding?
questions.a: Scoring makes a crisp, straight fold without cracking.

days.guide: Build a freestanding abstract sculpture ≥10 inches.

questions.q: What makes a paper sculpture stable?
questions.a: A wide base, triangular or folded structures, tabs and slots for joins and balanced weight.

days.guide: Photograph from three angles with a lamp.

questions.q: How does lighting change a sculpture?
questions.a: Shadows reveal or hide form; low side light creates dramatic shadows.

days.guide: Critique for balance, unity, negative space.

questions.q: What is sculpture 'in the round'?
questions.a: Freestanding sculpture meant to be viewed from all sides.

weeks.assessment_key: Paper sculpture: 4 = freestanding, ≥10 in, interesting from all sides, uses at least three paper techniques, intentional negative space, clean craftsmanship, three documented photos; 3 = minor issues; 2 = front-facing or unstable; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Air-dry clay, plastic knife, water cup, rolling pin, two slats for even slabs, fork or needle tool for scoring, plastic bag to keep clay moist. Safety: wipe surfaces with a damp sponge (no sweeping dry clay dust, which contains silica).
misconceptions: Joining pieces without scoring. Correct: score both surfaces, add slip, press and smooth (score and slip).
Uneven pinch pot walls. Correct: rotate and pinch evenly from the bottom up, about ¼ inch thick.

days.guide: Clay safety; wedge clay.

questions.q: Why clean clay with water instead of sweeping?
questions.a: Dry clay dust contains silica, which is harmful to breathe.

days.guide: Make a pinch pot.

questions.q: How do you start a pinch pot?
questions.a: Roll a ball, press the thumb into the center, then pinch and rotate to thin the walls evenly.

days.guide: Build a coil vessel with score and slip.

questions.q: What is slip?
questions.a: Clay mixed with water to a creamy consistency, used as glue between scored pieces.

days.guide: Construct a slab box with lid.

questions.q: How do you keep slabs even?
questions.a: Roll between two slats of equal thickness.

days.guide: Compare methods; choose one.

questions.q: Name the three hand-building methods.
questions.a: Pinch, coil, slab.

weeks.assessment_key: Three samples: 4 = pinch pot with even walls, coil vessel with secure scored joins, slab box with square joins and fitted lid, reflection compares methods; 3 = minor cracking or unevenness; 2 = joins fail; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Air-dry clay, acrylic paint, sealant (note: air-dry clay is not food-safe). Images: Maria Martinez's black-on-black pottery (San Ildefonso Pueblo) and Japanese Jōmon cord-marked pottery.
misconceptions: Carving designs when clay is too wet or dry. Correct: carve sgraffito at leather-hard.
Painting before fully dry. Correct: let air-dry clay dry completely (often several days) first.

days.guide: Study Martinez and Jōmon; sketch surface designs.

questions.q: What is Maria Martinez known for?
questions.a: Black-on-black pottery from San Ildefonso Pueblo, New Mexico — polished black surfaces with matte black designs, developed with her husband Julian.

days.guide: Build the vessel or sculpture.

questions.q: Why is Jōmon pottery significant?
questions.a: It is among the oldest pottery in the world (over 10,000 years old), named for its cord-marked ('jōmon') surfaces.

days.guide: Add texture or sgraffito at leather-hard.

questions.q: What is leather-hard?
questions.a: Clay that is partly dry — firm enough to hold shape but still carvable.

days.guide: Paint and seal after drying.

questions.q: What is sgraffito?
questions.a: Scratching through a surface layer (slip or paint) to reveal the color beneath.

days.guide: Write an artist statement explaining cultural inspiration.

questions.q: How do you respectfully use cultural inspiration?
questions.a: Learn and credit the tradition and its meaning, take inspiration from techniques or forms rather than copying sacred designs, and explain the connection.

weeks.assessment_key: Clay piece and statement: 4 = well-constructed form using a chosen method, surface texture/sgraffito, neat painting and sealing, statement accurately credits and explains the cultural inspiration; 3 = minor flaws; 2 = weak construction or no cultural connection; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Shoebox, found materials, camera, measuring tape. Images of Christo and Jeanne-Claude's 'Running Fence' (1976) and Yayoi Kusama's Infinity Mirror Rooms.
misconceptions: Thinking installation is just a big sculpture. Correct: installation transforms a space and the viewer's experience inside it.
Ignoring scale in the model. Correct: choose a scale (e.g., 1 inch = 1 foot) and apply it.

days.guide: Study 'Running Fence' and Kusama.

questions.q: Describe 'Running Fence.'
questions.a: A temporary 24.5-mile, 18-foot-tall white fabric fence across Sonoma and Marin County hills to the Pacific, installed in 1976 for two weeks.

days.guide: Photograph and measure a space.

questions.q: Why measure the site?
questions.a: To scale the model and plan materials accurately.

days.guide: Collaborate to sketch a proposal.

questions.q: What is site-specific art?
questions.a: Art created for a particular location, responding to its features and meaning.

days.guide: Build a scale model in a shoebox.

questions.q: If the scale is 1 inch = 1 foot, how big is a 6-foot wall in the model?
questions.a: 6 inches.

days.guide: Present proposal and model.

questions.q: How do Kusama's rooms change the viewer's experience?
questions.a: Mirrors and repeated lights or dots create an illusion of infinite space that surrounds the viewer.

weeks.assessment_key: Proposal and model: 4 = clear concept transforming a specific site, measured and correctly scaled model, materials list, explanation of viewer experience and collaboration; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = unscaled or unclear concept; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Mirror, pencils, drawing paper. Front-view proportion guide: eyes halfway down the head; face width about five eye-widths; bottom of the nose about halfway between eyes and chin; mouth about one-third of the way from nose to chin; ears between brow line and nose bottom.
misconceptions: Placing eyes too high. Correct: the eyes sit halfway — the forehead and hair are bigger than people think.
Drawing a flat top of the head. Correct: the skull extends well above the hairline.

days.guide: Draw a front-view guide.

questions.q: How many eye-widths wide is a face?
questions.a: About five, with one eye-width between the eyes.

days.guide: Six eye and nose studies.

questions.q: How do you show a nose without outlining it?
questions.a: Shade the sides and underside planes and the nostril shadows; leave the bridge light.

days.guide: Mouth and ear studies.

questions.q: Where do the corners of the mouth usually line up?
questions.a: Roughly under the pupils.

days.guide: Draw a family member's face from life with the guide.

questions.q: Where do the ears sit?
questions.a: Between the eyebrow line and the bottom of the nose.

days.guide: Compare to a photo; correct proportions.

questions.q: What's a common proportion error?
questions.a: Eyes too high, too large, or the head too short above the eyes.

weeks.assessment_key: Proportion studies: 4 = guide drawn correctly with labels, 6+ feature studies with shading, life drawing follows the guide and shows corrections; 3 = minor errors; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Mirror, drawing or painting materials. Images: Rembrandt self-portraits (he made around 80), Frida Kahlo self-portraits, Kehinde Wiley portraits with decorative backgrounds.
misconceptions: Copying a photo instead of observing. Correct: draw from the mirror for real form and light.
Adding symbols without meaning. Correct: each symbol should communicate something about you.

days.guide: Compare the three artists' symbols.

questions.q: How did Rembrandt's self-portraits change over time?
questions.a: They show him aging honestly, from a confident young man to an older man with lined face and humble clothing, recording his life and changing fortunes.

days.guide: Thumbnails with 3 personal symbols.

questions.q: How does Wiley use backgrounds symbolically?
questions.a: Ornate floral patterns reference his subjects' heritage and art-history traditions and elevate the sitters.

days.guide: Draw from the mirror.

questions.q: Why use a single light source for a self-portrait?
questions.a: It creates clear shadows that show the structure of the face.

days.guide: Add value or color and symbols.

questions.q: How can placement give a symbol importance?
questions.a: Placing it near the face, at a focal point, or larger in scale.

days.guide: Write an explanation of your symbols.

questions.q: What should the explanation include?
questions.a: Each symbol, what it represents and why it was placed where it is.

weeks.assessment_key: Self-portrait and statement: 4 = proportionally accurate face drawn from observation, full value range or intentional color, three meaningful integrated symbols, statement explains each; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = proportion errors or weak symbols; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Optional wooden manikin, pencils; image of Polykleitos's 'Doryphoros' (Spear-Bearer, c. 450–440 BCE, known from Roman marble copies). Family member to pose.
misconceptions: Drawing heads too large. Correct: an adult figure is about 7.5 heads tall.
Stiff, symmetrical poses. Correct: contrapposto shifts weight to one leg, tilting hips and shoulders in opposite directions.

days.guide: Teach the 7.5-heads rule; draw a chart.

questions.q: Where is the midpoint of an adult standing figure?
questions.a: Around the hips/groin (about 3.75–4 heads down).

days.guide: Twenty one-minute gestures.

questions.q: What is the 'line of action'?
questions.a: An imaginary curve through the body that shows the main direction and energy of the pose.

days.guide: Study 'Doryphoros'; draw contrapposto.

questions.q: What is contrapposto?
questions.a: A pose with weight on one leg so the hips tilt one way and the shoulders the other, creating a natural S-curve.

days.guide: 30-minute seated figure from life.

questions.q: How does sitting change proportions?
questions.a: The thighs foreshorten when they point toward the viewer, so they look shorter.

days.guide: Critique proportion with a partner.

questions.q: Why was the Doryphoros important?
questions.a: It illustrated Polykleitos's 'Canon' of ideal proportions and the use of contrapposto in Greek sculpture.

weeks.assessment_key: Figure drawing: 4 = proportions about 7.5 heads, convincing weight/contrapposto or seated foreshortening, gesture energy, value or line variation; 3 = minor proportion errors; 2 = stiff or distorted; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Museum images: Fayum mummy portraits (Roman Egypt, 1st–3rd century CE), Egyptian pharaoh portraits, Benin bronze/brass heads (Kingdom of Benin, Nigeria), Mughal miniature portraits (India, 16th–17th century), Modigliani and Alice Neel portraits. Quiz on traditions.
misconceptions: Judging non-Western portraits as 'less realistic' and therefore less skilled. Correct: styles reflect purpose — idealization, status, spiritual function.
Comparison essays that just describe. Correct: compare purpose, style and context with evidence.

days.guide: Compare Fayum and pharaoh portraits.

questions.q: How do Fayum portraits differ from pharaoh portraits?
questions.a: Fayum portraits are naturalistic, individual faces painted in encaustic (wax) on wood panels placed over mummies; pharaoh portraits are idealized, formal and timeless to show divine kingship.

days.guide: Study Benin bronzes and Mughal miniatures.

questions.q: What were Benin commemorative heads made for and how?
questions.a: Cast in brass/bronze by the lost-wax method to honor deceased Obas (kings) on royal ancestral altars; many were looted by British forces in 1897.

days.guide: Study Modigliani and Alice Neel.

questions.q: Describe Modigliani's portrait style.
questions.a: Elongated faces and necks, almond-shaped often blank eyes, simplified forms influenced by African and ancient sculpture.

days.guide: Write a comparison of two portraits citing visual evidence.

questions.q: What are Mughal miniature portraits like?
questions.a: Small, detailed paintings often showing rulers in profile, with fine brushwork, rich color and decorative borders, signaling status.

days.guide: Quiz.

questions.q: What medium were Fayum portraits painted in?
questions.a: Encaustic (pigment in hot wax) or tempera on wood panels.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Fayum – Roman Egypt, encaustic, naturalistic, funerary; Egyptian pharaohs – idealized, symbols of power; Benin – lost-wax brass heads honoring Obas, looted 1897; Mughal – detailed miniatures, profile portraits of rulers; Modigliani – elongated stylized faces; Neel – expressive, psychologically honest portraits of everyday New Yorkers. Essay: 4 = compares purpose, style, materials and context with specific visual evidence and a thesis.

weeks.prep: Painting or drawing materials, camera. Choose a subject (family member, mentor) and prepare interview questions.
misconceptions: Copying a photo without setting meaning. Correct: include objects and setting that reveal who the person is.
Rushing the face. Correct: build proportions with guidelines before details.

days.guide: Interview the subject; photograph in a meaningful setting.

questions.q: Give two good interview questions.
questions.a: 'What place feels most like you?' 'What object would you save in a fire and why?'

days.guide: Composition sketch with setting objects.

questions.q: How can composition emphasize the person?
questions.a: Place the face at a rule-of-thirds point, use contrast and lead lines toward the face.

days.guide: Begin the final portrait.

questions.q: Which proportion rules apply?
questions.a: Eyes halfway, five eye-widths across, ears between brow and nose, etc.

days.guide: Finish.

questions.q: How do you check likeness?
questions.a: Compare feature spacing and shapes to the photo; flip the image or view in a mirror to spot errors.

days.guide: Present to the subject; record reaction.

questions.q: Why record the subject's reaction?
questions.a: It shows how the portrait communicated and gives feedback for reflection.

weeks.assessment_key: Final portrait: 4 = accurate proportions and likeness, setting/objects reflect interview, strong composition, skilled media handling, reaction recorded; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = weak likeness or no setting meaning; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phone or digital camera; free editing app (Snapseed, built-in Photos). Images of Dorothea Lange's 'Migrant Mother' (1936) and Ansel Adams's Yosemite photographs.
misconceptions: Always shooting at noon. Correct: golden hour (just after sunrise and before sunset) gives warm, soft, directional light.
Over-editing. Correct: subtle adjustments; keep the image honest.

days.guide: Compare Lange and Adams.

questions.q: How did Adams's purpose differ from Lange's?
questions.a: Lange documented human suffering to prompt social aid; Adams celebrated the grandeur of wilderness and supported its preservation, using precise black-and-white tonal control (Zone System).

days.guide: Shoot 10 photos each technique.

questions.q: What is symmetry in photography?
questions.a: A balanced composition where both halves mirror each other.

days.guide: Photograph one object at three times; describe.

questions.q: How does noon light look compared with golden hour?
questions.a: Noon: harsh, overhead, short dark shadows, high contrast. Golden hour: warm, soft, long shadows.

days.guide: Edit best five: crop, exposure, black-and-white.

questions.q: Why convert to black and white?
questions.a: It emphasizes value, shape, texture and contrast over color.

days.guide: Present a 5-photo contact sheet.

questions.q: What is a contact sheet?
questions.a: A sheet of small thumbnail images for reviewing and selecting photos.

weeks.assessment_key: Contact sheet: 4 = five photos each clearly labeled and demonstrating a different technique (rule of thirds, leading lines, framing, symmetry, pattern), thoughtful edits, light study description; 3 = 4 clear; 2 = techniques unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Camera, notebook. Gordon Parks examples (e.g., 'American Gothic, Washington, D.C.,' 1942; LIFE photo essays like 'Flavio,' 1961). Permission script for photographing people and businesses.
misconceptions: Shooting without a plan. Correct: a shot list ensures variety (establishing, detail, portrait, action).
Photographing people without consent. Correct: ask permission, especially for close portraits and minors.

days.guide: Study Parks's photo essays and sequencing.

questions.q: Who was Gordon Parks?
questions.a: An African American photographer, writer and filmmaker who documented civil rights, poverty and Black American life for the FSA and LIFE magazine.

days.guide: Choose a subject; write a shot list.

questions.q: What shots belong on a shot list?
questions.a: Establishing/wide shot, medium action shots, close-up details, portraits, a closing image.

days.guide: Shoot 50+ photos with permissions.

questions.q: Why take many more photos than you need?
questions.a: To have choices for the strongest images and sequence.

days.guide: Select and sequence 8; write captions.

questions.q: What do good captions do?
questions.a: Give who/what/where/when and context without repeating what's obvious.

days.guide: Present; explain sequencing.

questions.q: Why does sequence matter?
questions.a: It creates a narrative arc — opening, development, closing — guiding the viewer's understanding.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo essay: 4 = 8 strong, varied photos in a narrative sequence with informative captions, permissions obtained, clear explanation of sequencing choices; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = weak narrative; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Magazines, photocopies of old photos (not originals), glue, acrylic paint. Images: Romare Bearden's collages of Harlem life (e.g., 'The Dove,' 1964) and Hannah Höch's photomontage ('Cut with the Kitchen Knife,' 1919–20).
misconceptions: Gluing too early. Correct: experiment with arrangements and photograph options before gluing.
Collages that feel random. Correct: use a theme and unify with color, paint or repeated shapes.

days.guide: Study Bearden and Höch.

questions.q: What did Bearden's collages depict?
questions.a: Everyday African American life — Harlem streets, music, family and the rural South — built from cut photos, paper and paint.

days.guide: Gather images around a theme.

questions.q: What is photomontage?
questions.a: Combining cut or edited photographs into a new image, used by Dada artists like Höch for social commentary.

days.guide: Experiment; photograph three options.

questions.q: Why photograph options?
questions.a: To compare compositions and remember arrangements.

days.guide: Glue down; unify with paint and drawing.

questions.q: How can you unify a collage?
questions.a: Repeat colors, add paint washes across pieces, use a dominant shape or line.

days.guide: Interpret a sibling's collage, then your own.

questions.q: What does 'interpret' mean in critique?
questions.a: Explain the meaning or message based on visual evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Collage and interpretation: 4 = clear theme, varied materials, intentional composition with unifying devices, interpretations use Feldman steps with visual evidence; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = random arrangement; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Computer or tablet with Krita (free) or a browser-based editor (e.g., Photopea). A scanned or photographed earlier drawing.
misconceptions: Working on one layer. Correct: use separate layers for sketch, line, color and effects so changes are easy.
Copying online images without permission. Correct: use your own photos or public-domain images.

days.guide: Learn layers, brushes, selection, opacity.

questions.q: What is a layer?
questions.a: A separate transparent sheet in a digital file that can be edited without affecting others.

days.guide: Recreate an earlier drawing digitally.

questions.q: What does lowering opacity do?
questions.a: Makes a layer more transparent.

days.guide: Original illustration combining photo and drawing.

questions.q: How do you blend a photo into a drawing?
questions.a: Use layer masks, opacity and blending modes.

days.guide: Refine color and layer effects.

questions.q: What is a layer mask?
questions.a: A non-destructive way to hide parts of a layer by painting black/white on a mask.

days.guide: Reflect on digital vs. traditional.

questions.q: Name one advantage of each workflow.
questions.a: Digital: undo, layers, easy color changes. Traditional: physical texture, unique original, no device needed.

weeks.assessment_key: Digital illustration: 4 = original image combining photo and drawing, uses multiple layers, masks/opacity effectively, cohesive color, reflection compares workflows with specifics; 3 = minor issues; 2 = single layer or copied; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Smithsonian Learning Lab access; sketchbook. Artists: Kara Walker (cut-paper silhouettes on slavery and race), El Anatsui (metal bottle-cap tapestries), Ai Weiwei (art and activism), Judy Baca ('The Great Wall of Los Angeles' mural).
misconceptions: Choosing a theme too broad ('life'). Correct: narrow to a specific idea you can show in three pieces.
A profile that only lists biography. Correct: analyze themes, media and specific works.

days.guide: Explore the four artists; note themes.

questions.q: What is El Anatsui known for?
questions.a: Shimmering, flexible wall hangings made of flattened bottle caps and aluminum joined with copper wire, addressing consumption, trade and history.

days.guide: Write a 400-word profile with images.

questions.q: What is Judy Baca's 'Great Wall of Los Angeles'?
questions.a: A half-mile-long mural in the Tujunga Wash painted with hundreds of youth beginning in 1976, depicting California history from the perspective of diverse communities.

days.guide: Mind map of personal themes.

questions.q: Why make a mind map?
questions.a: It generates connected ideas and helps narrow a theme.

days.guide: Write a 3-piece proposal with media and sketches.

questions.q: What makes a 'body of work'?
questions.a: A series of related pieces exploring one theme with consistent and varied approaches.

days.guide: Conference; revise.

questions.q: What questions should the conference ask?
questions.a: Is the theme clear? Are the media realistic? Do the three pieces vary while connecting?

weeks.assessment_key: Artist profile and proposal: profile 4 = ~400 words, analyzes themes, media and at least two specific works with images and sources; proposal 4 = focused theme, three distinct planned pieces, media, sketches and timeline, revised after conference; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Chosen media; phone for process photos.
misconceptions: Making three identical pieces. Correct: vary composition, scale or media while keeping the theme.
Skipping documentation. Correct: photograph each stage.

days.guide: Begin piece 1; document process.

questions.q: Why document process?
questions.a: It shows decisions and growth and supports the artist statement.

days.guide: Finish piece 1; write process notes.

questions.q: What should process notes include?
questions.a: Steps, challenges, decisions and changes.

days.guide: Begin piece 2 as a variation.

questions.q: Name two ways to vary a theme.
questions.a: Change viewpoint, scale, color scheme, medium or subject while keeping the idea.

days.guide: Finish piece 2.

questions.q: Does piece 2 connect to piece 1?
questions.a: Answers vary; explain the shared theme.

days.guide: Mid-project critique using criteria.

questions.q: What is one criterion you set?
questions.a: Answers vary; criteria should be specific and measurable.

weeks.assessment_key: Two pieces with documentation: 4 = both pieces complete, skilled, clearly connected yet varied, with dated process photos and notes, mid-project critique completed; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = one piece or weak documentation; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Chosen media; artist statement guide (theme, inspiration, media, process, what viewers should notice).
misconceptions: Statements full of vague words ('it's about feelings'). Correct: use specific language about subject, media and choices.
Not revising after critique. Correct: revise at least one piece.

days.guide: Create piece 3.

questions.q: How does piece 3 complete the series?
questions.a: Answers vary; it should conclude or extend the theme.

days.guide: Revise pieces based on critique.

questions.q: What did you revise and why?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers tie to critique.

days.guide: Draft a 250-word statement.

questions.q: What three things must the statement explain?
questions.a: Theme, media and process.

days.guide: Revise statement for clarity.

questions.q: Replace 'It shows emotions' with something specific.
questions.a: Example: 'Cool blue washes and empty chairs show the loneliness I felt after moving.'

days.guide: Self-evaluate with criteria.

questions.q: What does a strong self-evaluation include?
questions.a: Evidence from the work for each criterion and next steps.

weeks.assessment_key: Series and statement: 4 = three cohesive finished pieces with skillful media use, revisions evident, 250-word statement specific about theme, media and process, self-evaluation with evidence; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = incomplete series or vague statement; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Artwork, tape or hooks, label cards; a virtual museum exhibition (Google Arts & Culture or a museum website).
misconceptions: Hanging art too high or crowded. Correct: center works at about 57–60 inches from the floor with even spacing.
Labels without information. Correct: title, medium, date and a one-sentence description.

days.guide: Virtual tour; analyze grouping, labels, lighting.

questions.q: What does a curator do?
questions.a: Selects, organizes, interprets and presents artworks for an exhibition.

days.guide: Select 10–12 works including the series.

questions.q: How should works be grouped?
questions.a: By theme, medium or chronology so the show tells a clear story.

days.guide: Write wall labels.

questions.q: What goes on a wall label?
questions.a: Artist, title, date, medium and a short description.

days.guide: Install considering flow and lighting.

questions.q: What is the standard hanging height?
questions.a: Center of artwork about 57–60 inches from the floor.

days.guide: Walk through; adjust.

questions.q: Why walk through the show?
questions.a: To check flow, spacing, lighting and readability like a visitor.

weeks.assessment_key: Installed exhibition: 4 = 10–12 works including the series, logically grouped, consistent hanging height and spacing, complete labels, good lighting and flow; 3 = minor issues; 2 = disorganized; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Exhibition, guest book, refreshments optional; app or slides for a digital portfolio.
misconceptions: Talking only about technique at the opening. Correct: also share ideas and meaning.
A digital portfolio without captions. Correct: caption each work with title, medium, date and a sentence of context.

days.guide: Host the opening; short talk.

questions.q: What should an artist talk include?
questions.a: Welcome, the show's theme, highlights of the series and process, and an invitation to ask questions.

days.guide: Collect guest-book feedback; summarize.

questions.q: How do you summarize feedback?
questions.a: Group comments into themes (praise, questions, suggestions) and note patterns.

days.guide: Write about how an exhibition changed your view of an issue.

questions.q: Give an example of art changing a viewpoint.
questions.a: Example: Lange's 'Migrant Mother' made viewers see Depression-era farm workers as individuals deserving help.

days.guide: Create a captioned digital portfolio.

questions.q: Why keep a digital portfolio?
questions.a: For college/program applications and to track growth.

days.guide: Final reflection on growth and goals.

questions.q: What should the final reflection cover?
questions.a: Growth in skills and ideas with specific examples, favorite work, challenges and goals for next year.

weeks.assessment_key: Exhibition and reflection: 4 = successful opening with artist talk, feedback summarized into themes, thoughtful impact reflection, complete captioned digital portfolio, final reflection with specific evidence and goals; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = partial; 1 = incomplete.

WL.overview: Spanish II meets about 50 minutes a day and follows a weekly rhythm: new grammar or vocabulary early in the week, authentic reading/listening and conversation midweek, and a quiz, project, or performance assessment on Friday. Speak Spanish as much as possible, model each structure aloud before practice, and expect the student to speak and write every day. You do not need to be fluent: use the answers given here, SpanishDict for conjugations, and recordings of native speakers, and reteach any structure scored below 80% before moving on.

weeks.prep: Set up the Spanish notebook with sections (vocabulario, gramática, escritura) and create the Conjuguemos account. Make a present-tense chart for -ar/-er/-ir endings plus ser, estar, tener, ir, and the yo-go verbs. Have a phone ready to record the self-introduction.
misconceptions: Using 'estar' for personality (Estoy simpático): personality and traits use ser (Soy simpático); estar is for location and temporary states (Estoy cansado).
Saying 'Yo gusto la pizza': gustar works backward — the thing liked is the subject: Me gusta la pizza; Me gustan los perros.
Applying yo-go to every form (*nosotros tengamos): only the yo form adds -go (tengo); tener is also e→ie in other forms (tienes, tiene, tenemos).

days.guide: Model a short introduction aloud: 'Me llamo Ana. Tengo quince años. Soy creativa y un poco tímida. Me gusta leer y me gustan los gatos.' Your child writes a script with ser, tener, and gustar, practices it twice, then records about one minute; check for 'tengo ... años' (not 'soy ... años').

questions.q: How do you say 'I am 15 years old' in Spanish?
questions.a: Tengo quince años. (Age uses tener, not ser.)

questions.q: Say 'I like dogs' and 'I like to read.'
questions.a: Me gustan los perros. Me gusta leer. (gustan with a plural noun; gusta with an infinitive.)

days.guide: Review the endings: -ar (o, as, a, amos, áis, an), -er (o, es, e, emos, éis, en), -ir (o, es, e, imos, ís, en). Your child completes the Conjuguemos set, then writes 10 sentences about the week; check that each verb matches its subject.

questions.q: Conjugate vivir for nosotros and comer for ellos.
questions.a: vivimos; comen

questions.q: Translate: 'We study Spanish on Mondays.'
questions.a: Estudiamos español los lunes.

days.guide: Chant the yo-go forms (tengo, hago, salgo, pongo, vengo, digo, traigo) and show stem-changers as 'boot verbs' (all forms change except nosotros/vosotros). Your child does the timed drill twice and tries to beat the first time.

questions.q: Give the yo form of hacer, salir, and poner.
questions.a: hago, salgo, pongo

questions.q: Conjugate poder for tú and nosotros.
questions.a: puedes; podemos (nosotros does not change: o→ue only inside the 'boot').

days.guide: Help your child write 10 questions with question words (¿Cómo te llamas? ¿Qué te gusta hacer? ¿Dónde vives? ¿Cuántos hermanos tienes?). They interview you or a pen pal in Spanish and write the answers in third person (Mi mamá se llama...).

questions.q: Write the question 'Where do you live?' and answer it.
questions.a: ¿Dónde vives? — Vivo en (ciudad).

questions.q: Change 'Me gusta cocinar' to report what your mother said.
questions.a: A mi mamá le gusta cocinar.

days.guide: Give the present-tense quiz with notes closed. Grade it together, have your child correct each error with the rule, and score the recording with the rubric.

questions.q: Correct the error: 'Yo soy cansado hoy.'
questions.a: Yo estoy cansado hoy — a temporary condition uses estar.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (aim 80%+): sample key — hablar/yo: hablo; comer/tú: comes; vivir/nosotros: vivimos; tener/ella: tiene; hacer/yo: hago; salir/yo: salgo; poner/yo: pongo; querer/ellos: quieren; poder/tú: puedes; pedir/nosotros: pedimos. Recording rubric (4 pts each): 4 = 1 full minute, name/age/personality/likes all included, correct ser/tener/gustar, clear pronunciation; 3 = all content, 1–2 errors; 2 = missing a part or frequent errors; 1 = very short or mostly English.

weeks.prep: Make or print picture cards for the daily routine (waking, showering, brushing teeth, dressing, going to bed) and set out a clock with movable hands. Find a short Spanish 'mi rutina' video (search 'mi rutina diaria' on YouTube) and preview it.
misconceptions: Dropping the reflexive pronoun (Despierto a las seis): with reflexive verbs the pronoun matches the subject — Me despierto a las seis.
Attaching the pronoun wrongly (Me voy a ducharme): either 'Me voy a duchar' or 'Voy a ducharme', not both.
Forgetting stem changes inside reflexives: despertarse (e→ie) me despierto; acostarse (o→ue) me acuesto; vestirse (e→i) me visto.

days.guide: Show the pronoun chart (me, te, se, nos, os, se) and act out 'me lavo las manos' vs. 'lavo el carro' to show the action returns to the subject. Your child conjugates 10 routine verbs and labels the picture cards; check the pronouns and stem changes.

questions.q: Conjugate levantarse for yo, tú, and ellos.
questions.a: me levanto, te levantas, se levantan

questions.q: Why is it 'Me lavo las manos' and not 'Me lavo mis manos'?
questions.a: With reflexive verbs, Spanish uses the definite article for body parts because the pronoun already shows whose hands they are.

days.guide: Model telling time with a routine: 'A las seis y media me despierto. A las siete menos cuarto me ducho.' Your child writes the full weekday routine with times; check 'a la una' (singular) vs. 'a las dos'.

questions.q: Write 'At 7:15 I get dressed.'
questions.a: A las siete y cuarto me visto.

questions.q: Write 'At 1:00 I eat lunch.'
questions.a: A la una almuerzo.

days.guide: Play the routine video once just to listen, then again pausing to fill a timeline (time + activity). Your child compares the timeline with the speaker's words and you check two items by replaying.

questions.q: If the speaker says 'Me acuesto a las once de la noche,' what time does he go to bed?

days.guide: Explain that in Spain dinner is often around 9–10 p.m., the main meal (la comida) is around 2–3 p.m., and the long midday break is more common than a daily nap. Your child fills a Venn diagram comparing their routine to a Spanish teen's and writes 3 comparison sentences.

questions.q: Write a comparison: 'I eat dinner at 6; a teen in Spain eats at 9.'
questions.a: Yo ceno a las seis, pero un joven en España cena a las nueve.

questions.q: What is 'la comida' in Spain?
questions.a: The main midday meal, usually eaten around 2–3 p.m.

days.guide: Give the reflexive quiz, then have your child describe the routine aloud from memory using times and transition words (primero, luego, después, finalmente). Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Say 'First I wake up, then I shower, and finally I get dressed.'
questions.a: Primero me despierto, luego me ducho y finalmente me visto.

weeks.assessment_key: Reflexive quiz sample key: 1) yo/levantarse — me levanto 2) tú/ducharse — te duchas 3) ella/vestirse — se viste 4) nosotros/acostarse — nos acostamos 5) ellos/despertarse — se despiertan 6) yo/cepillarse los dientes — me cepillo los dientes. Oral routine rubric: 4 = 8+ routine actions in order with times and correct pronouns; 3 = 6–7 actions, minor errors; 2 = under 6 actions or frequent pronoun errors; 1 = isolated words.

weeks.prep: Copy the child's class schedule onto the template; prepare stem-changer playing cards (verb on one side, subject on the other). Find a short reading on a school day in Mexico or Argentina (e.g., a textbook reading or a Spanish blog about 'la escuela secundaria').
misconceptions: Changing the stem in nosotros (*empiezamos): nosotros and vosotros keep the original stem — empezamos, almorzamos, pedimos.
Confusing e→ie and e→i: preferir becomes prefiero (ie), but pedir becomes pido (i). Memorize each with its pattern.
Saying 'Me gusta la matemática' for school subjects: the subject is usually plural — Me gustan las matemáticas.

days.guide: Model: 'Tengo matemáticas a las nueve. Me gustan porque son interesantes, pero son difíciles.' Your child writes 10 sentences about classes and opinions; check that adjectives agree with the subject (las ciencias son fascinantes).

questions.q: Write 'History is boring but art is fun.'
questions.a: La historia es aburrida, pero el arte es divertido.

questions.q: How do you say 'school subject' and 'schedule'?
questions.a: la asignatura (or la materia); el horario

days.guide: Sort verbs into three 'boots': e→ie (empezar, querer, preferir), o→ue (almorzar, poder, dormir), e→i (pedir, servir, repetir). Play the card game: flip a verb and a subject and say the form; then complete the written drill.

questions.q: Conjugate almorzar for yo and nosotros.
questions.a: almuerzo; almorzamos

questions.q: Conjugate pedir for ella.
questions.a: pide

days.guide: Read the article together; your child lists five differences (e.g., uniforms, morning or afternoon shifts called turnos in Mexico, students staying in one classroom while teachers move, calling teachers 'maestro/profe'). Check that each difference comes from the reading.

questions.q: Write a sentence about a difference: 'In Mexico, many students wear uniforms.'
questions.a: En México, muchos estudiantes llevan uniforme.

days.guide: Act out a conversation: '¿Qué prefieres hacer después de las clases?' — 'Prefiero jugar al fútbol. ¿Y tú?' Your child must use preferir and querer at least three times each and ask follow-up questions.

questions.q: Answer: '¿Qué quieres hacer esta tarde?' (You want to swim.)
questions.a: Quiero nadar esta tarde.

questions.q: Ask a friend 'Do you prefer soccer or basketball?'
questions.a: ¿Prefieres el fútbol o el básquetbol?

days.guide: Give the stem-changer quiz and score the role-play from day 4 with the rubric. Have your child re-conjugate any missed verb in all six forms.

questions.q: Conjugate dormir in all six present forms.
questions.a: duermo, duermes, duerme, dormimos, dormís, duermen

weeks.assessment_key: Stem-changer quiz sample key: empezar/yo — empiezo; almorzar/tú — almuerzas; preferir/ella — prefiere; pedir/nosotros — pedimos; querer/ellos — quieren; dormir/yo — duermo; servir/tú — sirves; poder/ustedes — pueden; volver/él — vuelve; repetir/yo — repito. Role-play rubric: 4 = asks and answers 5+ questions with correct stem changes and natural follow-ups; 3 = 4 exchanges, few errors; 2 = short answers, several errors; 1 = cannot sustain.

weeks.prep: Print the IPA task sheet and find an authentic school-schedule or school-life article (e.g., from a Spanish-language school website or a teen magazine). Plan the 3-minute conversation prompts and gather Unit 1 flashcards. Write the unit test covering present tense, reflexives, stem-changers, routine, and school vocabulary.
misconceptions: Translating word-for-word from English in the email: encourage short, known structures (Me levanto a las siete) rather than invented phrases.
Forgetting greetings and closings in an email: use 'Hola, ...' / 'Querido/a ...' and 'Un abrazo' or 'Saludos'.

days.guide: Your child reads the article independently, highlighting cognates first, then answers the comprehension questions in English or simple Spanish. Afterward, discuss which clues (cognates, numbers, times) helped.

questions.q: What strategy helps when you meet an unknown word in an authentic text?
questions.a: Look for cognates (e.g., 'horario' near times and class names), use context, and skip words not needed for the question.

days.guide: Hold the 3-minute conversation using questions like ¿A qué hora te levantas? ¿Cuál es tu clase favorita? ¿Qué haces después de las clases? Keep it natural; note errors but don't interrupt. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: How would you answer '¿A qué hora te acuestas?' (11:00 p.m.)
questions.a: Me acuesto a las once de la noche.

days.guide: Your child writes the 150-word email to a new exchange student, including a greeting, routine with times, classes, and a question for the student. Check reflexive pronouns and word count.

questions.q: Write a good closing sentence asking a question back.
questions.a: Example: ¿Y tú? ¿Cómo es tu rutina? ¡Escríbeme pronto! Saludos, (nombre)

days.guide: Review all Unit 1 flashcards; sort into 'know' and 'don't know' piles and redo the second pile until it is empty. Your child corrects errors from the IPA tasks and writes the rule beside each.

questions.q: Translate: 'to brush one's teeth,' 'to get up,' 'to go to bed.'
questions.a: cepillarse los dientes, levantarse, acostarse

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test without notes. Grade, go over errors together, and log scores.

questions.q: Correct: 'Nosotros nos acuestamos tarde.'
questions.a: Nosotros nos acostamos tarde (no stem change in nosotros).

weeks.assessment_key: IPA rubric (each mode, 4 levels): Interpretive — 4 = identifies main idea and 5+ details accurately; 3 = main idea and 3–4 details; 2 = some details; 1 = isolated words. Interpersonal — 4 = sustains 3 minutes, asks and answers questions, mostly accurate present/reflexive verbs; 3 = sustains with some pauses; 2 = mostly short answers; 1 = cannot sustain. Presentational — 4 = ~150 words, greeting/closing, routine in sequence with times, accurate reflexives; 3 = complete with minor errors; 2 = under 100 words or many errors; 1 = fragments. Unit test sample items: me ducho; nosotros almorzamos; ella se viste; 'A las ocho y media empiezo las clases.'

weeks.prep: Gather 3–5 childhood photos. Make an imperfect chart: -ar: -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban; -er/-ir: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían; irregulars ser (era), ir (iba), ver (veía).
misconceptions: Forgetting the accent on -ía (*comia): every -er/-ir imperfect form has an accent on the í (comía, vivíamos).
Missing the accent on nosotros -ar (*hablabamos): it is hablábamos.
Using the preterite for habitual past actions: 'used to / would' habits take the imperfect (Siempre jugaba en el parque).

days.guide: Explain that the imperfect describes how things were or used to be. Model 'De niña, yo jugaba mucho y comía helado.' Your child conjugates the 20 verbs; check accents.

questions.q: Conjugate estudiar in the imperfect for yo and nosotros.
questions.a: estudiaba; estudiábamos

questions.q: Conjugate escribir for ellos.
questions.a: escribían

days.guide: List frequency words (siempre, a menudo, todos los días, cada verano, a veces, nunca). Your child writes 10 'used to' sentences about childhood, each with a frequency word.

questions.q: Translate: 'Every summer we used to go to the beach.'
questions.a: Cada verano íbamos a la playa.

questions.q: Translate: 'I often watched cartoons.'
questions.a: A menudo veía dibujos animados.

days.guide: Teach the only three irregulars: ser (era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran), ir (iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban), ver (veía, veías...). Your child writes two sentences for each.

questions.q: Translate: 'My grandmother was very kind.'
questions.a: Mi abuela era muy amable.

questions.q: Translate: 'We used to go to the park.'
questions.a: Íbamos al parque.

days.guide: Your child chooses a photo and describes it aloud: age (Tenía cinco años), place (Vivíamos en...), people, and what they used to do. Ask two follow-up questions.

questions.q: How do you say 'I was five years old'?
questions.a: Tenía cinco años (age in the past uses tener in the imperfect).

days.guide: Give the imperfect quiz and score the photo description with the rubric. Review any missed accents.

questions.q: Fill in: Cuando yo ___ (ser) niño, ___ (vivir) en Texas.
questions.a: era; vivía

weeks.assessment_key: Imperfect quiz sample key: hablar/yo — hablaba; comer/nosotros — comíamos; vivir/ellos — vivían; jugar/tú — jugabas; ser/yo — era; ir/nosotros — íbamos; ver/ella — veía; tener/ustedes — tenían; 'When I was little, I used to play soccer' — Cuando era pequeño/a, jugaba al fútbol. Photo description rubric: 4 = 6+ imperfect sentences describing age, place, people, and activities, accurate forms; 3 = 4–5 sentences; 2 = few verbs or mixed tenses; 1 = isolated words.

weeks.prep: Find short Spanish readings or videos on rayuela (hopscotch), trompo (spinning top), lotería, and canicas (marbles). Print or buy a lotería set (printable sets are free online) and prepare a Venn diagram.
misconceptions: Thinking lotería is a number game like bingo: it uses pictures with names (El gallo, La sirena, La luna), often called with a riddle or rhyme.
Assuming games are identical across cultures: many are shared (hide-and-seek = escondidas/escondite) but names and rules vary by country.

days.guide: Read the short texts together, pausing to match each game with a picture. Your child writes one sentence per game in Spanish (La rayuela es un juego con tiza y una piedra).

questions.q: What is la rayuela?
questions.a: Hopscotch — a chalk grid where you toss a stone and hop through the squares.

questions.q: What do you need to play el trompo?
questions.a: A wooden top and a string (cuerda) to wind and throw it.

days.guide: Play lotería: the caller (your child first) reads each card in Spanish; players mark with beans. Switch callers so everyone practices pronunciation.

questions.q: What do players say when they win?
questions.a: ¡Lotería! (some families also say ¡Buenas!)

days.guide: Your child asks a family member: ¿A qué jugabas de niño? ¿Con quién jugabas? ¿Dónde jugaban? and takes notes in Spanish using the imperfect.

questions.q: Write the question 'What did you used to play when you were a child?'
questions.a: ¿A qué jugabas cuando eras niño/a?

questions.q: Report: 'My dad used to play marbles with his brothers.'
questions.a: Mi papá jugaba a las canicas con sus hermanos.

days.guide: Your child compares two games (e.g., U.S. hopscotch vs. rayuela, or bingo vs. lotería) in a Venn diagram and writes three comparison sentences in Spanish.

questions.q: Write: 'Both games use cards.'
questions.a: Los dos juegos usan cartas (or tarjetas).

days.guide: Give the short reading check and review the interview notes with the rubric.

questions.q: How do you say 'to hide' and 'hide-and-seek'?
questions.a: esconderse; las escondidas (Latin America) or el escondite (Spain)

weeks.assessment_key: Reading check sample key: 1) La rayuela = hopscotch, drawn with chalk and played by tossing a stone; 2) El trompo = a wooden spinning top wound with string; 3) La lotería = a Mexican picture game played with tablas and frijoles as markers; 4) Las canicas = marbles; 5) 'jugar a las escondidas' = to play hide-and-seek. Interview notes rubric: 4 = 8+ notes in Spanish using the imperfect (Mi papá jugaba...), with details on where/with whom; 3 = 5–7 notes; 2 = few notes or mostly English; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather drawing paper. Find a short story told in the imperfect (a Spanish-learner podcast like 'Cuentos de mi niñez' or a graded reader). Prepare a list of describing adjectives (alto, bajo, simpático, travieso, tranquilo).
misconceptions: Using 'era' for location (*La casa era en el centro): location uses estar — La casa estaba en el centro.
Pluralizing 'había' (*habían muchos árboles): había (there was/were) is always singular — Había muchos árboles.
Adjective agreement errors: mi maestra era simpática (feminine), mis vecinos eran ruidosos (plural).

days.guide: Model: 'Mi casa era grande. Tenía tres dormitorios. Había un parque cerca.' Your child draws the childhood home and neighborhood and writes 8 sentences using era, tenía, había, and estaba.

questions.q: Translate: 'There were many children in my neighborhood.'
questions.a: Había muchos niños en mi vecindario (barrio).

questions.q: Translate: 'The school was near my house.'
questions.a: La escuela estaba cerca de mi casa.

days.guide: Your child writes a 6-sentence description of a friend or teacher: appearance (era alto, tenía pelo rizado), personality, and what they used to do together.

questions.q: Translate: 'She had brown eyes and was very funny.'
questions.a: Tenía ojos marrones (or café) y era muy graciosa (or divertida).

days.guide: Play the story twice; your child answers questions and lists imperfect verbs heard. Discuss how the imperfect sets the scene.

questions.q: Why does a story often begin 'Había una vez...'?
questions.a: It means 'Once upon a time there was...' — the imperfect sets background, like describing the scene.

days.guide: Use prompts: ¿Dónde vivías? ¿Cómo era tu escuela? ¿Quién era tu mejor amigo? You answer about your own childhood; your child compares (Yo vivía en..., pero tú vivías en...).

questions.q: Ask: 'What was your school like?'
questions.a: ¿Cómo era tu escuela?

days.guide: Give the writing quiz: describe a childhood place and a person in at least 8 sentences. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Correct: 'Habían muchos árboles y la casa era en una calle tranquila.'
questions.a: Había muchos árboles y la casa estaba en una calle tranquila.

weeks.assessment_key: Writing quiz rubric (descriptive paragraph in the past): 4 = 8+ sentences, correct era/estaba/tenía/había, adjectives agree, varied vocabulary; 3 = 6–7 sentences, few errors; 2 = 4–5 sentences or frequent errors; 1 = fragments. Proficient sample: 'Mi casa era pequeña y azul. Estaba cerca de un parque. Había un árbol grande en el jardín. Mi vecina se llamaba Rosa; era alta y muy simpática.'

weeks.prep: Gather photos or drawings, construction paper or a slide template, and glue. Print an editing checklist: imperfect endings and accents, ser/ir/ver forms, noun–adjective agreement. Write the Unit 2 test (imperfect forms, childhood vocabulary, games, describing the past).
misconceptions: Mixing present tense into captions (Vivo en...): captions about childhood need the imperfect (Vivía en...).
Reading the presentation word-for-word: use photos as cues and speak from memory.

days.guide: Help your child choose a photo or drawing for each page topic: home, family, school, games, food, holidays. List key vocabulary for each page in the notebook.

questions.q: Give a Spanish title for the food page.
questions.a: Example: La comida de mi niñez / Lo que comía de niño/a

days.guide: Your child writes 3–4 imperfect captions per page (Vivíamos en una casa amarilla. Siempre jugaba con mi perro.). Circulate and point out good examples.

questions.q: Write a caption: 'On holidays we always ate tamales.'
questions.a: En los días festivos siempre comíamos tamales.

days.guide: Your child edits with the checklist, underlining every verb and checking its ending and accent. You spot-check one page and mark errors with a symbol (not the correction).

questions.q: Find and fix: 'Mis abuelos vivia en Chicago.'
questions.a: Mis abuelos vivían en Chicago.

days.guide: Your child presents the book for 2 minutes using pictures as cues, then answers two questions you ask (¿Cuál era tu juguete favorito? ¿Qué te gustaba comer?).

questions.q: Answer: '¿Cuál era tu juguete favorito?'
questions.a: Example: Mi juguete favorito era un oso de peluche.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test. Grade and review.

questions.q: Conjugate ver in the imperfect for all forms.
questions.a: veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían

weeks.assessment_key: Memory book rubric: Content — 6 pages with 3–4 captions each; Language — accurate imperfect forms and agreement; Presentation — 2 minutes, not read, answers 2 questions; Visuals — clear and labeled. 4 = all criteria met with few errors; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing pages or many errors; 1 = incomplete. Unit test sample: 1) nosotros/ir — íbamos 2) yo/ver — veía 3) ellos/ser — eran 4) 'jugábamos a las canicas' = we used to play marbles 5) 'Había' = there was/were.

weeks.prep: Make a preterite chart: -ar: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron; -er/-ir: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. Have a calendar to talk about 'ayer, anoche, la semana pasada'.
misconceptions: Missing accents that change meaning: hablo (I speak) vs. habló (he spoke).
Forgetting spelling changes in yo forms: buscar → busqué, llegar → llegué, empezar → empecé.
Confusing nosotros forms: -ar/-ir nosotros are the same in present and preterite (hablamos, vivimos); context and time words tell which.

days.guide: Explain the preterite tells completed actions at a specific time. Model 'Ayer comí pizza y miré una película.' Your child conjugates 20 verbs; check accents on yo and él forms.

questions.q: Conjugate cantar in the preterite for yo, él, and ellos.
questions.a: canté, cantó, cantaron

questions.q: Conjugate salir for tú.
questions.a: saliste

days.guide: Review time expressions (ayer, anoche, anteayer, el fin de semana pasado, el año pasado). Your child writes 10 sentences about yesterday or last weekend.

questions.q: Translate: 'Last night I studied and then I slept.'
questions.a: Anoche estudié y luego dormí.

days.guide: Show why: to keep the sound, c→qu, g→gu, z→c before é. Practice busqué, saqué, toqué, llegué, pagué, jugué, empecé, almorcé, comencé.

questions.q: Give the yo preterite of tocar, pagar, and almorzar.
questions.a: toqué, pagué, almorcé

questions.q: Why is 'él buscó' spelled with c but 'yo busqué' with qu?
questions.a: Before o the c already sounds like k; before é it must be qu to keep the k sound.

days.guide: Your child writes a 120-word paragraph about the last birthday: who came, what you ate, what you did. Check that all completed actions are in the preterite.

questions.q: Translate: 'My cousins came and we ate cake.'
questions.a: Mis primos vinieron y comimos pastel (or torta).

questions.q: Translate: 'I opened the gifts.'
questions.a: Abrí los regalos.

days.guide: Give the preterite quiz and review any spelling-change errors.

questions.q: Fill in: Ayer yo ___ (llegar) tarde y ___ (empezar) la tarea a las nueve.
questions.a: llegué; empecé

weeks.assessment_key: Preterite quiz sample key: hablar/yo — hablé; comer/tú — comiste; vivir/ella — vivió; bailar/nosotros — bailamos; abrir/ellos — abrieron; buscar/yo — busqué; llegar/yo — llegué; empezar/yo — empecé; jugar/yo — jugué; celebrar/ustedes — celebraron.

weeks.prep: Gather ofrenda materials (photo, candles or LED candles, paper marigolds or cempasúchil images, papel picado, small foods) or a slide template. Preview a respectful reading on Día de los Muertos. Chart the irregular preterites: ser/ir (fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron), hacer (hice, hiciste, hizo...), tener (tuve...), estar (estuve...), poder (pude...).
misconceptions: Thinking Día de los Muertos is 'Mexican Halloween': it is a celebration (Nov. 1–2) honoring and remembering loved ones who have died, not a scary holiday.
Adding accents to irregular preterites (*tuvó, *hizó): the irregular 'stem' preterites have no written accents — tuve, tuvo, hice, hizo.
Confusing fui = 'I went' and 'I was': ser and ir share preterite forms; context decides.

days.guide: Teach the irregulars as patterns (hacer: hic/hiz-, tener: tuv-, estar: estuv-, poder: pud-, all with endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron). Drill with quick oral prompts.

questions.q: Translate: 'We went to the cemetery.'
questions.a: Fuimos al cementerio.
